The chain rule already hands you the exact formula for the gradient of your loss with respect to every single parameter. So here is the paradox: why does writing that formula down naively, and just evaluating it, blow up to exponential time? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_3:diamond_graph>> <<SECTION:The diamond graph|id=sec-1>> Let me build the smallest graph that exposes the problem. Here is an <<FOCUS:node-x>> input node x at the bottom. From x <<FOCUS:node-y>> we compute y, and then <<FOCUS:node-z>> from y we compute z, but x also feeds forward again so that <<FOCUS:node-w>> the output w depends on both y and z. Watch the <<FOCUS:edge-x-y+edge-x-z>> two paths leave x and <<FOCUS:node-w>> re-converge at the top. Now I want the <<FOCUS:node-w+node-x>> gradient of the output w with respect to x. The chain rule says: <<FOCUS:chain-rule>> sum over every path from x to w, multiplying derivatives along each path. There are <<FOCUS:edge-y-w+edge-z-w>> two paths, so two terms. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The gradient of the output with respect to x is the sum over both paths from x to w, multiplying the derivatives along each path. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}|id=eq-chain>> Here it is written out. Each term is a product of derivatives along one route from x up to w. Now here is the trap. Suppose z is itself a function of y. Then the <<FOCUS:edge-y-w-label>> derivative of w with respect to y is not atomic; it must in turn account for the path through z. So the piece dw/dy <<FOCUS:edge-z-w-label>> secretly contains dw/dz inside it. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> If you expand everything symbolically and then evaluate, that inner subexpression dw/dz gets written out, and computed, in two separate places. One diamond duplicates it once. Stack diamonds on diamonds, layer after layer, and ask: how many times does the deepest subexpression get recomputed? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> It doubles at every layer. With n stacked diamonds you recompute the shared piece on the order of two-to-the-n times. That is the exponential blow-up: the formula is short, but the naive evaluation is astronomically wasteful. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:The fix: compute once, store, reuse|id=sec-2>> The cure is the move every smart student already makes. Do the <<FOCUS:shared-subexpr>> shared sub-calculation once, write the answer in the margin, and copy it wherever it is needed instead of redoing the arithmetic. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Chain rule = WHAT to compute. Backprop = compute each subexpression ONCE, store, reuse.|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That is exactly what back-propagation does. It computes the gradient at each node exactly once, stores it, and feeds it to the parents below. The chain rule tells you what to compute; back-propagation is the discipline of <<FOCUS:shared-subexpr>> never recomputing a shared subexpression. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> <<WRITE_TEXT:store -> O(graph) time, more memory; recompute -> less memory, more time|id=text-tradeoff>>Notice this is a genuine trade-off, not a free lunch. Storing intermediate gradients costs memory but makes the runtime linear in the size of the graph. Recomputing saves memory but pays in time, and for tangled graphs that time is the exponential cost we just saw. So the algorithm proceeds backward through the graph in a careful order: visit the output, then each node once, accumulating the gradient flowing into it before passing it down. Same answer the chain rule promised, computed in a single sweep instead of an exponential explosion.

The chain rule is one line of calculus you've known for years. So why does running it backwards through a network decide whether you train a model in an hour or in a century? <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_4:chain_graph>> Let's strip the network down to its bones: <<FOCUS:node-w+edge-wx+node-x+edge-xy+node-y+edge-yz+node-z>> a single chain, where we apply the very same function f at every step. We start with an <<FOCUS:node-w>> input w. Then <<FOCUS:node-x>> x is f of w, <<FOCUS:node-y>> y is f of x, and finally <<FOCUS:node-z>> z is f of y. <<WRITE_TEXT:x=f(w), y=f(x), z=f(y)|id=text-chain>> Now we ask the gradient question: <<FOCUS:node-w+node-z>> if I nudge w, how much does the output z move? <<SECTION:Expanding the chain rule|id=sec-chain>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The chain rule answers cleanly: multiply the local derivatives along the path, partial z over partial y, times partial y over partial x, times partial x over partial w. Multiply the local derivatives <<FOCUS:edge-yz+edge-xy+edge-wx>> along the path: partial z over partial y, times partial y over partial x, times partial x over partial w. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial z}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\,\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\,\frac{\partial x}{\partial w}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's the moment to watch. Each of those local derivatives is f prime evaluated at the node before it, so <<FOCUS:expansion>> written out fully, the gradient becomes f prime of f of f of w, times f prime of f of w, times f prime of w. <<UNFOCUS>> Each local derivative is f prime evaluated at the node before it, so the whole thing becomes f prime of f of f of w, times f prime of f of w, times f prime of w. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial z}{\partial w} = f'(f(f(w)))\,f'(f(w))\,f'(w)|id=eq-2|boxed>> Stare at that expression and you'll see the <<FOCUS:expansion>> same subexpression, f of w, appearing again and again, nested deeper each time. <<UNFOCUS>> So you face a genuine fork in the road. You can recompute f of w fresh every single time the chain rule asks for it, which costs no memory but explodes the work, or you can compute it once, <<FOCUS:node-x>> store it as the value x, and reuse it everywhere downstream. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Back-propagation <<FOCUS:backward-flow>> takes the second road. <<WRITE_KEY:Backprop = chain rule + store each repeated subexpression once|id=key-backprop>> <<UNFOCUS>> It is exactly the chain rule, plus the single decision to compute every repeated subexpression once and store it. That one choice trades a little memory for an enormous cut in runtime. <<PAUSE:short>> And this is precisely why the forward pass matters beyond just producing a prediction. <<SECTION:Forward caches, backward reuses|id=sec-mlp>> As we push the input through each layer, multiplying by weights, adding biases, applying activations, we are quietly caching every intermediate activation. <<PAUSE:short>> Then the backward pass <<FOCUS:backward-flow>> sweeps right to left through the same graph, and at every node it reuses the exact value the forward pass already stored, multiplying it by the local derivative to assemble each weight and bias gradient in a single sweep. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. Let w be the single input to the graph, and we use the same function f at every step of a chain. So x equals f of w, then y equals f of x, and z equals f of y. Our goal is to compute the derivative of z with respect to w. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: x = f(w), y = f(x), z = f(y) — find dz/dw|id=ex-q-1>> We start by applying the chain rule. That gives us a product: the derivative of z with respect to y, times the derivative of y with respect to x, times the derivative of x with respect to w. <<WRITE_STEP:dz/dw = (dz/dy)(dy/dx)(dx/dw)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we rewrite each factor using f. This equals f prime of y, times f prime of x, times f prime of w. <<WRITE_STEP:= f'(y) · f'(x) · f'(w)|id=ex-step-1-2>> If we expand it fully by substituting x equals f of w and y equals f of f of w, watch what happens: <<FOCUS:expansion>> f of w appears multiple times in the expression. <<WRITE_STEP:= f'(f(f(w))) · f'(f(w)) · f'(w)|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's the payoff. Back-propagation computes the value of f of w only once and <<FOCUS:node-x>> stores it in the variable x, then reuses it. <<UNFOCUS>> The alternative approach recomputes f of w each time it is needed, which wastes work. <<PAUSE:short>> So the answer is the same product either way, but back-propagation gets it more efficiently. <<WRITE_ANSWER:dz/dw = f'(f(f(w))) · f'(f(w)) · f'(w), with f(w) computed once and stored|id=ex-ans-1>> In a fully-connected MLP this is the whole story repeated layer by layer: one forward pass fills the cache, one backward pass drains it into gradients, and nothing is ever computed twice. <<PAUSE:short>> This toy chain uses one function and one input on purpose. Real frameworks generalize the same idea to any computational graph and process a whole minibatch at once, but the engine underneath is exactly what you just saw: store once, reuse everywhere.

What if back-propagation never touched a single number, and instead handed you back a brand-new graph that already knows how to compute every gradient? <<SECTION:Symbols versus numbers|id=sec-1>> Think about a formula like velocity equals u plus a times t. The letters are symbols; they stand for values without committing to any actual number yet. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_5:s2s_graph>> A computational graph is exactly the same kind of object: it's the recipe for a calculation, drawn as nodes and edges, before you plug in any ingredients. You hand it the graph plus actual inputs, and it crunches through and returns numbers, the gradient at exactly those values. Torch and Caffe work this way. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Symbol-to-symbol: back-prop adds new graph nodes that symbolically describe the derivative|id=key-1>> But there's a cleverer style. Symbol-to-symbol differentiation never looks at a number. Instead it takes your graph and <<FOCUS:deriv-node-dzdy+deriv-node-dydx+deriv-node-dxdw>> appends new nodes that are themselves a symbolic description of the derivative. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Watch what back-propagation actually builds. It walks the chain and, for each link, creates a node holding the local derivative: <<FOCUS:deriv-node-dzdy>> f prime of y, <<FOCUS:deriv-node-dydx>> then f prime of x, <<FOCUS:deriv-node-dxdw>> then f prime of w. Then it wires those local pieces together with multiply nodes, chaining d z d y times d y d x <<FOCUS:mult-node-dzdx>> into d z d x, and multiplying once more by d x d w <<FOCUS:mult-node-dzdw>> to get d z d w. That's the chain rule, <<FOCUS:deriv-edges>> drawn as graph. <<UNFOCUS>> The chain rule, drawn as graph, says the derivative of z with respect to w is the product of the local derivatives at each link in the chain. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{dz}{dw} = f'(y)\,f'(x)\,f'(w)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{dz}{dw} = f'(y)\,f'(x)\,f'(w)|id=eq-1>> And notice: not one number was needed to build any of this. The result is just <<FOCUS:forward-edges+deriv-edges>> a bigger graph that computes both the original expression and its derivative. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Why this is powerful|id=sec-3>> <<UNFOCUS>> The first payoff is uniformity: the derivative is written in the very same language as the original. A generic evaluation engine can later plug in any numbers you like; nothing special required. Here's the truly beautiful part: if the derivative is just another computational graph, what stops you from running back-propagation on it again? <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. When we actually use or train a neural network, the symbols alone aren't enough — we have to assign specific values to them. In particular, we replace a symbolic input to the network, x, with a specific numeric value. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Replace symbolic input x with a concrete numeric vector|id=ex-q-1>> So we start by taking x, which up to now has just been a symbol, and we swap it for an actual vector of numbers. Here that vector is one point one, two, three point seven six five, and negative one point eight. <<WRITE_STEP:x is symbolic — assign a concrete vector|id=ex-step-1-1>> And the answer is: the symbolic input x now becomes the numeric vector one point one, two, three point seven six five, negative one point eight, which is exactly what flows through the network when we run it. <<WRITE_ANSWER:x = [1.1, 2, 3.765, -1.8]|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We begin with a graph that represents <<FOCUS:node-w+node-x+node-y+node-z>> z equals f of f of f of w. <<UNFOCUS>> So it's the same function f composed with itself three times, applied to w. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Start from a graph for z = f(f(f(w))); build a graph for dz/dw|id=ex-q-1>> Now we run the back-propagation algorithm, but here's the twist: instead of asking it for a number, we instruct it to construct the graph for the expression corresponding to the derivative of z with respect to w. The key point is that no specific numeric values are accessed during this construction. <<WRITE_STEP:Run back-prop in symbol-to-symbol mode: emit graph nodes for dz/dw|id=ex-step-1-1>> And the result is exactly what we wanted: a <<FOCUS:mult-node-dzdw>> brand-new computational graph that gives a symbolic description of the derivative of z with respect to w. Back-propagation has simply <<FOCUS:deriv-node-dzdy+deriv-node-dydx+deriv-node-dxdw>> added new nodes that describe how to compute the derivative, rather than computing the derivative itself. <<WRITE_ANSWER:A graph that symbolically describes dz/dw, with no numbers ever evaluated|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Derivatives are graphs, so differentiate them again for higher-order derivatives|id=key-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> Nothing stops you. You feed the derivative graph back into the same machinery and get the derivative of the derivative, and so on, for arbitrarily high-order derivatives. The machinery composes with itself. <<PAUSE:short>> That self-composing flexibility, derivatives that are themselves differentiable graphs, is exactly why symbol-to-symbol systems like Theano and TensorFlow became the backbone of deep learning. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_6>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_6:comp_graph_backprop>> A deep network can route the same intermediate quantity to the loss through thousands of different paths — so if you differentiated naively, you would recompute that quantity an exponential number of times. Yet back-propagation finds every gradient in roughly the time of one forward pass. <<PAUSE:short>> Forget neural networks for a moment. Picture any computation as a graph: each node holds a number computed by applying some operation to the numbers flowing in from its parents, and at the very top sits a <<FOCUS:node-loss>> single scalar we care about — the loss. <<SECTION:The shared subexpression|id=sec-1>> Now look at <<FOCUS:node-shared>> this interior node. Notice <<FOCUS:node-child-a+node-child-b>> it has two children — its value feeds upward <<FOCUS:edge-shared-a+edge-shared-b>> along two different paths to the loss. <<WRITE_TEXT:want df_loss / d every input|id=text-1>> What we want is how the final loss changes when we <<FOCUS:node-param>> nudge each input node — in practice, each parameter of the model. Here is the honest question: if <<FOCUS:node-shared>> that shared node influences the loss <<FOCUS:node-child-a+node-child-b>> through both of these children, how do we account for both paths without walking the whole tree of paths separately? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The trick is to run a second graph in exactly the reverse order. We start at the top, where the gradient of the loss <<FOCUS:grad-arrow-loss>> with respect to itself is simply one, and then we work our way down. <<SECTION:Gradient flows backward|id=sec-2>> To get the <<FOCUS:grad-arrow-shared>> gradient at our shared node, we collect contributions from each of its children. <<FOCUS:node-child-a>> From this child we take the gradient already computed there and multiply by the <<FOCUS:edge-shared-a>> local derivative of that child with respect to the shared node. <<PAUSE:short>> We do the same <<FOCUS:node-child-b+edge-shared-b>> along the second child, and then we add the two contributions together. That sum is the <<FOCUS:grad-arrow-shared>> gradient at the shared node — both paths handled, no tree walked. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:grad[node] = sum over children of grad[child] times local derivative|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That summing rule is just the chain rule applied across all children of a node, and it is the entire engine of back-propagation. <<PAUSE:short>> The gradient of the loss with respect to a node equals the sum, over every child of that node, of the loss-gradient already known at the child times the local derivative of the child with respect to the node. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial u^{(n)}}{\partial u^{(j)}} = \sum_{i\,:\,j \in Pa(u^{(i)})} \frac{\partial u^{(n)}}{\partial u^{(i)}}\,\frac{\partial u^{(i)}}{\partial u^{(j)}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> We store every gradient in a table as we compute it, so when a node lower down needs the gradient of its child, it is already sitting there — never recomputed. In practice we read each child's gradient straight out of a stored table and accumulate it into the entry for the current node, so nothing is computed twice. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{grad\_table}[u^{(j)}] \leftarrow \sum_{i\,:\,j \in Pa(u^{(i)})} \text{grad\_table}[u^{(i)}]\,\frac{\partial u^{(i)}}{\partial u^{(j)}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<SECTION:Why it is cheap|id=sec-3>> Now count the work. <<FOCUS:edge-shared-a+edge-shared-b+edge-param-shared+edge-a-loss+edge-b-loss>> Each edge of the graph is touched exactly once: one local partial derivative, one multiplication, one addition. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the total cost scales with the number of edges — the same order as the forward pass. That is how back-propagation defeats the exponential explosion: it remembers shared subexpressions instead of recomputing them, trading memory for speed. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_7>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_7:forward_prop_chain>> Every prediction a deep network ever makes is just one input, passed hand to hand down a chain of layers, like a baton in a relay race, transformed at every exchange. Before the race even starts, the network needs four things: how deep it is, the depth l, a weight matrix and a bias vector for every layer, and the input x with the target y we are aiming for. <<SECTION:Forward Propagation|id=sec-fwd>> Here is the first, almost silly move: the <<FOCUS:input-node>> activation of layer zero is just the input itself. <<UNFOCUS>> The input is the very first runner holding the baton. The activation of layer zero is defined to be the input itself. <<WRITE_EQUATION:h^{(0)} = x|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now we hand off. The signal <<TRACE:edge-input-to-1>> flows along this edge, where it gets multiplied by the weight matrix and shifted by the bias. <<WRITE_STEP:a-one equals b-one plus W-one times h-zero|id=step-preact>> That mixing <<FOCUS:layer-1-preact>> gives us the pre-activation: take the bias for the layer, and add the weight matrix times the activation coming in. <<UNFOCUS>> It is a pure affine map, a linear combine plus a nudge. <<PAUSE:short>> The pre-activation of layer k is the bias plus the weight matrix times the previous layer's activation. <<WRITE_EQUATION:a^{(k)} = b^{(k)} + W^{(k)} h^{(k-1)}|id=eq-2|boxed>> If we stopped there, stacking layers would collapse into one big linear map. So we bend the pre-activation through a nonlinear activation function f, and <<FOCUS:layer-1-act>> that bent output is the activation h-one. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The activation of layer k is the pre-activation passed through the nonlinear function f. <<WRITE_EQUATION:h^{(k)} = f\left(a^{(k)}\right)|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Each layer: affine map, then nonlinearity, then pass forward|id=key-recipe>> And here is the whole engine in one sentence: each layer computes a pre-activation by an affine map, bends it through a nonlinearity, and that output <<TRACE:edge-1-to-2>> becomes the next layer's input. <<PAUSE:short>> We just keep repeating the same two steps, layer after layer, the baton moving down the chain, <<TRACE:edge-2-to-L>> until we reach the final layer. The activation of that last layer is the finish line: <<FOCUS:layer-L-act>> it is our prediction, y-hat. <<UNFOCUS>> The prediction is simply the activation of the final layer. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\hat{y} = h^{(l)}|id=eq-4|boxed>> <<SECTION:Measuring the Result|id=sec-cost>> But how do we know if the prediction is any good, and what stops the weights from blowing up to fit every quirk in the data? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Cost equals loss plus lambda times regularizer|id=key-cost>> We answer both <<FOCUS:cost-node>> with the cost. Its first part is the loss, <<FOCUS:layer-L-act+cost-node>> comparing y-hat to the true y. <<UNFOCUS>> Its second part is a regularizer, scaled by lambda, that gently penalizes large parameters so the network learns instead of memorizes. <<PAUSE:short>> The total cost is the loss between prediction and target plus lambda times a regularizer on the parameters. <<WRITE_EQUATION:J = L(\hat{y}, y) + \lambda\,\Omega(\theta)|id=eq-5|boxed>> Add those two together and you have the full cost the network drives downward. One input, walked forward through every layer, <<FOCUS:cost-node>> ending in a single number measuring how wrong we were: that is one complete forward pass.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_8>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_8:backprop_graph_annotated>> The back-propagation you've learned is correct, complete, and elegant — and yet if you typed it up exactly as we drew it, no serious deep learning library would ship it. Why not? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Complications under the hood|id=sec-1>> The answer is that our clean algorithm answers the mathematical question — what is the gradient — but stays silent on four engineering questions that every real implementation must confront. Let me walk you through them on a graph. <<PAUSE:short>> First wrinkle. We defined an operation as a function returning a single tensor. But suppose you want <<FOCUS:multi-output-node>> both the maximum value in a tensor and the index where it lives. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Scanning that memory twice would be wasteful, so a good implementation does both in one pass and <<FOCUS:multi-out-value+multi-out-argmax>> returns two outputs from a single operation — which means the graph machinery must allow a node to emit more than one result tensor. <<WRITE_TEXT:op may emit several output tensors|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the very first generalization is structural: an operation is a map from input tensors to a tuple of output tensors, and every output carries its own gradient contribution backward. Second wrinkle: memory. <<FOCUS:fan-in-node>> Look at this node — during the backward pass, gradient contributions arrive <<FOCUS:gradient-edge-a+gradient-edge-b+gradient-edge-c>> along three separate edges, and back-propagation must sum them. <<UNFOCUS>> The naive recipe computes all three, holds every one in memory, then adds them at the end. For a node with thousands of consumers, that peak memory is brutal. So how do we add them without ever storing them all at once? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Accumulate in place: one buffer, add each gradient as it arrives|id=key-1>> You keep <<FOCUS:accumulation-buffer>> one running buffer at the node and add each contribution into it the instant it's computed, then free that contribution — so peak memory is one tensor, not the whole crowd of them. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:in-place sum trades a second pass for O(1) extra tensors|id=step-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> This is the same idea as accumulating a running total instead of building a list and summing later — a constant-memory reduction folded directly into the backward traversal. <<SECTION:Types and undefined gradients|id=sec-2>> Third wrinkle: numbers themselves. The same edge might carry thirty-two-bit floats, sixty-four-bit floats, or integers, and each type needs its own carefully designed policy for casting, accumulation, and overflow during the backward pass. Fourth wrinkle: some operations have no well-defined gradient at all — think of an integer rounding step or <<FOCUS:nondiff-edge>> an argmax index. <<UNFOCUS>> The software must mark such edges and decide whether the gradient the user actually requested even exists. Notice the pattern: none of these are flaws in the theory. Multi-output ops, in-place accumulation, type policies, undefined-gradient tracking — each is the answer to a concrete systems constraint sitting on top of the math. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Clean theory complete; production layers engineering on top|id=key-2>> So the clean algorithm you learned is genuinely complete as an idea — it gives you the real intellectual machinery for computing derivatives. When you open a professional library, the extra complexity isn't confusion; it's engineering serving memory, compute, and numerical correctness, and now you know exactly why each piece is there. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_9>>
Back-propagation can compute the gradient of a billion-parameter network for roughly the price of one forward pass, and yet it is provably not the optimal way to compute a gradient. Both of those are true at once. The deep learning world grew up a little isolated, and invented its own habits for derivatives. But step outside, and there's an entire field called automatic differentiation whose only job is computing derivatives by algorithm. <<SECTION:Automatic Differentiation|id=sec-ad>> Back-propagation is just one member of that family. Specifically, back-propagation belongs to a class called reverse mode accumulation: we evaluate the chain rule starting from the output and work backwards toward the inputs. <<WRITE_TEXT:backprop = reverse-mode autodiff|id=text-rev>> Other methods just evaluate the same chain rule pieces in a different order. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_9:jacobian_chain>> Here's the cleanest way to see what order means. Think of the chain rule for a deep composition as a product of Jacobian matrices, <<FOCUS:matrix-A+matrix-B+matrix-C+matrix-D>> A times B times C times D. Suppose the <<FOCUS:matrix-D>> rightmost factor D is a tall column vector and the <<FOCUS:matrix-A>> leftmost A has many rows: that's a graph with many inputs and a single scalar output, exactly our loss. <<UNFOCUS>> The gradient of a deep composition is a product of Jacobian matrices, one per layer, chained from output back to input. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\nabla = A\,B\,C\,D \quad (\text{Jacobian chain})|id=eq-1|boxed>> So in which order should we multiply this chain to spend the least arithmetic? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Multiply from the right: <<FOCUS:right-bracket>> C times D first. Because D is a vector, every product stays a cheap <<FOCUS:rev-cost>> matrix-times-vector. Keep going <<TRACE:reverse-arrow>> right-to-left and you never build a single big matrix-matrix product. That is exactly <<FOCUS:reverse-label+right-bracket-label>> reverse mode, exactly back-propagation. <<PAUSE:short>> Multiply from the left instead, <<FOCUS:left-bracket>> A times B first, and you're grinding out full <<FOCUS:fwd-cost>> matrix-matrix products, vastly more expensive when there's only one output. <<WRITE_KEY:Cheapest order depends on the shapes: many inputs, one output favors reverse mode|id=key-shapes>> <<UNFOCUS>> The answer is identical; only the cost differs. <<PAUSE:short>> Flip the situation. If A is short, few outputs, but D is wide, many of them, then <<TRACE:forward-arrow>> multiplying left-to-right is the cheap direction. That is <<FOCUS:forward-label+left-bracket-label>> forward mode accumulation, and it also saves memory because you don't store the whole graph. <<UNFOCUS>> Now the guarantee that makes reverse mode beloved. When the graph has one output and each local partial derivative costs a constant, every edge's derivative is computed exactly once, with one multiply and one add. So the gradient costs the same order as the forward pass: order, number of edges. <<PAUSE:short>> With one scalar output and constant-cost local derivatives, reverse mode computes the whole gradient in time of the same order as the forward pass, growing with the number of edges in the graph. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{cost}(\nabla) = O(\#\text{edges})|id=eq-2|boxed>> But beloved is not optimal. Picture building a softmax from exponentials, a sum, and a division, then a cross-entropy loss on top. A human spots that the derivative of the loss with respect to a logit collapses to a gorgeous q minus p. A human notices the softmax-plus-cross-entropy gradient with respect to a logit simplifies to predicted probability minus true probability — a shortcut pure back-propagation cannot find on its own. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial J}{\partial z_i} = q_i - p_i|id=eq-3|boxed>> Back-propagation can't see that shortcut. It dutifully pushes gradients through every logarithm and exponential in the graph. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial J}{\partial z_i} = q_i - p_i|id=eq-qmp>> Libraries like Theano and TensorFlow bolt on pattern-matching heuristics to simplify, but plain back-prop won't. Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose we have variables p one through p n representing probabilities, and variables z one through z n representing unnormalized log probabilities. We define q i equals exp of z i divided by the sum over i of exp of z i — that's the softmax, built out of exponentiation, summation, and division operations. From these we construct a cross-entropy loss J equals negative sum over i of p i times log of q i. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the derivative of the softmax-plus-cross-entropy loss J with respect to z i.|id=ex-q-1>> A human mathematician looks at this whole expression and notices something beautiful. We start by writing down the loss and the softmax together. <<WRITE_EQUATION:J = -\sum_i p_i \log q_i, \quad q_i = \frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_i \exp(z_i)}|id=ex-eq-1>> When you differentiate J with respect to z i by hand, all the logarithms and exponentials cancel against each other algebraically, and the messy expression collapses. <<WRITE_STEP:Differentiate J w.r.t. z_i; logs and exps cancel|id=ex-step-1-1>> And the answer is wonderfully simple: the derivative of J with respect to z i equals q i minus p i. <<WRITE_ANSWER:dJ/dz_i = q_i - p_i|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's the catch. Back-propagation cannot spot this shortcut. Instead it will explicitly propagate gradients through every single logarithm and exponentiation operation in the original graph. Some software libraries, such as Theano, can perform some kinds of algebraic substitution to improve over the graph that pure back-propagation proposes. And finding the truly cheapest evaluation order in general? That's N P complete, because it can require simplifying the algebra into its least expensive form. So nobody has a fast, general optimal method. One last cultural difference: outside machine learning, people differentiate raw Python or C code directly. Deep learning libraries instead use explicit graph structures, which forces a hand-written backward rule for every operation. That limits you to defined ops, but it lets experts hand-craft clever rules for speed and numerical stability. So back-propagation isn't the only way, nor the optimal way, but it is wonderfully practical and serves us extremely well.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_10>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_10:backprop_graph>> Here's a strange idea: instead of building a graph that spits out numbers, what if we built a graph that spits out its own derivatives — and then never had to decide when to run anything? <<SECTION:Symbol-to-symbol|id=sec-1>> The trick is what each node contains. In the ordinary view, a node holds a number. In the symbol-to-symbol view, a node holds another operation — so the derivatives themselves live inside the graph as differentiable nodes you can keep evaluating. <<PAUSE:short>> And because the derivative graph is just more graph, you don't decide ahead of time when each operation fires. A generic engine evaluates any node the instant its parents are ready. <<SECTION:The backward pass|id=sec-2>> Now the heart of it. Suppose <<FOCUS:node-z>> z is our final scalar and we want to know how z responds to <<FOCUS:node-x>> some earlier variable x. <<UNFOCUS>> Where do we even start? <<PAUSE:long>> We start the backward pass with the simplest fact there is: the <<FOCUS:grad-seed>> gradient of z with respect to itself is one, because anything changes itself one-for-one. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial z}{\partial z} = 1|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Seed the backward pass with dz/dz = 1|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> We start at z itself, and we seed the gradient with the most obvious fact in mathematics: the gradient of z with respect to z is one. Anything changes itself one-for-one. <<PAUSE:short>> Then we <<TRACE:back-z-y1>> walk backwards along an edge. At each operation, we multiply our current gradient by <<FOCUS:jac-z-y1>> that operation's Jacobian — the matrix that says how the operation turned its inputs into its outputs. We keep multiplying Jacobians, edge after edge, traveling backwards through the graph, until <<FOCUS:node-x>> we finally arrive at x. <<UNFOCUS>> That product of Jacobians is the gradient. To get the gradient at any node, take each operation that consumed it, push the gradient backward through that operation's Jacobian, and add up the contributions from every path. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} z = \sum_{i} \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}_i}{\partial \mathbf{x}} \right)^{\top} \nabla_{\mathbf{y}_i} z|id=eq-2|boxed>> But look — <<FOCUS:edge-x-y1+edge-x-y2>> x feeds two operations, not one. So going backward, <<FOCUS:back-y1-x+back-y2-x>> two gradients arrive at x along two different paths. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:At a shared node, SUM the gradients from every path|id=step-1>> When a node is reached by more than one backward path, you simply <<FOCUS:merge-sum>> add the arriving gradients. <<UNFOCUS>> That sum is not a detail — it's the chain rule honestly accounting for every way x influenced z. <<PAUSE:short>> So the whole rule, written out, is a sum over consumers: for each operation that used x, transpose its Jacobian, apply it to that operation's gradient, and add them all up. <<PAUSE:short>> To make this general in code, each node holds a tensor — scalar, vector, matrix, whatever — and knows three things: which operation created it, who its parents are, and who its consumers are. And every operation carries one back-propagation rule that computes exactly that Jacobian-vector product. Those tiny pieces — <<FOCUS:grad-seed>> seed at one, <<FOCUS:jac-z-y1+jac-y1-x>> multiply by Jacobians, <<FOCUS:merge-sum>> sum at the merges — assemble into the entire algorithm.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_6>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_6:depth_as_composition>> Take two networks with the exact same number of parameters. Make <<FOCUS:shallow-layer>> one shallow and wide, <<FOCUS:deep-stage-1+deep-stage-2+deep-stage-3>> the other deep and narrow — and the deep one keeps winning. <<UNFOCUS>> Why should rearranging the same parameters into more layers matter at all? <<PAUSE:long>> This isn't a one-off. Across many tasks, holding the parameter count roughly fixed, depth tended to beat width. The empirical result was clear long before the explanation was. The honest answer comes from one word: a prior. <<SECTION:Depth as a prior|id=sec-1>> A prior is an assumption you bake into the model before it sees a single data point — a belief about what good solutions ought to look like. Picture the <<FOCUS:function-space>> whole space of functions the model could represent. A prior is just a statement that <<FOCUS:favored-region>> some corner of this space is far more plausible than the rest. <<UNFOCUS>> So what corner does depth bet on? Watch the deep path. <<FOCUS:input-node>> The input enters, the <<FOCUS:deep-stage-1>> first stage extracts low-level features, the next stage combines those <<FOCUS:deep-stage-2>> into mid-level features, the next <<FOCUS:deep-stage-3>> builds higher-level ones still. <<UNFOCUS>> A deep network just says the answer is built by passing the input through one stage, then feeding that into the next, again and again — a chain of composed functions. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f(x) = f^{(L)} \circ f^{(L-1)} \circ \cdots \circ f^{(1)}(x)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:f(x) = f^{(L)} \circ \cdots \circ f^{(1)}(x)|id=eq-1>> Each layer is a function, and the network is those functions composed in a chain — the output of one becomes the input of the next. The crucial move is right here. Notice how a later stage doesn't start from scratch — <<FOCUS:reuse-arrow>> it reuses and recombines whatever the stage below it discovered. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> That is the prior. <<WRITE_KEY:Depth = the prior that f is a composition of reused simpler steps|id=key-1>> Choosing depth quietly tells the model: I believe the function we want factors into many simple steps, each one building on the features below it. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's the question that makes this matter: why would such an oddly specific assumption ever help? Surely committing to compositional functions just throws away flexibility. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Because the problems we actually care about are built that way. Edges compose into shapes, shapes into objects; phonemes into words, words into meaning. The <<FOCUS:favored-region>> shaded region the deep prior prefers is exactly where the real-world target functions tend to live. <<UNFOCUS>> So depth isn't a lucky trick that happened to work. The structure of deep networks lines up with the structure of the problems, and that alignment is what makes the prior useful. <<PAUSE:short>> Carry this framing forward. <<WRITE_TEXT:depth, weight sharing, specialized layers = priors|id=text-1>> Almost every architectural decision you'll meet later — depth, weight sharing, convolution, attention — is the same move: a built-in belief that nudges the model toward the solutions we expect to be correct. <<PAUSE:short>>

lecture_plan.chapter_arc: We begin with a single problem a linear model cannot solve — XOR — and use it to motivate hidden layers and nonlinearity, then build up the full machinery of training: cost functions grounded in maximum likelihood, the right output and hidden units to pair with them, and why depth helps. The chapter then turns to the engine that makes all of this trainable at scale, back-propagation, developing it from the chain rule through computational graphs to the fully general algorithm. The student leaves understanding not just what a deep network is, but how gradients flow through one and why that flow is so general.
lecture_plan.opening_hook: A single straight line cannot separate the four points of the XOR function — so how does adding one hidden layer suddenly make the impossible trivial? That tiny puzzle holds the whole secret of deep feedforward networks.

coverage_checklist.description: Show concretely why a linear model fails on XOR and how a single nonlinear hidden layer solves it, writing out the complete network
Establish that training a deep network is gradient-based and not fundamentally different from training linear/SVM models, except for nonconvexity
Ground cost functions in maximum likelihood / cross-entropy and explain the unboundedness caveat
Pair output units (sigmoid, softmax, Gaussian with precision) with the correct cost and explain why
Compare ReLU, sigmoid/tanh, and other hidden units, and explain saturation and gradient flow
State the universal approximation theorem and explain empirically why depth helps over width
Develop back-propagation from the chain rule through computational graphs to the fully general recursive algorithm
Explain why back-propagation is so general — each operation handles its own local gradient — and connect it to automatic differentiation

lecture_plan.closing_summary: We started with four points that no straight line could separate, and we end knowing exactly how a network conquers them: a hidden layer bends the space with a nonlinearity, an output unit and a maximum-likelihood cost turn that representation into predictions, and gradient-based learning tunes every weight. The deep insight is that the whole machine — every output type, every activation function, every layer — is trained by one general idea: back-propagation, which is nothing more than the chain rule applied systematically over a computational graph, where each operation only needs to know its own local derivative. That locality is what makes it so general, and depth is what makes these networks so powerful. The XOR puzzle was the smallest possible window into all of it.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_3:xor_feature_transform>> Four points in a plane. No straight line on Earth can split the XOR answers apart — and yet I'm going to show you a network that solves it using nothing but straight lines with a single bend. Here are <<FOCUS:input-point-00+input-point-01+input-point-10+input-point-11>> the four inputs. The point at the origin and the point at the far corner <<FOCUS:input-point-00+input-point-11>> both want the answer zero; the two off-diagonal points <<FOCUS:input-point-01+input-point-10>> both want the answer one. <<WRITE_TEXT:No single line separates the filled dots from the open circles|id=text-1>> Try to <<FOCUS:input-point-01+input-point-10+input-point-00+input-point-11>> draw one straight line with the filled dots on one side and the open circles on the other. <<UNFOCUS>> You can't — that is exactly why a plain linear model dies on XOR. So we insert one hidden layer in between. In words: take the input, multiply by a first weight matrix, add a bias, then squash the result through a function that keeps positives but zeros out negatives — and finally take a weighted sum to get the output. Written out in plain language: take the input, apply the first weights and bias, bend it with the rectified linear unit, then take a final weighted sum plus a last bias. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{W},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{w},b)=\mathbf{w}^\top \max\{0,\;\mathbf{W}^\top\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{c}\}+b|id=eq-1|boxed>> That squashing function is the rectified linear unit, the ReLU. It keeps any positive number exactly as it is and turns every negative number into zero. Notice it is almost a straight line — it has just one bend, right at zero. The rectified linear unit keeps any positive number unchanged and turns every negative number into zero — almost a straight line, but with one bend at the origin. <<WRITE_EQUATION:g(z)=\max\{0,\,z\}|id=eq-2|boxed>> Now watch what the first layer does before the bend. With the right weights and bias, all four points get squeezed <<TRACE:collapsed-line>> onto a single straight line in the hidden space, sliding along it with slope one. <<UNFOCUS>> And here's the trap: along that line the output has to start at zero, rise to one, then fall back to zero. No straight line can go up and then back down — so a linear model is still stuck. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Then the ReLU's single bend fires. Every negative coordinate gets clamped to zero, and that clamp <<FOCUS:folded-point-cluster>> physically folds the line. The two class-one points pile onto one spot while the class-zero points pull apart — they no longer lie on a single line. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:One ReLU bend folds the points off their line so a linear layer can separate them|id=key-1>> And now <<TRACE:separating-line>> a single straight cut does the job. <<UNFOCUS>> The bend bought us exactly the nonlinearity we needed; the final weighted sum just reads off which side each point landed on. <<PAUSE:short>> The book's lovely point: just as a Turing machine builds everything from cells storing zero or one, we can build a universal function approximator out of these humble rectified linear pieces. But here we cheated — we simply wrote down the perfect weights by hand. With billions of parameters you cannot guess. So what changes when you have to actually learn them? <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter where we specify a complete solution to the XOR problem. Let W be the two-by-two matrix with all entries equal to one. Let c be the vector with entries zero and negative one. Let w be the vector with entries one and negative two, and let b equal zero. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Solve XOR with W (all ones), c = (0, -1), w = (1, -2), b = 0|id=ex-q-1>> We start by writing down the input matrix X, which contains all four points in the binary input space, one example per row: the rows are zero-zero, zero-one, one-zero, and one-one. The first step is to multiply this input matrix by the first layer's weight matrix W, giving X times W with rows zero-zero, one-one, one-one, and two-two. <<WRITE_STEP:X has rows (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:XW has rows (0,0), (1,1), (1,1), (2,2)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Next, we add the bias vector c, which has entries zero and negative one, to obtain rows zero-negative-one, one-zero, one-zero, and two-one. Notice that in this space all of the examples <<TRACE:collapsed-line>> lie along a line with slope one. <<UNFOCUS>> As we move along that line the output needs to start at zero, rise to one, then drop back to zero, and a linear model simply cannot do that. <<WRITE_STEP:XW + c has rows (0,-1), (1,0), (1,0), (2,1)|id=ex-step-1-3>> To finish computing the hidden values, we apply the rectified linear transformation, taking the max of zero and each value, which gives rows zero-zero, one-zero, one-zero, and two-one. This changes the relationship between the examples: they <<FOCUS:folded-point-cluster>> no longer lie on a single line, and now a linear model can solve the problem. <<WRITE_STEP:ReLU = max(0, value): rows (0,0), (1,0), (1,0), (2,1)|id=ex-step-1-4>> <<UNFOCUS>> We finish by multiplying by the output weight vector w, with entries one and negative two, giving outputs zero, one, one, zero. These match the four target XOR outputs zero, one, one, zero exactly, so the network has obtained the correct answer for every example in the batch. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Outputs (0, 1, 1, 0) = XOR targets, all correct|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:nonlinearity makes the loss surface non-convex|id=text-2>> This is the answer, and it's the whole reason deep learning feels different. The very nonlinearity that solved XOR makes the loss surface bumpy — non-convex — so unlike linear regression or an SVM there's no global-convergence guarantee. <<PAUSE:short>> So instead of solving, we descend. The point at the origin and the point at the far corner both want the answer zero; the two off-diagonal points both want the answer one. <<POINT:input-point-01>> <<POINT:input-point-01>> <<FOCUS:input-point-11>> <<WRITE_TEXT:No single line separates the filled dots from the open circles|id=text-1>>Try to draw one straight line with the filled dots on one side and the open circles on the other. segments.narration_chapter: Stack a linear layer on top of another linear layer, train forever with all the gradient descent you want, and you have learned absolutely nothing a single linear layer couldn't already do. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_2:feedforward_chain>> Here is <<FOCUS:input-node-x+hidden-node-h+output-node-y>> the network we are trying to build. Your <<FOCUS:input-node-x+edge-W>> input x runs through a first function to produce a <<FOCUS:hidden-node-h>> layer of hidden units h, and then h runs through a <<FOCUS:edge-w+output-node-y>> second function to give your prediction y. <<SECTION:The composition|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> The second function is the easy part. It is just a linear regression model, but applied to h instead of to x. So the whole model is two functions chained together, and the only real design freedom we have is <<FOCUS:edge-W>> this first function. <<UNFOCUS>> The big question is: what should it compute? <<PAUSE:long>> Linear models have served us beautifully so far, so the tempting answer is to make the first function linear too. Let us follow that temptation and see exactly where it breaks. <<WRITE_STEP:Let h = W x and y = h w|id=step-1>> Suppose the first function is just h equals W times x, and the second is y equals h times w. Substitute the first into the second and watch what happens. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:y = (W x) w = x (W w)|id=step-2>> You get y equals x times the product of W and w. Those two weight matrices <<FOCUS:edge-W+edge-w>> fold into one single matrix, so the whole network collapses back into a single linear map. <<UNFOCUS>> This is the payoff: stacking linear on top of linear is still linear, and depth bought you nothing. <<PAUSE:short>> When both layers are linear, the two weight matrices multiply into one single matrix, and the whole network is just the input times that combined matrix. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}\,\mathbf{w}', \quad \mathbf{w}' = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{w}|id=eq-1|boxed>> That collapse is not a quirk of this example. Any composition of linear maps is itself a linear map, which is exactly why we cannot get away with a linear hidden layer. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:The fix: affine then nonlinear|id=sec-2>> So we must describe our features with a nonlinear function. Because h is now a whole vector of hidden units, not a single number, we need a whole vector of biases. Stacking a linear function on top of another linear function gives you just one linear function, so linear hidden layers add no power. <<WRITE_ANSWER:f(x) = x w-prime with w-prime = W w — still a single linear function|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. segments.narration_chapter: Here is something strange: you almost never have to invent a loss function. The moment you decide what your network is allowed to predict, the loss is already chosen for you. Start with the reassuring part. The cost functions we use for deep networks are essentially the same ones we use for linear models. Nothing exotic — you are reusing familiar ideas, just stacked on top of a more flexible function inside. <<SECTION:Maximum Likelihood|id=sec-1>> The key move is that in most cases the network does not output a single number — it outputs an entire conditional distribution, p of y given x, parametrized by theta. Given an input, it tells you how probable every possible answer is. So what should we ask of that distribution? Just this: make the answers that actually appeared in the training data as probable as possible. That single demand is the principle of maximum likelihood. Maximizing a product of probabilities is awkward, so we take the logarithm and flip the sign. <<WRITE_TEXT:cost = average penalty for low probability of the true answer|id=text-1>> Maximizing likelihood becomes minimizing the negative log-likelihood — penalize the model every time it assigns low probability to a correct answer. Written as an expectation over the training data, the cost is the negative expected log-probability the model assigns to the true outputs. This quantity is exactly the cross-entropy between the data distribution and the model. The cost is the negative expected log-probability the model assigns to the true outputs — that is the cross-entropy between the data and the model. <<WRITE_EQUATION:J(\theta) = -\mathbb{E}_{x,y\sim\hat{p}_{\text{data}}}\,\log p_{\text{model}}(y\mid x)|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now the beautiful consequence. Once you have committed to a form for p of y given x, there is nothing left to choose. The negative log of that distribution IS your cost function. <<PAUSE:long>> Let me make that concrete. Suppose your model predicts a Gaussian centered on its guess f of x — a bell curve whose mean is the network's output. What cost does maximum likelihood hand back? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Write down the log of a Gaussian and almost everything is a constant. <<WRITE_EQUATION:J(\theta) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\,\lVert y - f(x;\theta)\rVert^2 + \text{const}|id=eq-mse>> What survives is one half the squared distance between the true value and the prediction — the mean squared error. You did not invent it; it fell out. <<PAUSE:short>> And this equivalence does not care how complicated f is. Linear model, hundred-layer network — if it predicts the mean of a Gaussian, maximum likelihood gives you mean squared error. <<WRITE_KEY:Choose the distribution, and its negative log-likelihood IS the loss.|id=key-1>> Specifying the distribution automatically determines the cost. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_2_1:saturation_gradient_plot>> <<SECTION:Keeping the Gradient Alive|id=sec-2>> There is one more reason this framework is not just elegant but practical. For learning to work, the gradient must stay large and informative. Look at a typical output unit, <<TRACE:sigmoid-curve>> the sigmoid: out in the far negative region it flattens completely. <<FOCUS:saturated-region>> In that flat tail the slope is essentially zero. If our loss lived directly on this curve, the gradient would vanish and learning would simply stall — the model would get no signal to correct a confident, wrong prediction. <<PAUSE:long>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose our model's conditional distribution is a Gaussian, that is, p model of y given x equals the normal distribution N of y, with mean f of x semicolon theta, and covariance the identity matrix. So the mean of the Gaussian is exactly the network output f of x semicolon theta, and the covariance is the identity matrix. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: If p_model(y|x) = N(y; f(x;theta), I), what cost function do we recover from maximum likelihood?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by taking the negative log likelihood of this Gaussian. When you write out the log of a normal density, you get the squared difference between y and f of x semicolon theta, scaled by one half, plus a constant term that does not depend on theta. <<WRITE_STEP:-log p_model(y|x) = (1/2) ||y - f(x;theta)||^2 + const|id=ex-step-1-1>> That leading term is just the mean squared error, the squared difference between y and f of x semicolon theta, carrying the scaling factor of one half. The constant term comes from the variance of the Gaussian, which in this case we chose not to parametrize, so it does not depend on theta and we discard it. And the answer is that maximum likelihood here reduces to the mean squared error cost: J of theta equals one half, the expectation over x and y of the squared norm of y minus f of x semicolon theta, plus a constant, up to a scaling factor of one half and a term that does not depend on theta. <<WRITE_ANSWER:J(theta) = (1/2) E_{x,y ~ p_data} ||y - f(x;theta)||^2 + const  (mean squared error)|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here is the rescue. The sigmoid hides an exp of a negative argument, which is exactly what saturates. The log in negative log-likelihood <<FOCUS:nll-curve>> undoes that exp. <<PAUSE:short>> So instead of flattening, the cost <<FOCUS:nll-slope-marker>> keeps climbing with a steep, predictable slope right where the model is most wrong. The logarithm cancels the exponential and <<FOCUS:nll-curve+saturated-region>> the gradient stays healthy. <<UNFOCUS>> In practice you then add a regularization term, like weight decay, to keep the whole model well behaved. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: Here is something strange about the cross-entropy cost we train almost every classifier with: most of the time, it has no minimum. But a sigmoid can only creep toward one — it never gets there, so there is always a little more reward to chase. <<WRITE_TEXT:cross-entropy has no true minimum|id=text-1>> For real-valued outputs it is even sharper. Let the model learn how spread out its predictions are, and it can pile unbounded probability density right onto the training answers, sending the cross-entropy toward negative infinity. That is exactly why we will later need regularization. <<PAUSE:short>> Now step back. Often we do not want the whole distribution — we want one summary number, like the average value of y given x. If the network is powerful enough to represent essentially any function, then the cost stops being a function of a few parameters and becomes a functional: a rule that takes an entire function and returns one number. <<SECTION:Which statistic does the cost reward?|id=sec-1>> So learning is now choosing a function. Switch to mean absolute error and you get a different statistic entirely — the conditional median. The cost function literally chooses what the network learns. <<PAUSE:short>> This is why the cost and the output unit are tied together at the hip. Suppose we want that conditional mean for real-valued targets. And because a linear unit never saturates — its slope is constant everywhere — the gradient never dies, so optimization stays smooth. <<SECTION:Binary outputs and the sigmoid|id=sec-2>> But now switch to a binary target. We model y with a Bernoulli distribution, so the network only needs one number: the probability that y equals one. Right when the model is most wrong, it learns nothing. For a binary target we squash the linear pre-activation through the logistic sigmoid so the output is always a valid probability with a gradient that never dies. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\hat{y} = \sigma(w^\top h + b)|id=eq-3|boxed>> The sigmoid solves exactly this. It also approaches zero and one, but <<TRACE:sigmoid-curve>> it never goes flat — it only asymptotes. <<UNFOCUS>> So even a badly wrong prediction sits on a curve with real slope. <<FOCUS:wrong-answer-point>> Look at this point: the true label is one, but the model outputs almost zero. On the clipped unit this <<FOCUS:dead-gradient-region>> lives on a dead shoulder. <<FOCUS:sigmoid-curve>> On the sigmoid, paired with cross-entropy, there is still a strong gradient pulling it back toward the right answer. <<UNFOCUS>> So the whole chain locks together: the cost functional picks the statistic, and the output unit keeps the gradient alive while it learns. Linear units give you the Gaussian mean, sigmoid units give you a Bernoulli probability — and cross-entropy, even without a minimum, beats squared error precisely because saturating units would otherwise strangle the gradient. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: The rectified linear unit has a sharp corner at zero where its derivative literally does not exist. So why is it the single most trusted building block in modern deep learning? But before we open up that unit, let's tie off a loose end. Everything we have built so far predicts a single number or a single category — yet sometimes we want a network to output something far richer, like a whole sentence, a sequence of characters strung together. The guiding idea does not change at all: we still write down a probability model for the output given the input, p of y given the parameters omega of x, and we push the network to make the real answers as likely as possible. <<SECTION:Rich structured outputs|id=sec-outputs>> That is still pure maximum likelihood. What changes is that the model for a structured y gets complicated fast — so we set those cases aside for later chapters. There is one beautiful picture worth holding onto, though: a network can output the parameters of a mixture of several Gaussian bells, letting every mean, every spread, and every mixing weight bend nonlinearly with the input. Now we turn to something special to feedforward networks: how to choose the hidden units, those little computing pieces in the middle layers. And here is an honest truth — this is an active research area with very few firm theoretical rules. So what is the practical method, if theory can't tell us which unit is best in advance? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> It is trial and error, plain and simple. You intuit that some unit might work, you train the network with it, and you check its performance on a validation set. And the default you reach for first, almost always, is the rectified linear unit. <<SECTION:The anatomy of a hidden unit|id=sec-anatomy>> Here is the unifying view. Strip away the names, and almost every hidden unit does the same three things: it takes an input vector x, computes an affine transformation — multiply by a weight matrix W and add a bias b — and then applies a nonlinear function g element by element. <<PAUSE:short>> A hidden unit takes the input vector, multiplies it by a weight matrix and adds a bias to get z, then applies the nonlinearity g element by element to get the unit's output. <<WRITE_EQUATION:z = Wx + b, \quad h = g(z)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Hidden unit = affine transform then element-wise nonlinearity; only g changes|id=key-anatomy>> So the entire zoo of hidden units differs in essentially one place: the choice of that activation function g. Everything else is shared scaffolding. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_4:relu_corner>> Now back to our opening puzzle. <<TRACE:relu-curve>> Let's actually draw the most common g, the rectified linear unit: g of z equals the max of zero and z. <<WRITE_EQUATION:g(z) = \max\{0, z\}|id=eq-relu>> Watch what happens <<FOCUS:kink-point>> right here at the origin. To the left, <<FOCUS:left-slope-label>> the function is flat, so its slope — the left derivative — is exactly zero. To the right, <<FOCUS:right-slope-label>> it climbs at forty-five degrees, so the right derivative is exactly one. The two don't match, and that is precisely what makes the function <<FOCUS:kink-point>> non-differentiable at this corner. Just to the left of zero the slope is zero, and just to the right of zero the slope is one — <<FOCUS:left-slope-label+right-slope-label>> the left and right derivatives disagree, which is exactly why the function is not differentiable at the corner. <<WRITE_EQUATION:g'_-(0) = 0, \quad g'_+(0) = 1|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> You might think that single broken point kills gradient descent. Here is why it doesn't. <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. Take the rectified linear function, g of z, which outputs the maximum of zero and z. The book points out that this function is not differentiable at z equals zero. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Is g(z) = max(0, z) differentiable at z = 0?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's look at the two sides of that corner. Coming in from the left, where z is negative, <<FOCUS:left-slope-label>> the function is flat at zero, so the left derivative at zero is zero. Coming in from the right, where z is positive, the function <<FOCUS:right-slope-label>> rises like z itself, so the right derivative at zero is one. <<WRITE_STEP:Left derivative at z = 0 is 0|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Right derivative at z = 0 is 1|id=ex-step-1-2>> Because the left derivative, zero, doesn't match the right derivative, one, <<FOCUS:kink-point>> the slope jumps at the corner and the derivative is technically undefined there. <<UNFOCUS>> But this is harmless in practice: software implementations of neural network training usually just return one of the one-sided derivatives rather than reporting that the derivative is undefined or raising an error. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Not differentiable at z = 0 (left deriv 0, right deriv 1) — software returns one one-sided value|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Training never actually arrives at a clean local minimum, and it essentially never lands on z exactly equal to zero — a digital computer carries rounding error anyway, so the value was almost certainly some tiny nonzero number that got rounded. When the corner is hit, the software simply returns one of the two one-sided slopes and moves on. <<PAUSE:short>> So the corner is a mathematical curiosity, not a practical obstacle: we can safely disregard the non-differentiability of these activation functions. <<WRITE_TEXT:non-differentiable points: ignore them|id=text-ignore>> Remember the two takeaways — every hidden unit is an affine map followed by an element-wise g, and ReLU's broken derivative simply does not bite. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_3_1:relu_family_graph>> The activation function powering most of modern deep learning is barely a function at all — it's just a kinked straight line, and that brokenness is exactly why it works. <<FOCUS:relu-curve>> Here it is. <<SECTION:Rectified Linear Units|id=sec-relu>> For positive input, the unit <<FOCUS:active-slope-label>> passes the value straight through, slope one, no distortion. For negative input, <<FOCUS:dead-region>> it outputs flat zero. The rectified linear unit outputs <<FOCUS:kink-point>> the larger of zero and its input — pass positive values through, clamp everything negative to zero. <<WRITE_EQUATION:g(z) = \max\{0, z\}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> Look at the positive half. The output equals the input, so <<FOCUS:active-slope-label>> the slope is exactly one — and crucially, it stays one. <<WRITE_KEY:Active ReLU: first derivative = 1, second derivative = 0|id=key-grad>> <<UNFOCUS>> The second derivative is zero, meaning the gradient that flows back is large, constant, and never bent by curvature. <<PAUSE:short>> Why should you care that the second derivative is zero? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Because second-order effects are what corrupt the gradient direction. With a saturating sigmoid the slope changes as you move, so the descent direction lies to you. A ReLU's active region has no such curvature — the gradient direction is honest, and that is the single biggest reason these networks optimize so smoothly. <<PAUSE:short>> You almost always put a ReLU on top of an affine transformation — a weighted sum plus a bias. In practice you apply the rectifier on top of an affine transformation: a weighted sum of the inputs plus a bias. <<WRITE_EQUATION:h = g(W^\top x + b)|id=eq-2|boxed>> There's a clean initialization trick: set every bias to a small positive number, like zero point one. <<WRITE_TEXT:init bias to +0.1 so units start active|id=text-init>> That makes most units start active, so gradient can flow from the very first step. But here is the flaw. Across <<FOCUS:dead-region>> this whole negative half, the output is flat zero, so the gradient is zero. <<UNFOCUS>> A unit stuck here is dead — it gets no signal and can never recover. <<SECTION:Leaky, Parametric, and Absolute-Value Rectifiers|id=sec-leaky>> The fix is to give the negative side <<TRACE:leaky-branch>> a small slope alpha instead of zero, so a tiny gradient always leaks through. <<WRITE_EQUATION:g(z) = \max(0,z) + \alpha\,\min(0,z)|id=eq-leaky>> <<UNFOCUS>> Fix alpha at zero point zero one and you get a leaky ReLU; let alpha be learned and it's a parametric ReLU; set it to negative one and you get the absolute value, useful when a feature shouldn't care about light polarity. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_3_1:maxout_construction>> <<SECTION:Maxout Units|id=sec-maxout>> Maxout goes further still. Instead of fixing the shape, give the unit <<FOCUS:affine-line-1+affine-line-2+affine-line-3>> several affine lines and let it output the maximum at every point. <<FOCUS:affine-line-2>> Add a second line, <<FOCUS:affine-line-3>> a third, each with its own learned weights and bias. The price is k times the parameters, so it needs more regularization — but its redundancy resists catastrophic forgetting. <<TRACE:max-envelope>> A maxout unit splits its inputs into groups and outputs the maximum value within each group. <<WRITE_EQUATION:g(z)_i = \max_{j \in \mathbb{G}(i)} z_j|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:max-envelope>> Step back and the common thread is one idea: models are easier to optimize when their behavior stays close to linear. <<WRITE_KEY:Stay near-linear and gradients stay well-behaved|id=key-principle>>That's why rectifiers beat saturating units, and the same principle even reaches recurrent networks — the LSTM carries information through time by simple summation, the most linear operation there is. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:relu-curve>> So the kink is not a defect to apologize for — it is just enough nonlinearity to be expressive, sitting on top of behavior that stays gloriously, optimizably linear. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_3_2:sigmoid_tanh_curves>> Here is a curve that was the heart of nearly every neural network for two decades, and today we tell you: never put it in a hidden layer. <<SECTION:Squashing functions|id=sec-1>> This is <<FOCUS:sigmoid-curve>> the logistic sigmoid. <<UNFOCUS>> It takes any real number you throw at it and squashes it into the open interval between zero and one. Its cousin, <<FOCUS:tanh-curve>> the hyperbolic tangent, which we call tanh, does the same kind of squashing but into the interval between negative one and positive one. <<UNFOCUS>> You can write the hyperbolic tangent directly in terms of the sigmoid: it is two times sigmoid of two z, minus one, which means they are the same shape just stretched and shifted. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\tanh(z) = 2\sigma(2z) - 1|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:\tanh(z) = 2\sigma(2z) - 1|id=eq-rel>> And these two are not really different beasts. You can write tanh as two times sigmoid of two z, minus one. Same shape, just stretched and shifted. Now look at the tails. Out here on the right, the curve has <<FOCUS:saturated-tail-right>> flattened against its ceiling. Out here on the left, it lies <<FOCUS:saturated-tail-left>> flat against its floor. <<WRITE_TEXT:flat tails = near-zero slope|id=text-sat>> <<UNFOCUS>> This flattening is what we call saturation. And where the curve is flat, its slope, its gradient, is nearly zero. The function only truly responds in <<FOCUS:responsive-region>> this narrow band near z equals zero. <<UNFOCUS>> Everywhere else, it has stopped listening to its input. So here is the honest question: if the gradient is essentially zero across most of the domain, what happens to a network that learns by following gradients? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Saturation drives the gradient to zero almost everywhere, so learning crawls to a halt|id=key-sat>> Learning crawls to a halt. The gradient signal that should update the weights is multiplied down to almost nothing. This is exactly why we now discourage sigmoidal units in hidden layers. <<PAUSE:short>> They are still perfectly fine as output units, though, as long as you pair them with a cost function, like the cross-entropy loss, that cancels the saturation exactly where you read off the prediction. <<SECTION:Why tanh wins|id=sec-2>> But if you absolutely must use a sigmoidal function in a hidden layer, tanh is the better choice. Look at where each curve <<FOCUS:origin-point>> crosses the vertical axis. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Tanh of zero is zero, while sigmoid of zero is one half. So near the origin, tanh hugs <<FOCUS:tangent-line-near-origin>> this straight line through the origin. <<UNFOCUS>> It behaves almost exactly like the identity function. <<PAUSE:short>> When the activations stay small, every tanh acts like the identity, so the whole deep network collapses into a plain product of weight matrices, which is just a linear model. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\hat{y} = w^{\top}\tanh(U\tanh(Vx)) \approx w^{\top}UVx|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Small-activation tanh network behaves like a linear model, easing early training|id=key-tanh>> That is the payoff. A deep tanh network, while its activations stay small, behaves almost like a simple linear model stacked layer on layer, and that linear-like behavior makes the early stages of training far easier. <<PAUSE:short>> And do not write these functions off entirely. In recurrent networks, in many probabilistic models, and in some autoencoders, special requirements rule out piecewise linear units, so the smooth, saturating sigmoid still earns its place, saturation and all.

segments.narration_chapter: A feedforward network whose hidden activation is the cosine of W times x plus b reaches under one percent error on handwritten digits, which is competitive with the rectifier and the sigmoid you already know. So why does almost nobody ever use cosine? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Because almost any differentiable function works about equally well, and that is the honest, slightly humbling truth of this whole topic. <<WRITE_KEY:Almost any differentiable g works as a hidden unit|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here is the consequence: countless activation functions never even get published, because researchers only bother to write up a new unit when it clearly beats the existing ones. A unit that merely ties is so common it is uninteresting. <<WRITE_TEXT:new unit published only if it clearly wins|id=text-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:The linear hidden unit|id=sec-2>> So if everything works, let us look at the most extreme choice of all: no activation function at all, the identity. You might object that stacking linear layers is pointless, because a chain of linear maps collapses into a single linear map. And that objection is correct for a whole network. But it is perfectly acceptable for just some layers to be purely linear, and here is where it becomes a clever trick rather than a mistake. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_3_3:weight_factorization>> Picture one ordinary layer that maps <<FOCUS:input-block+output-block>> n inputs to p outputs through a <<FOCUS:weight-matrix-w>> single weight matrix W. That dense block costs <<FOCUS:param-count-original>> n times p parameters. Now what happens if we split it into two linear stages, first compressing the n inputs down to a <<FOCUS:bottleneck-block>> narrow bottleneck of size q, then expanding from q back up to p outputs? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> We have factored the matrix W into two smaller matrices, <<FOCUS:matrix-u>> U feeding the bottleneck and <<FOCUS:matrix-v>> V leaving it. Count the parameters: U holds n times q, V holds q times p, so together it is <<FOCUS:param-count-factored>> n plus p, all times q. <<WRITE_EQUATION:W \approx VU,\quad U\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times n},\ V\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}|id=eq-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> When q is small, n plus p times q is far less than n times p, a real saving in parameters and compute. <<WRITE_KEY:linear bottleneck: np params become (n+p)q|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> The original dense layer <<FOCUS:param-count-original>> needs n times p parameters; the factored pair through a bottleneck of size q <<FOCUS:param-count-factored>> needs only n plus p, all multiplied by q. <<WRITE_EQUATION:n p \;\longrightarrow\; (n+p)\,q|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> The price is honest: you have forced the transformation to be low rank, rank at most q. But in practice those low-rank relationships are very often sufficient, which is exactly why this trick is worth knowing. <<WRITE_TEXT:cost = rank capped at q, often fine|id=text-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:A zoo of distinctive units|id=sec-3>> A few other units are worth naming. Softmax, usually an output, can act as a soft switch inside memory networks. A radial basis function fires only when the input is near a template and saturates to zero almost everywhere, which makes it hard to optimize. Here's an example from the chapter. The authors wanted to see whether an unusual choice of activation function could still work, so they built a feedforward network using the activation h equals the cosine of W times x plus b. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Can a cosine activation, h = cos(Wx + b), compete with conventional hidden units?|id=ex-q-1>> They took this cosine-based network and trained it on the MNIST dataset, the classic handwritten digit benchmark. <<WRITE_STEP:Hidden unit: h = cos(Wx + b)|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Train and evaluate on MNIST|id=ex-step-1-2>> And the result: the network obtained an error rate of less than one percent, which is competitive with results from more conventional activation functions. The takeaway is that many differentiable functions can serve as hidden units. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Error rate less than one percent on MNIST — competitive with conventional activations.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Consider a neural network layer with n inputs and p outputs, computing h equals g of W times x plus b. The weight matrix W <<FOCUS:weight-matrix-w>> contains n times p parameters. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Layer with n inputs, p outputs, h = g(Wx+b). Reduce parameters?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by replacing this single layer with two layers, one using <<FOCUS:matrix-u>> weight matrix U and the <<FOCUS:matrix-v>> other using weight matrix V. The trick is that the first layer, <<FOCUS:matrix-u>> the one with U, has no activation function. <<WRITE_STEP:Replace W with two layers: U then V, U has no activation|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Because that first layer is linear, we've essentially factored the original weight matrix. The factored computation becomes h equals g of V times U times x plus b. <<WRITE_STEP:h = g(VUx + b)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now let's count parameters. If <<FOCUS:bottleneck-block>> U produces q outputs, then U and V together contain <<FOCUS:param-count-factored>> only n plus p, all times q, parameters, while the <<FOCUS:param-count-original>> original W contains n times p parameters. <<WRITE_STEP:U and V: (n + p)q params vs W: np params|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<UNFOCUS>> And the answer is this: for small q, the factored layers use only n plus p times q parameters, a considerable saving compared to n times p, though it constrains the transformation to be low rank. <<WRITE_ANSWER:For small q, (n+p)q parameters — a big saving, but the transformation is constrained to be low rank|id=ex-ans-1>> Softplus, the smooth log of one plus e to the a, is a differentiable version of the rectifier — and counterintuitively it performs worse, so smoothness buys you nothing here. Hard tanh simply clamps its input between negative one and one. <<WRITE_TEXT:softplus smooth but worse; hard tanh clamps to [-1,1]|id=text-3>> The deeper lesson stands: hidden-unit design is still open, active research. Because so many functions tie, you do not reason your way to the best unit, you find it by experiment, watching the validation error. <<WRITE_KEY:pick the unit empirically, by validation error|id=key-3>> <<PAUSE:short>>
