segments.narration_chapter: A single hidden layer can approximate any function you want, to any accuracy you want. So why does anyone ever build a deep network? <<PAUSE:long>> Let's start from the humble linear model: it takes your inputs, multiplies by a weight matrix, adds a bias, and stops. <<WRITE_TEXT:Linear model: straight lines only|id=text-lin>> Clean to train, but it can only ever draw straight-line relationships. The world, though, is full of curves and twists. You might guess that every new kind of nonlinearity needs its own hand-designed model — and that guess is wrong. <<SECTION:Universal Approximation|id=sec-uat>> Insert one hidden layer with a squashing nonlinearity, like the logistic sigmoid, between two linear maps, and something remarkable happens. One hidden layer is just a linear map, then a nonlinearity applied element-wise, then another linear map on top. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{W}^{(2)}\,g\!\left(\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)}\right) + \mathbf{b}^{(2)}|id=eq-1|boxed>> This is the universal approximation theorem: that one hidden layer, given enough units, can approximate any continuous function on a closed, bounded region, to any accuracy you choose — and later work extended it to the rectified linear unit too. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> But here is the honest catch. <<WRITE_KEY:Representing a function is not the same as learning it|id=key-rep>> Being able to represent a function is not the same as being able to learn it. Optimization can fail to find the weights, or it can overfit and memorize. <<PAUSE:short>> And the theorem is silent on size. How many hidden units does that single layer actually need? <<PAUSE:long>> The number of distinct Boolean functions on n bits is two raised to the power two-to-the-n — a doubly exponential explosion, which is why a shallow network might need exponentially many units to pin one down. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\left|\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}\right| = 2^{2^n}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> In the worst case, an exponential number. Count the Boolean functions on n bits: there are two raised to the power two-to-the-n of them, so just to distinguish them all you may need one hidden unit per input configuration. <<SECTION:Why Depth|id=sec-depth>> So a shallow net can represent anything, but it might need to be impossibly wide. This is exactly where depth earns its keep. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_4_1:folding_regions>> Picture <<FOCUS:input-axis>> the input as a single axis. A hidden unit with an absolute-value rectifier <<FOCUS:fold-line>> picks a fold line, and folds the space across it — so whatever pattern lives on one side <<FOCUS:base-pattern+mirrored-pattern>> gets mirrored onto the other. <<PAUSE:short>> Watch: <<FOCUS:base-pattern>> the bump on the right reflects across the fold line <<FOCUS:mirrored-pattern>> into an identical copy on the left. One fold turned one pattern into two regions — and stacking another layer folds those, giving four, then eight, <<FOCUS:region-count-label>> doubling with every layer. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The number of linear regions a deep rectifier network carves out grows exponentially in the depth l — that is the formal statement of the folding picture. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\#\text{regions} = O\!\left(\binom{n}{d}^{d(l-1)} n^{d}\right)|id=eq-3|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose our inputs are binary vectors v in the set zero-one to the power n. We want to count how many possible binary functions there are on these vectors, and ask how many degrees of freedom a single-layer network would need to capture an arbitrary one. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How many degrees of freedom to select an arbitrary binary function on v in {0,1}^n?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's count. Each input vector lives in the set zero-one to the power n, and a binary function assigns each of those inputs an output of zero or one. The number of possible binary functions on these vectors is two raised to the power of two-to-the-n. <<WRITE_STEP:Number of binary functions = 2^(2^n)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now, to single out one specific function from that enormous collection, we need enough information to name it. Selecting one such function requires two-to-the-n bits, one bit for each of the two-to-the-n possible inputs. <<WRITE_STEP:Selecting one function requires 2^n bits|id=ex-step-1-2>> And so the answer: capturing an arbitrary binary function in general requires order two-to-the-n degrees of freedom, which means a single-layer network may be forced to use an exponentially large number of units. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Requires O(2^n) degrees of freedom — exponentially many units|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. The main theorem from Montufar and colleagues, two thousand fourteen, looks at a deep rectifier network with d inputs, depth l, and n units per hidden layer, and asks how many linear regions it can carve out of its input space. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How many linear regions does a deep rectifier network with d inputs, depth l, and n units per layer create?|id=ex-q-1>> The theorem states that the number of linear regions for this deep rectifier network is on the order of n over d, raised to the power d times the quantity l minus one, all multiplied by n to the power d. <<WRITE_STEP:Number of linear regions = order of ((n/d) to the power d times (l minus 1)) times (n to the power d)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Notice the key feature: the depth l sits up in the exponent, so this count is exponential in the depth l. That's the formal reason depth buys efficiency over width. And for the related case of maxout networks with k filters per unit, the number of linear regions is on the order of k to the power l minus one, plus d. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Regions ~ ((n/d)^(d(l-1))) * (n^d), exponential in depth l; maxout with k filters: ~ k^(l-1) + d|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_KEY:Linear regions grow exponentially with depth|id=key-depth>> That is the engine: the number of linear regions a deep rectifier network carves out grows exponentially in its depth, so depth can replace exponential width. <<PAUSE:short>> There's a deeper reason to like this too: choosing a deep model encodes a belief that your target function is a composition of simpler functions — a program of reusable steps. And empirically, across a wide range of tasks, deeper really does generalize better.

One hidden layer is just a linear map, then a nonlinearity applied element-wise, then another linear map on top. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{W}^{(2)}\,g\!\left(\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)}\right) + \mathbf{b}^{(2)}|id=eq-1|boxed>> This is the universal approximation theorem: that one hidden layer, given enough units, can approximate any continuous function on a closed, bounded region, to any accuracy you choose — and later work extended it to the rectified linear unit too. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> But here is the honest catch. <<WRITE_KEY:Representing a function is not the same as learning it|id=key-rep>>Being able to represent a function is not the same as being able to learn it. Optimization can fail to find the weights, or it can overfit and memorize. <<PAUSE:short>> And the theorem is silent on size. How many hidden units does that single layer actually need? <<PAUSE:long>> The number of distinct Boolean functions on n bits is two raised to the power two-to-the-n — a doubly exponential explosion, which is why a shallow network might need exponentially many units to pin one down. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\left|\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}\right| = 2^{2^n}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> In the worst case, an exponential number. Count the Boolean functions on n bits: there are two raised to the power two-to-the-n of them, so just to distinguish them all you may need one hidden unit per input configuration. <<SECTION:Why Depth|id=sec-depth>>So a shallow net can represent anything, but it might need to be impossibly wide. This is exactly where depth earns its keep. <<FOCUS:fold-line>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_4_1:folding_regions>> Picture the input as a single axis. A hidden unit with an absolute-value rectifier picks a fold line, and folds the space across it — so whatever pattern lives on one side gets mirrored onto the other. <<TRACE:fold-line>> <<POINT:fold-line>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:mirrored-pattern>> Watch: the bump on the right reflects across the fold line into an identical copy on the left. One fold turned one pattern into two regions — and stacking another layer folds those, giving four, then eight, doubling with every layer. <<TRACE:mirrored-pattern>> <<PAUSE:short>> The number of linear regions a deep rectifier network carves out grows exponentially in the depth l — that is the formal statement of the folding picture. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\#\text{regions} = O\!\left(\binom{n}{d}^{d(l-1)} n^{d}\right)|id=eq-3|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose our inputs are binary vectors v in the set zero-one to the power n. We want to count how many possible binary functions there are on these vectors, and ask how many degrees of freedom a single-layer network would need to capture an arbitrary one. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How many degrees of freedom to select an arbitrary binary function on v in {0,1}^n?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's count. Each input vector lives in the set zero-one to the power n, and a binary function assigns each of those inputs an output of zero or one. The number of possible binary functions on these vectors is two raised to the power of two-to-the-n. <<WRITE_STEP:Number of binary functions = 2^(2^n)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now, to single out one specific function from that enormous collection, we need enough information to name it. Selecting one such function requires two-to-the-n bits, one bit for each of the two-to-the-n possible inputs. <<WRITE_STEP:Selecting one function requires 2^n bits|id=ex-step-1-2>> And so the answer: capturing an arbitrary binary function in general requires order two-to-the-n degrees of freedom, which means a single-layer network may be forced to use an exponentially large number of units. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Requires O(2^n) degrees of freedom — exponentially many units|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. The main theorem from Montufar and colleagues, two thousand fourteen, looks at a deep rectifier network with d inputs, depth l, and n units per hidden layer, and asks how many linear regions it can carve out of its input space. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How many linear regions does a deep rectifier network with d inputs, depth l, and n units per layer create?|id=ex-q-1>> The theorem states that the number of linear regions for this deep rectifier network is on the order of n over d, raised to the power d times the quantity l minus one, all multiplied by n to the power d. <<WRITE_STEP:Number of linear regions = order of ((n/d) to the power d times (l minus 1)) times (n to the power d)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Notice the key feature: the depth l sits up in the exponent, so this count is exponential in the depth l. That's the formal reason depth buys efficiency over width. And for the related case of maxout networks with k filters per unit, the number of linear regions is on the order of k to the power l minus one, plus d. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Regions ~ ((n/d)^(d(l-1))) * (n^d), exponential in depth l; maxout with k filters: ~ k^(l-1) + d|id=ex-ans-1>> <<FOCUS:region-count-label>> <<WRITE_KEY:Linear regions grow exponentially with depth|id=key-depth>>That is the engine: the number of linear regions a deep rectifier network carves out grows exponentially in its depth, so depth can replace exponential width. <<POINT:region-count-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> There's a deeper reason to like this too: choosing a deep model encodes a belief that your target function is a composition of simpler functions — a program of reusable steps. And empirically, across a wide range of tasks, deeper really does generalize better.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_4_2:depth_vs_width_graph>> Take a network that already works, then pour in forty million extra parameters. Sometimes accuracy jumps; sometimes it barely moves. Same budget, completely different payoff — and the deciding factor is not how many parameters, but how you arrange them. Here is the actual experiment, transcribing multi-digit street numbers from photographs. The <<FOCUS:param-axis>> horizontal axis is the number of parameters; the <<FOCUS:accuracy-axis>> vertical axis is test accuracy. <<TRACE:shallow-curve>> Watch the shallow model. <<SECTION:Depth versus width|id=sec-depth>> It climbs at first, then stalls and <<FOCUS:overfit-knee>> starts overfitting at around twenty million parameters — adding more width buys it almost nothing. <<TRACE:deep-curve>> Now the deep model. With far fewer parameters early on it already does better, and crucially it <<FOCUS:deep-benefit-region>> keeps improving past sixty million parameters, long after the shallow one gave up. <<UNFOCUS>> So here is the honest question: if both models can have the same number of parameters, why does stacking them deep beat spreading them wide? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Because depth is not extra power — it is a belief. <<WRITE_KEY:Depth encodes a prior: target = composition of many simpler functions|id=key-depth>> Choosing a deep model says you believe the function you want is built by composing many simpler functions: edges into corners, corners into shapes, or one sequential step feeding the next. <<PAUSE:short>> When that belief matches reality, depth gives you generalization almost for free, while the wide model just memorizes. <<WRITE_TEXT:wide -> memorize; deep -> compose|id=text-prior>>That is why the same parameter count pays off so differently. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_4_2:skip_connection_net>> But the chain of layers is only the starting point. <<SECTION:Wiring beyond the chain|id=sec-wiring>> Real architectures break the straight line on purpose, and the reasons are mechanical. <<FOCUS:main-chain-edges>> Here is the main chain — input, layer i, i plus one, i plus two. Now add a skip connection: an edge that <<TRACE:skip-edge>> jumps from layer i straight to layer i plus two. <<UNFOCUS>> Why bother? Remember that during training the <<TRACE:gradient-flow-arrow>> gradient flows backward from the output toward the input. The skip edge gives that gradient a shortcut — <<FOCUS:skip-edge+gradient-flow-arrow>> a second, shorter path home, so it arrives at the early layers without being squeezed through every step. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The second lever is how you wire a pair of layers. segments.narration_chapter: A modern network has hundreds of millions of weights, and to take one training step you need the derivative of the loss with respect to every single one of them. Naively that's hundreds of millions of separate calculations — so how does a network train in milliseconds? <<PAUSE:long>> Before we answer that, remember the setup: to apply gradient-based learning we must make two choices first. <<SECTION:Two choices come first|id=sec-setup>> We choose a cost function — how we measure wrongness — and we choose an output representation — what form the model's answer takes. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:cost J = how wrong; backprop serves it|id=text-setup>> Everything that follows — all the careful machinery — exists only to compute slopes of that cost. Back-propagation is the servant of those two choices, not a thing unto itself. <<PAUSE:short>> The cost J is just a loss function comparing the network's output y-hat to the target y — that single scalar is what we differentiate. <<WRITE_EQUATION:J = L(\hat{y}, y)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5:comp_graph_mlp>> Here's the key reframing. Don't think of the network as layers of neurons. Think of it as a single long composition of functions, <<FOCUS:node-x+node-z+node-h+node-y+node-J>> a computational graph, where <<FOCUS:node-J>> the cost J is just the final node. <<UNFOCUS>> Watch it flow forward. <<FOCUS:node-x>> The input x <<FOCUS:node-z>> maps to a pre-activation z, then through a nonlinearity to <<FOCUS:node-h>> the hidden activation h, then <<FOCUS:node-y>> to the output y-hat, and finally to <<FOCUS:node-J>> the scalar cost J. <<UNFOCUS>> Now the honest question: J depends on a weight buried way back near x. The chain rule says its derivative is a product of <<FOCUS:edge-x-z+edge-z-h+edge-h-y+edge-y-J>> local derivatives along the path. <<UNFOCUS>> If I compute that product separately for every weight, am I doing redundant work? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Look at the path. Every weight near the front shares <<FOCUS:edge-y-J+edge-h-y+edge-z-h>> the same downstream factors — the derivative of J with respect to y-hat, of y-hat with respect to h, of h with respect to z. <<UNFOCUS>> Compute those shared pieces once, store them, and reuse them. That's the whole trick. The derivative of the cost with respect to a buried weight is a product of local derivatives along the path from that weight to the cost — and the front factors are shared by every early weight. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial J}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial \hat{y}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial h} \cdot \frac{\partial h}{\partial z} \cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial w}|id=eq-2|boxed>> So we run the chain rule <<TRACE:backward-flow>> from right to left. <<WRITE_KEY:One backward pass computes ALL gradients, cost approx one forward pass|id=key-back>> <<FOCUS:grad-J>> Start at the cost with the trivial seed: the derivative of J with respect to itself is one. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> We seed the backward pass with the only derivative we know for free: the derivative of the cost with respect to itself is one. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial J}{\partial J} = 1|id=eq-3|boxed>> Then sweep that gradient <<TRACE:backward-flow>> backward across the graph. <<UNFOCUS>> At each node we multiply the incoming gradient by the local derivative of that node's operation, and pass it further back. Every node is visited exactly once. Because each shared sub-derivative is computed once and reused by everything upstream of it, <<FOCUS:backward-flow>> a single backward pass delivers the gradient for all hundreds of millions of weights, at about the cost of one forward pass. <<UNFOCUS>> That's the answer to our opening puzzle. <<PAUSE:short>> And notice — back-propagation isn't one rigid recipe. It's a family: the same right-to-left chain-rule bookkeeping generalizes to any computational graph, which is exactly why it scales from a tiny example to enormous modern models. <<WRITE_TEXT:choose cost + output -> backprop computes the slope|id=text-tie>>So hold two things together: you choose the cost and the output representation, and back-propagation is the efficient algorithm that turns those choices into a gradient for every weight in one organized sweep. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: Every neural network diagram you've ever drawn — circles, arrows, neurons — is a useful lie. To make back-propagation rigorous, we need to throw it out and draw something exact instead. The informal picture conflates two completely different things: the values flowing through the network, and the operations that transform them. <<WRITE_TEXT:Informal nets blur values and operations|id=text-1>> To be precise, we have to pull those apart. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_1:comp_graph_logistic>> <<SECTION:The computational graph|id=sec-1>> So here is the new rule, and it is dead simple. Every node in the graph <<FOCUS:node-x+node-w+node-u+node-b+node-z+node-yhat>> stands for one variable. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And when I say variable, I mean it in the broadest sense — it might be a scalar, a single number, or a vector, a list of numbers, or a matrix, a grid, or even a tensor, a higher-dimensional grid. A node just holds a value, whatever shape that value takes. Nodes by themselves are inert — they just sit there holding values. What gives the graph life is the edges. <<WRITE_TEXT:Node = variable, edge = operation|id=text-2>> <<FOCUS:edge-dot+edge-add+edge-sigmoid>> An edge is an operation: a simple function of one or more variables. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Watch what happens with a real example — a logistic-regression prediction. We feed in <<FOCUS:node-x+node-w>> the input x and the weights w, and the first operation is a dot product, <<FOCUS:node-u>> producing an intermediate variable u. That arrow from x and w into u is <<FOCUS:edge-dot>> labelled with its operation, the dot product. <<UNFOCUS>> The drawing rule is exactly this: if a variable is computed by applying an operation to other variables, draw a directed edge into it. The first intermediate node holds the dot product of the weight vector with the input vector. <<WRITE_EQUATION:u = w^\top x|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now we take that u, <<FOCUS:node-b>> add the bias b, and get <<FOCUS:node-z>> another intermediate variable z. <<UNFOCUS>> Notice the recipe is building up — each node is one clean step. Here's a question worth pausing on: each operation returns only a single output variable. Isn't that hopelessly restrictive — surely real computations branch into many outputs? <<PAUSE:long>> The whole prediction is just the sigmoid of that dot product plus a bias — and notice it's nothing but <<FOCUS:edge-dot+edge-add+edge-sigmoid>> those three operation nodes composed end to end. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\hat{y} = \sigma\!\left(w^\top x + b\right)|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> It costs us nothing. That single output can itself be a vector with many entries, so anything multi-valued just rides inside one richer variable. Software allows multiple outputs for convenience, but conceptually one-output-per-operation loses no generality. The final edge <<FOCUS:edge-sigmoid>> applies the sigmoid to z, giving us <<FOCUS:node-yhat>> the prediction y-hat. <<WRITE_KEY:Complex function = composition of simple operations|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> And look at the whole picture: a complicated function is nothing but simple operations chained together — that chaining is called composition. <<PAUSE:short>> Step back and read the whole graph as a recipe: <<FOCUS:node-x+node-w>> inputs flow in on the left, operations transform them edge by edge, <<FOCUS:node-yhat>> the output emerges on the right. <<UNFOCUS>> Every value has a place, every transformation is explicit. This is the precise language we were missing. Nodes are variables, edges are operations, and any function is their composition — and that exactness is exactly what lets us state back-propagation rigorously in the very next step. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter:
When a deep network gets something wrong, how does a weight buried twenty layers deep know it was even partly to blame? The nudge can't teleport from x straight to z. It has to <<FOCUS:node-y>> pass through y first. segments.narration_chapter: The chain rule already hands you the exact formula for the gradient of your loss with respect to every single parameter. So here is the paradox: why does writing that formula down naively, and just evaluating it, blow up to exponential time? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_3:diamond_graph>> <<SECTION:The diamond graph|id=sec-1>> Let me build the smallest graph that exposes the problem. Here is an <<FOCUS:node-x>> input node x at the bottom. From x <<FOCUS:node-y>> we compute y, and then <<FOCUS:node-z>> from y we compute z, but x also feeds forward again so that <<FOCUS:node-w>> the output w depends on both y and z. Watch the <<FOCUS:edge-x-y+edge-x-z>> two paths leave x and <<FOCUS:node-w>> re-converge at the top. Now I want the <<FOCUS:node-w+node-x>> gradient of the output w with respect to x. The chain rule says: <<FOCUS:chain-rule>> sum over every path from x to w, multiplying derivatives along each path. There are <<FOCUS:edge-y-w+edge-z-w>> two paths, so two terms. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The gradient of the output with respect to x is the sum over both paths from x to w, multiplying the derivatives along each path. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}|id=eq-chain>> Here it is written out. Each term is a product of derivatives along one route from x up to w. Now here is the trap. Suppose z is itself a function of y. Then the <<FOCUS:edge-y-w-label>> derivative of w with respect to y is not atomic; it must in turn account for the path through z. So the piece dw/dy <<FOCUS:edge-z-w-label>> secretly contains dw/dz inside it. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> If you expand everything symbolically and then evaluate, that inner subexpression dw/dz gets written out, and computed, in two separate places. One diamond duplicates it once. Stack diamonds on diamonds, layer after layer, and ask: how many times does the deepest subexpression get recomputed? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> It doubles at every layer. With n stacked diamonds you recompute the shared piece on the order of two-to-the-n times. That is the exponential blow-up: the formula is short, but the naive evaluation is astronomically wasteful. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:The fix: compute once, store, reuse|id=sec-2>> The cure is the move every smart student already makes. Do the <<FOCUS:shared-subexpr>> shared sub-calculation once, write the answer in the margin, and copy it wherever it is needed instead of redoing the arithmetic. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Chain rule = WHAT to compute. Backprop = compute each subexpression ONCE, store, reuse.|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That is exactly what back-propagation does. It computes the gradient at each node exactly once, stores it, and feeds it to the parents below. The chain rule tells you what to compute; back-propagation is the discipline of <<FOCUS:shared-subexpr>> never recomputing a shared subexpression. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> <<WRITE_TEXT:store -> O(graph) time, more memory; recompute -> less memory, more time|id=text-tradeoff>>Notice this is a genuine trade-off, not a free lunch. Storing intermediate gradients costs memory but makes the runtime linear in the size of the graph. Recomputing saves memory but pays in time, and for tangled graphs that time is the exponential cost we just saw. So the algorithm proceeds backward through the graph in a careful order: visit the output, then each node once, accumulating the gradient flowing into it before passing it down. Same answer the chain rule promised, computed in a single sweep instead of an exponential explosion.

segments.narration_chapter: The chain rule is one line of calculus you've known for years. So why does running it backwards through a network decide whether you train a model in an hour or in a century? <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_4:chain_graph>> Let's strip the network down to its bones: <<FOCUS:node-w+edge-wx+node-x+edge-xy+node-y+edge-yz+node-z>> a single chain, where we apply the very same function f at every step. We start with an <<FOCUS:node-w>> input w. Then <<FOCUS:node-x>> x is f of w, <<FOCUS:node-y>> y is f of x, and finally <<FOCUS:node-z>> z is f of y. <<WRITE_TEXT:x=f(w), y=f(x), z=f(y)|id=text-chain>> Now we ask the gradient question: <<FOCUS:node-w+node-z>> if I nudge w, how much does the output z move? <<SECTION:Expanding the chain rule|id=sec-chain>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The chain rule answers cleanly: multiply the local derivatives along the path, partial z over partial y, times partial y over partial x, times partial x over partial w. Multiply the local derivatives <<FOCUS:edge-yz+edge-xy+edge-wx>> along the path: partial z over partial y, times partial y over partial x, times partial x over partial w. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial z}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\,\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\,\frac{\partial x}{\partial w}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's the moment to watch. Each of those local derivatives is f prime evaluated at the node before it, so <<FOCUS:expansion>> written out fully, the gradient becomes f prime of f of f of w, times f prime of f of w, times f prime of w. <<UNFOCUS>> Each local derivative is f prime evaluated at the node before it, so the whole thing becomes f prime of f of f of w, times f prime of f of w, times f prime of w. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial z}{\partial w} = f'(f(f(w)))\,f'(f(w))\,f'(w)|id=eq-2|boxed>> Stare at that expression and you'll see the <<FOCUS:expansion>> same subexpression, f of w, appearing again and again, nested deeper each time. <<UNFOCUS>> So you face a genuine fork in the road. You can recompute f of w fresh every single time the chain rule asks for it, which costs no memory but explodes the work, or you can compute it once, <<FOCUS:node-x>> store it as the value x, and reuse it everywhere downstream. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Back-propagation <<FOCUS:backward-flow>> takes the second road. <<WRITE_KEY:Backprop = chain rule + store each repeated subexpression once|id=key-backprop>> <<UNFOCUS>> It is exactly the chain rule, plus the single decision to compute every repeated subexpression once and store it. That one choice trades a little memory for an enormous cut in runtime. <<PAUSE:short>> And this is precisely why the forward pass matters beyond just producing a prediction. <<SECTION:Forward caches, backward reuses|id=sec-mlp>> As we push the input through each layer, multiplying by weights, adding biases, applying activations, we are quietly caching every intermediate activation. <<PAUSE:short>> Then the backward pass <<FOCUS:backward-flow>> sweeps right to left through the same graph, and at every node it reuses the exact value the forward pass already stored, multiplying it by the local derivative to assemble each weight and bias gradient in a single sweep. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. Let w be the single input to the graph, and we use the same function f at every step of a chain. So x equals f of w, then y equals f of x, and z equals f of y. Our goal is to compute the derivative of z with respect to w. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: x = f(w), y = f(x), z = f(y) — find dz/dw|id=ex-q-1>> We start by applying the chain rule. That gives us a product: the derivative of z with respect to y, times the derivative of y with respect to x, times the derivative of x with respect to w. <<WRITE_STEP:dz/dw = (dz/dy)(dy/dx)(dx/dw)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we rewrite each factor using f. This equals f prime of y, times f prime of x, times f prime of w. <<WRITE_STEP:= f'(y) · f'(x) · f'(w)|id=ex-step-1-2>> If we expand it fully by substituting x equals f of w and y equals f of f of w, watch what happens: <<FOCUS:expansion>> f of w appears multiple times in the expression. <<WRITE_STEP:= f'(f(f(w))) · f'(f(w)) · f'(w)|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's the payoff. Back-propagation computes the value of f of w only once and <<FOCUS:node-x>> stores it in the variable x, then reuses it. <<UNFOCUS>> The alternative approach recomputes f of w each time it is needed, which wastes work. <<PAUSE:short>> So the answer is the same product either way, but back-propagation gets it more efficiently. <<WRITE_ANSWER:dz/dw = f'(f(f(w))) · f'(f(w)) · f'(w), with f(w) computed once and stored|id=ex-ans-1>> In a fully-connected MLP this is the whole story repeated layer by layer: one forward pass fills the cache, one backward pass drains it into gradients, and nothing is ever computed twice. <<PAUSE:short>> This toy chain uses one function and one input on purpose. segments.narration_chapter: What if back-propagation never touched a single number, and instead handed you back a brand-new graph that already knows how to compute every gradient? <<SECTION:Symbols versus numbers|id=sec-1>> Think about a formula like velocity equals u plus a times t. The letters are symbols; they stand for values without committing to any actual number yet. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_5:s2s_graph>> A computational graph is exactly the same kind of object: it's the recipe for a calculation, drawn as nodes and edges, before you plug in any ingredients. Here's one for <<FOCUS:node-w+node-x+node-y+node-z>> z equals f of f of f of w. <<UNFOCUS>> Only when you actually run or train the network do you replace the symbol w with a concrete list of numbers, like one point one, two, and three point seven six five. <<SECTION:Two styles of differentiation|id=sec-2>> So when we want gradients, here's the honest question: does back-propagation have to know those numbers to give us derivatives? <<PAUSE:long>> In one style, called symbol-to-number differentiation, the answer is yes. You hand it the graph plus actual inputs, and it crunches through and returns numbers, the gradient at exactly those values. segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_6:comp_graph_backprop>> A deep network can route the same intermediate quantity to the loss through thousands of different paths — so if you differentiated naively, you would recompute that quantity an exponential number of times. Yet back-propagation finds every gradient in roughly the time of one forward pass. <<PAUSE:short>> Forget neural networks for a moment. Picture any computation as a graph: each node holds a number computed by applying some operation to the numbers flowing in from its parents, and at the very top sits a <<FOCUS:node-loss>> single scalar we care about — the loss. <<SECTION:The shared subexpression|id=sec-1>> Now look at <<FOCUS:node-shared>> this interior node. Notice <<FOCUS:node-child-a+node-child-b>> it has two children — its value feeds upward <<FOCUS:edge-shared-a+edge-shared-b>> along two different paths to the loss. <<WRITE_TEXT:want df_loss / d every input|id=text-1>> What we want is how the final loss changes when we <<FOCUS:node-param>> nudge each input node — in practice, each parameter of the model. Here is the honest question: if <<FOCUS:node-shared>> that shared node influences the loss <<FOCUS:node-child-a+node-child-b>> through both of these children, how do we account for both paths without walking the whole tree of paths separately? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The trick is to run a second graph in exactly the reverse order. We start at the top, where the gradient of the loss <<FOCUS:grad-arrow-loss>> with respect to itself is simply one, and then we work our way down. <<SECTION:Gradient flows backward|id=sec-2>> To get the <<FOCUS:grad-arrow-shared>> gradient at our shared node, we collect contributions from each of its children. <<FOCUS:node-child-a>> From this child we take the gradient already computed there and multiply by the <<FOCUS:edge-shared-a>> local derivative of that child with respect to the shared node. <<PAUSE:short>> We do the same <<FOCUS:node-child-b+edge-shared-b>> along the second child, and then we add the two contributions together. That sum is the <<FOCUS:grad-arrow-shared>> gradient at the shared node — both paths handled, no tree walked. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:grad[node] = sum over children of grad[child] times local derivative|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That summing rule is just the chain rule applied across all children of a node, and it is the entire engine of back-propagation. <<PAUSE:short>> The gradient of the loss with respect to a node equals the sum, over every child of that node, of the loss-gradient already known at the child times the local derivative of the child with respect to the node. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial u^{(n)}}{\partial u^{(j)}} = \sum_{i\,:\,j \in Pa(u^{(i)})} \frac{\partial u^{(n)}}{\partial u^{(i)}}\,\frac{\partial u^{(i)}}{\partial u^{(j)}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> We store every gradient in a table as we compute it, so when a node lower down needs the gradient of its child, it is already sitting there — never recomputed. segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_7:forward_prop_chain>> Every prediction a deep network ever makes is just one input, passed hand to hand down a chain of layers, like a baton in a relay race, transformed at every exchange. Before the race even starts, the network needs four things: how deep it is, the depth l, a weight matrix and a bias vector for every layer, and the input x with the target y we are aiming for. <<SECTION:Forward Propagation|id=sec-fwd>> Here is the first, almost silly move: the <<FOCUS:input-node>> activation of layer zero is just the input itself. <<UNFOCUS>> The input is the very first runner holding the baton. The activation of layer zero is defined to be the input itself. <<WRITE_EQUATION:h^{(0)} = x|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now we hand off. The signal <<TRACE:edge-input-to-1>> flows along this edge, where it gets multiplied by the weight matrix and shifted by the bias. <<WRITE_STEP:a-one equals b-one plus W-one times h-zero|id=step-preact>> That mixing <<FOCUS:layer-1-preact>> gives us the pre-activation: take the bias for the layer, and add the weight matrix times the activation coming in. <<UNFOCUS>> It is a pure affine map, a linear combine plus a nudge. <<PAUSE:short>> The pre-activation of layer k is the bias plus the weight matrix times the previous layer's activation. <<WRITE_EQUATION:a^{(k)} = b^{(k)} + W^{(k)} h^{(k-1)}|id=eq-2|boxed>> If we stopped there, stacking layers would collapse into one big linear map. So we bend the pre-activation through a nonlinear activation function f, and <<FOCUS:layer-1-act>> that bent output is the activation h-one. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The activation of layer k is the pre-activation passed through the nonlinear function f. <<WRITE_EQUATION:h^{(k)} = f\left(a^{(k)}\right)|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Each layer: affine map, then nonlinearity, then pass forward|id=key-recipe>> And here is the whole engine in one sentence: each layer computes a pre-activation by an affine map, bends it through a nonlinearity, and that output <<TRACE:edge-1-to-2>> becomes the next layer's input. <<PAUSE:short>> We just keep repeating the same two steps, layer after layer, the baton moving down the chain, <<TRACE:edge-2-to-L>> until we reach the final layer. The activation of that last layer is the finish line: <<FOCUS:layer-L-act>> it is our prediction, y-hat. <<UNFOCUS>> The prediction is simply the activation of the final layer. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\hat{y} = h^{(l)}|id=eq-4|boxed>> <<SECTION:Measuring the Result|id=sec-cost>> But how do we know if the prediction is any good, and what stops the weights from blowing up to fit every quirk in the data? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Cost equals loss plus lambda times regularizer|id=key-cost>> We answer both <<FOCUS:cost-node>> with the cost. segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_8:backprop_graph_annotated>> The back-propagation you've learned is correct, complete, and elegant — and yet if you typed it up exactly as we drew it, no serious deep learning library would ship it. Why not? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Complications under the hood|id=sec-1>> The answer is that our clean algorithm answers the mathematical question — what is the gradient — but stays silent on four engineering questions that every real implementation must confront. Let me walk you through them on a graph. <<PAUSE:short>> First wrinkle. We defined an operation as a function returning a single tensor. But suppose you want <<FOCUS:multi-output-node>> both the maximum value in a tensor and the index where it lives. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Scanning that memory twice would be wasteful, so a good implementation does both in one pass and <<FOCUS:multi-out-value+multi-out-argmax>> returns two outputs from a single operation — which means the graph machinery must allow a node to emit more than one result tensor. <<WRITE_TEXT:op may emit several output tensors|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the very first generalization is structural: an operation is a map from input tensors to a tuple of output tensors, and every output carries its own gradient contribution backward. Second wrinkle: memory. <<FOCUS:fan-in-node>> Look at this node — during the backward pass, gradient contributions arrive <<FOCUS:gradient-edge-a+gradient-edge-b+gradient-edge-c>> along three separate edges, and back-propagation must sum them. <<UNFOCUS>> The naive recipe computes all three, holds every one in memory, then adds them at the end. For a node with thousands of consumers, that peak memory is brutal. So how do we add them without ever storing them all at once? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Accumulate in place: one buffer, add each gradient as it arrives|id=key-1>> You keep <<FOCUS:accumulation-buffer>> one running buffer at the node and add each contribution into it the instant it's computed, then free that contribution — so peak memory is one tensor, not the whole crowd of them. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:in-place sum trades a second pass for O(1) extra tensors|id=step-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> This is the same idea as accumulating a running total instead of building a list and summing later — a constant-memory reduction folded directly into the backward traversal. <<SECTION:Types and undefined gradients|id=sec-2>> Third wrinkle: numbers themselves. The same edge might carry thirty-two-bit floats, sixty-four-bit floats, or integers, and each type needs its own carefully designed policy for casting, accumulation, and overflow during the backward pass. Fourth wrinkle: some operations have no well-defined gradient at all — think of an integer rounding step or <<FOCUS:nondiff-edge>> an argmax index. <<UNFOCUS>> The software must mark such edges and decide whether the gradient the user actually requested even exists. Notice the pattern: none of these are flaws in the theory. Multi-output ops, in-place accumulation, type policies, undefined-gradient tracking — each is the answer to a concrete systems constraint sitting on top of the math. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Clean theory complete; production layers engineering on top|id=key-2>> So the clean algorithm you learned is genuinely complete as an idea — it gives you the real intellectual machinery for computing derivatives. When you open a professional library, the extra complexity isn't confusion; it's engineering serving memory, compute, and numerical correctness, and now you know exactly why each piece is there. <<PAUSE:short>>

But suppose you want both the maximum value in a tensor and the index where it lives. <<POINT:multi-output-node>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:multi-output-node>> Scanning that memory twice would be wasteful, so a good implementation does both in one pass and returns two outputs from a single operation — which means the graph machinery must allow a node to emit more than one result tensor. <<TRACE:multi-output-node>> <<FOCUS:multi-output-node>> <<WRITE_TEXT:op may emit several output tensors|id=text-1>>So the very first generalization is structural: an operation is a map from input tensors to a tuple of output tensors, and every output carries its own gradient contribution backward. <<FOCUS:fan-in-node>> Second wrinkle: memory. Look at this node — during the backward pass, gradient contributions arrive along three separate edges, and back-propagation must sum them. <<POINT:fan-in-node>> <<FOCUS:gradient-edge-a>> The naive recipe computes all three, holds every one in memory, then adds them at the end. For a node with thousands of consumers, that peak memory is brutal. So how do we add them without ever storing them all at once? <<TRACE:gradient-edge-a>> <<TRACE:gradient-edge-a>> <<TRACE:gradient-edge-a>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:accumulation-buffer>> <<WRITE_KEY:Accumulate in place: one buffer, add each gradient as it arrives|id=key-1>>You keep one running buffer at the node and add each contribution into it the instant it's computed, then free that contribution — so peak memory is one tensor, not the whole crowd of them. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:in-place sum trades a second pass for O(1) extra tensors|id=step-1>>This is the same idea as accumulating a running total instead of building a list and summing later — a constant-memory reduction folded directly into the backward traversal. <<POINT:accumulation-buffer>> <<FOCUS:gradient-edge-b>> <<SECTION:Types and undefined gradients|id=sec-2>>Third wrinkle: numbers themselves. The software must mark such edges and decide whether the gradient the user actually requested even exists. <<TRACE:nondiff-edge>> <<FOCUS:fan-in-node>> Notice the pattern: none of these are flaws in the theory. When you open a professional library, the extra complexity isn't confusion; it's engineering serving memory, compute, and numerical correctness, and now you know exactly why each piece is there. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: Back-propagation can compute the gradient of a billion-parameter network for roughly the price of one forward pass, and yet it is provably not the optimal way to compute a gradient. Both of those are true at once. The deep learning world grew up a little isolated, and invented its own habits for derivatives. But step outside, and there's an entire field called automatic differentiation whose only job is computing derivatives by algorithm. <<SECTION:Automatic Differentiation|id=sec-ad>> Back-propagation is just one member of that family. Specifically, back-propagation belongs to a class called reverse mode accumulation: we evaluate the chain rule starting from the output and work backwards toward the inputs. <<WRITE_TEXT:backprop = reverse-mode autodiff|id=text-rev>> Other methods just evaluate the same chain rule pieces in a different order. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_9:jacobian_chain>> Here's the cleanest way to see what order means. Think of the chain rule for a deep composition as a product of Jacobian matrices, <<FOCUS:matrix-A+matrix-B+matrix-C+matrix-D>> A times B times C times D. Suppose the <<FOCUS:matrix-D>> rightmost factor D is a tall column vector and the <<FOCUS:matrix-A>> leftmost A has many rows: that's a graph with many inputs and a single scalar output, exactly our loss. <<UNFOCUS>> The gradient of a deep composition is a product of Jacobian matrices, one per layer, chained from output back to input. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\nabla = A\,B\,C\,D \quad (\text{Jacobian chain})|id=eq-1|boxed>> So in which order should we multiply this chain to spend the least arithmetic? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Multiply from the right: <<FOCUS:right-bracket>> C times D first. Because D is a vector, every product stays a cheap <<FOCUS:rev-cost>> matrix-times-vector. Keep going <<TRACE:reverse-arrow>> right-to-left and you never build a single big matrix-matrix product. That is exactly <<FOCUS:reverse-label+right-bracket-label>> reverse mode, exactly back-propagation. <<PAUSE:short>> Multiply from the left instead, <<FOCUS:left-bracket>> A times B first, and you're grinding out full <<FOCUS:fwd-cost>> matrix-matrix products, vastly more expensive when there's only one output. <<WRITE_KEY:Cheapest order depends on the shapes: many inputs, one output favors reverse mode|id=key-shapes>> <<UNFOCUS>> The answer is identical; only the cost differs. <<PAUSE:short>> Flip the situation. If A is short, few outputs, but D is wide, many of them, then <<TRACE:forward-arrow>> multiplying left-to-right is the cheap direction. That is <<FOCUS:forward-label+left-bracket-label>> forward mode accumulation, and it also saves memory because you don't store the whole graph. <<UNFOCUS>> Now the guarantee that makes reverse mode beloved. When the graph has one output and each local partial derivative costs a constant, every edge's derivative is computed exactly once, with one multiply and one add. So the gradient costs the same order as the forward pass: order, number of edges. <<PAUSE:short>> With one scalar output and constant-cost local derivatives, reverse mode computes the whole gradient in time of the same order as the forward pass, growing with the number of edges in the graph. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{cost}(\nabla) = O(\#\text{edges})|id=eq-2|boxed>> But beloved is not optimal. Picture building a softmax from exponentials, a sum, and a division, then a cross-entropy loss on top. A human spots that the derivative of the loss with respect to a logit collapses to a gorgeous q minus p. A human notices the softmax-plus-cross-entropy gradient with respect to a logit simplifies to predicted probability minus true probability — a shortcut pure back-propagation cannot find on its own. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial J}{\partial z_i} = q_i - p_i|id=eq-3|boxed>> Back-propagation can't see that shortcut. It dutifully pushes gradients through every logarithm and exponential in the graph. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial J}{\partial z_i} = q_i - p_i|id=eq-qmp>> Libraries like Theano and TensorFlow bolt on pattern-matching heuristics to simplify, but plain back-prop won't. Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose we have variables p one through p n representing probabilities, and variables z one through z n representing unnormalized log probabilities. We define q i equals exp of z i divided by the sum over i of exp of z i — that's the softmax, built out of exponentiation, summation, and division operations. From these we construct a cross-entropy loss J equals negative sum over i of p i times log of q i. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the derivative of the softmax-plus-cross-entropy loss J with respect to z i.|id=ex-q-1>> A human mathematician looks at this whole expression and notices something beautiful. We start by writing down the loss and the softmax together. <<WRITE_EQUATION:J = -\sum_i p_i \log q_i, \quad q_i = \frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_i \exp(z_i)}|id=ex-eq-1>> When you differentiate J with respect to z i by hand, all the logarithms and exponentials cancel against each other algebraically, and the messy expression collapses. <<WRITE_STEP:Differentiate J w.r.t. z_i; logs and exps cancel|id=ex-step-1-1>> And the answer is wonderfully simple: the derivative of J with respect to z i equals q i minus p i. <<WRITE_ANSWER:dJ/dz_i = q_i - p_i|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's the catch. Back-propagation cannot spot this shortcut. Instead it will explicitly propagate gradients through every single logarithm and exponentiation operation in the original graph. Some software libraries, such as Theano, can perform some kinds of algebraic substitution to improve over the graph that pure back-propagation proposes. And finding the truly cheapest evaluation order in general? That's N P complete, because it can require simplifying the algebra into its least expensive form. So nobody has a fast, general optimal method. One last cultural difference: outside machine learning, people differentiate raw Python or C code directly. Deep learning libraries instead use explicit graph structures, which forces a hand-written backward rule for every operation. That limits you to defined ops, but it lets experts hand-craft clever rules for speed and numerical stability. So back-propagation isn't the only way, nor the optimal way, but it is wonderfully practical and serves us extremely well.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_10:backprop_graph>> Here's a strange idea: instead of building a graph that spits out numbers, what if we built a graph that spits out its own derivatives — and then never had to decide when to run anything? <<SECTION:Symbol-to-symbol|id=sec-1>> The trick is what each node contains. In the ordinary view, a node holds a number. In the symbol-to-symbol view, a node holds another operation — so the derivatives themselves live inside the graph as differentiable nodes you can keep evaluating. <<PAUSE:short>> And because the derivative graph is just more graph, you don't decide ahead of time when each operation fires. A generic engine evaluates any node the instant its parents are ready. <<SECTION:The backward pass|id=sec-2>> Now the heart of it. Suppose <<FOCUS:node-z>> z is our final scalar and we want to know how z responds to <<FOCUS:node-x>> some earlier variable x. <<UNFOCUS>> Where do we even start? <<PAUSE:long>> We start the backward pass with the simplest fact there is: the <<FOCUS:grad-seed>> gradient of z with respect to itself is one, because anything changes itself one-for-one. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial z}{\partial z} = 1|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Seed the backward pass with dz/dz = 1|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> We start at z itself, and we seed the gradient with the most obvious fact in mathematics: the gradient of z with respect to z is one. Anything changes itself one-for-one. <<PAUSE:short>> Then we <<TRACE:back-z-y1>> walk backwards along an edge. At each operation, we multiply our current gradient by <<FOCUS:jac-z-y1>> that operation's Jacobian — the matrix that says how the operation turned its inputs into its outputs. We keep multiplying Jacobians, edge after edge, traveling backwards through the graph, until <<FOCUS:node-x>> we finally arrive at x. <<UNFOCUS>> That product of Jacobians is the gradient. To get the gradient at any node, take each operation that consumed it, push the gradient backward through that operation's Jacobian, and add up the contributions from every path. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} z = \sum_{i} \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}_i}{\partial \mathbf{x}} \right)^{\top} \nabla_{\mathbf{y}_i} z|id=eq-2|boxed>> But look — <<FOCUS:edge-x-y1+edge-x-y2>> x feeds two operations, not one. So going backward, <<FOCUS:back-y1-x+back-y2-x>> two gradients arrive at x along two different paths. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:At a shared node, SUM the gradients from every path|id=step-1>> When a node is reached by more than one backward path, you simply <<FOCUS:merge-sum>> add the arriving gradients. <<UNFOCUS>> That sum is not a detail — it's the chain rule honestly accounting for every way x influenced z. <<PAUSE:short>> So the whole rule, written out, is a sum over consumers: for each operation that used x, transpose its Jacobian, apply it to that operation's gradient, and add them all up. <<PAUSE:short>> To make this general in code, each node holds a tensor — scalar, vector, matrix, whatever — and knows three things: which operation created it, who its parents are, and who its consumers are. And every operation carries one back-propagation rule that computes exactly that Jacobian-vector product. Those tiny pieces — <<FOCUS:grad-seed>> seed at one, <<FOCUS:jac-z-y1+jac-y1-x>> multiply by Jacobians, <<FOCUS:merge-sum>> sum at the merges — assemble into the entire algorithm.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_6:depth_as_composition>> Take two networks with the exact same number of parameters. Make <<FOCUS:shallow-layer>> one shallow and wide, <<FOCUS:deep-stage-1+deep-stage-2+deep-stage-3>> the other deep and narrow — and the deep one keeps winning. <<UNFOCUS>> Why should rearranging the same parameters into more layers matter at all? <<PAUSE:long>> This isn't a one-off. Across many tasks, holding the parameter count roughly fixed, depth tended to beat width. The empirical result was clear long before the explanation was. The honest answer comes from one word: a prior. <<SECTION:Depth as a prior|id=sec-1>> A prior is an assumption you bake into the model before it sees a single data point — a belief about what good solutions ought to look like. Picture the <<FOCUS:function-space>> whole space of functions the model could represent. A prior is just a statement that <<FOCUS:favored-region>> some corner of this space is far more plausible than the rest. <<UNFOCUS>> So what corner does depth bet on? Watch the deep path. <<FOCUS:input-node>> The input enters, the <<FOCUS:deep-stage-1>> first stage extracts low-level features, the next stage combines those <<FOCUS:deep-stage-2>> into mid-level features, the next <<FOCUS:deep-stage-3>> builds higher-level ones still. <<UNFOCUS>> A deep network just says the answer is built by passing the input through one stage, then feeding that into the next, again and again — a chain of composed functions. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f(x) = f^{(L)} \circ f^{(L-1)} \circ \cdots \circ f^{(1)}(x)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:f(x) = f^{(L)} \circ \cdots \circ f^{(1)}(x)|id=eq-1>> Each layer is a function, and the network is those functions composed in a chain — the output of one becomes the input of the next. The structure of deep networks lines up with the structure of the problems, and that alignment is what makes the prior useful. <<PAUSE:short>> Carry this framing forward. <<WRITE_TEXT:depth, weight sharing, specialized layers = priors|id=text-1>> Almost every architectural decision you'll meet later — depth, weight sharing, convolution, attention — is the same move: a built-in belief that nudges the model toward the solutions we expect to be correct. <<PAUSE:short>>
