choreography.narration: Take a network that already works, then pour in forty million extra parameters. Sometimes accuracy jumps; sometimes it barely moves. Same budget, completely different payoff — and the deciding factor is not how many parameters, but how you arrange them.
Here is the actual experiment, transcribing multi-digit street numbers from photographs. The horizontal axis is the number of parameters; the vertical axis is test accuracy.

Watch the shallow model. <<SECTION:Depth versus width|id=sec-depth>>It climbs at first, then stalls and starts overfitting at around twenty million parameters — adding more width buys it almost nothing.
Now the deep model. With far fewer parameters early on it already does better, and crucially it keeps improving past sixty million parameters, long after the shallow one gave up.
So here is the honest question: if both models can have the same number of parameters, why does stacking them deep beat spreading them wide?

Because depth is not extra power — it is a belief. <<WRITE_KEY:Depth encodes a prior: target = composition of many simpler functions|id=key-depth>>Choosing a deep model says you believe the function you want is built by composing many simpler functions: edges into corners, corners into shapes, or one sequential step feeding the next.

When that belief matches reality, depth gives you generalization almost for free, while the wide model just memorizes. <<WRITE_TEXT:wide -> memorize; deep -> compose|id=text-prior>>That is why the same parameter count pays off so differently.
But the chain of layers is only the starting point. <<SECTION:Wiring beyond the chain|id=sec-wiring>>Real architectures break the straight line on purpose, and the reasons are mechanical.
Here is the main chain — input, layer i, i plus one, i plus two. Now add a skip connection: an edge that jumps from layer i straight to layer i plus two.

Why bother? Remember that during training the gradient flows backward from the output toward the input. The skip edge gives that gradient a shortcut — a second, shorter path home, so it arrives at the early layers without being squeezed through every step.
The second lever is how you wire a pair of layers. The default is fully connected: every input unit touches every output unit — maximum parameters, maximum computation.

But you can deliberately make it sparse, so each input only connects to a small local group of outputs. Convolutional networks do exactly this — far fewer parameters, far less computation, and a pattern tuned to the structure of images.

So the real lesson is this: architecture is how you spend your parameters and steer your gradients. <<WRITE_KEY:Architecture = controlling gradient flow + spending parameters wisely|id=key-arch>>Skip connections and sparse wiring are not decoration — they decide whether the gradient can flow and whether the parameters are spent on the right assumptions.
Depth picks the right family of functions; wiring decides whether you can actually train them. Get both right, and forty million extra parameters become a leap instead of dead weight.

lesson_plans.title: Back-Propagation: Computing the Gradient Without Going Bankrupt

hook.text: A modern network has hundreds of millions of weights. To take one training step, you need the derivative of the loss with respect to every single one of them. Naively, that sounds like hundreds of millions of separate calculations. So how does a network train in milliseconds?

crucial_facts: Back-propagation computes the gradient with respect to ALL parameters in a single backward pass, costing about the same as one forward pass, by reusing shared sub-derivatives via the chain rule.

Before any back-propagation can happen, two design choices come first: the cost function (how wrong are we) and the output representation (what form the answer takes) — back-propagation exists only to serve those choices.

diagrams.purpose: Show the loss as the output of a chain of operations, so that the chain rule and the backward reuse of sub-derivatives become visually obvious.

required_elements.description: Input node x at the far left of the computational graph.
Pre-activation node z = W x + b, second from left.
Hidden activation node h = g(z).
Network output node y-hat produced from h.
Scalar cost node J, the loss, at the far right of the graph.
Forward edge from x to z carrying the linear map.
Forward edge from z to h carrying the activation g.
Forward edge from h to output y-hat.
Forward edge from y-hat to cost J.
A backward arrow sweeping right-to-left across the whole graph representing the propagation of derivatives.
Seed gradient dJ/dJ = 1 attached at the cost node J.

choreography.narration: A modern network has hundreds of millions of weights, and to take one training step you need the derivative of the loss with respect to every single one of them. Naively that's hundreds of millions of separate calculations — so how does a network train in milliseconds?

Before we answer that, remember the setup: to apply gradient-based learning we must make two choices first. <<SECTION:Two choices come first|id=sec-setup>>We choose a cost function — how we measure wrongness — and we choose an output representation — what form the model's answer takes.

<<WRITE_TEXT:cost J = how wrong; backprop serves it|id=text-setup>>Everything that follows — all the careful machinery — exists only to compute slopes of that cost. Back-propagation is the servant of those two choices, not a thing unto itself.
Here's the key reframing. Don't think of the network as layers of neurons. Think of it as a single long composition of functions, a computational graph, where the cost J is just the final node.
Watch it flow forward. The input x maps to a pre-activation z, then through a nonlinearity to the hidden activation h, then to the output y-hat, and finally to the scalar cost J.

Now the honest question: J depends on a weight buried way back near x. The chain rule says its derivative is a product of local derivatives along the path. If I compute that product separately for every weight, am I doing redundant work?

Look at the path. Every weight near the front shares the same downstream factors — the derivative of J with respect to y-hat, of y-hat with respect to h, of h with respect to z. Compute those shared pieces once, store them, and reuse them. That's the whole trick.

So we run the chain rule from right to left. <<WRITE_KEY:One backward pass computes ALL gradients, cost approx one forward pass|id=key-back>>Start at the cost with the trivial seed: the derivative of J with respect to itself is one.

Then sweep that gradient backward across the graph. At each node we multiply the incoming gradient by the local derivative of that node's operation, and pass it further back. Every node is visited exactly once.

Because each shared sub-derivative is computed once and reused by everything upstream of it, a single backward pass delivers the gradient for all hundreds of millions of weights, at about the cost of one forward pass. That's the answer to our opening puzzle.

And notice — back-propagation isn't one rigid recipe. It's a family: the same right-to-left chain-rule bookkeeping generalizes to any computational graph, which is exactly why it scales from a tiny example to enormous modern models.

<<WRITE_TEXT:choose cost + output -> backprop computes the slope|id=text-tie>>So hold two things together: you choose the cost and the output representation, and back-propagation is the efficient algorithm that turns those choices into a gradient for every weight in one organized sweep.

equations.explanation_in_words: The cost J is just a loss function comparing the network's output y-hat to the target y — that single scalar is what we differentiate.

equations.latex: \frac{\partial J}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial \hat{y}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial h} \cdot \frac{\partial h}{\partial z} \cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial w}
equations.explanation_in_words: The derivative of the cost with respect to a buried weight is a product of local derivatives along the path from that weight to the cost — and the front factors are shared by every early weight.
We seed the backward pass with the only derivative we know for free: the derivative of the cost with respect to itself is one.

lesson_plans.title: Computational Graphs: The Exact Language of Computation

hook.text: Every neural network diagram you've ever drawn — circles, arrows, neurons — is a lie. A useful lie, but a lie. To make back-propagation rigorous, we need to throw it out and draw something exact instead.

crucial_facts: A computational graph is a directed graph where every node is a variable (scalar, vector, matrix, or tensor) and every edge is an operation applied to produce one node from another.
Any function, no matter how complex, is just a composition of simple operations chained through the graph — and each operation returns exactly one output variable without loss of generality.

diagrams.purpose: Show that a real expression — a logistic-regression prediction — decomposes into a chain of single-operation nodes, making the node-is-variable / edge-is-operation convention concrete and revealing the composition structure that back-prop will later exploit.

required_elements.description: Input node labelled x, the feature vector entering the computation, drawn as a circle on the left.
Input node labelled w, the weight vector, drawn as a circle on the left below x.
Intermediate node u holding the dot product of w and x, drawn as a circle in the middle.
Input node labelled b, the bias scalar, drawn lower middle.
Intermediate node z holding u plus b, drawn right of u.
Output node y-hat holding the sigmoid of z, the final prediction, drawn on the right.
Directed edges from x and w into u, annotated 'dot product'.
Directed edges from u and b into z, annotated 'plus'.
Directed edge from z into y-hat, annotated 'sigmoid'.

choreography.narration: Every neural network diagram you've ever drawn — circles, arrows, neurons — is a useful lie. To make back-propagation rigorous, we need to throw it out and draw something exact instead.

The informal picture conflates two completely different things: the values flowing through the network, and the operations that transform them. <<WRITE_TEXT:Informal nets blur values and operations|id=text-1>>To be precise, we have to pull those apart.
<<SECTION:The computational graph|id=sec-1>>So here is the new rule, and it is dead simple. Every node in the graph stands for one variable.

And when I say variable, I mean it in the broadest sense — it might be a scalar, a single number, or a vector, a list of numbers, or a matrix, a grid, or even a tensor, a higher-dimensional grid. A node just holds a value, whatever shape that value takes.

Nodes by themselves are inert — they just sit there holding values. What gives the graph life is the edges. <<WRITE_TEXT:Node = variable, edge = operation|id=text-2>>An edge is an operation: a simple function of one or more variables.
Watch what happens with a real example — a logistic-regression prediction. We feed in the input x and the weights w, and the first operation is a dot product, producing an intermediate variable u.

That arrow from x and w into u is labelled with its operation, the dot product. The drawing rule is exactly this: if a variable is computed by applying an operation to other variables, draw a directed edge into it.
Now we take that u, add the bias b, and get another intermediate variable z. Notice the recipe is building up — each node is one clean step.
Here's a question worth pausing on: each operation returns only a single output variable. Isn't that hopelessly restrictive — surely real computations branch into many outputs?

It costs us nothing. That single output can itself be a vector with many entries, so anything multi-valued just rides inside one richer variable. Software allows multiple outputs for convenience, but conceptually one-output-per-operation loses no generality.

The final edge applies the sigmoid to z, giving us the prediction y-hat. <<WRITE_KEY:Complex function = composition of simple operations|id=key-1>>And look at the whole picture: a complicated function is nothing but simple operations chained together — that chaining is called composition.

Step back and read the whole graph as a recipe: inputs flow in on the left, operations transform them edge by edge, the output emerges on the right. Every value has a place, every transformation is explicit.

This is the precise language we were missing. Nodes are variables, edges are operations, and any function is their composition — and that exactness is exactly what lets us state back-propagation rigorously in the very next step.

equations.explanation_in_words: The first intermediate node holds the dot product of the weight vector with the input vector.
The whole prediction is just the sigmoid of that dot product plus a bias — and notice it's nothing but those three operation nodes composed end to end.

lesson_plans.title: The Chain Rule: The Engine of Back-Propagation

hook.text: When a deep network gets something wrong, how does a weight buried twenty layers deep know it was even partly to blame?

crucial_facts: The gradient flowing into any variable is the Jacobian of the next variable with respect to it, times the gradient already computed for that next variable.
Back-propagation is nothing more than one Jacobian-times-gradient product per operation in the computational graph.

diagrams.purpose: Show the scalar composition z depends on y depends on x, so the derivative flows backward as a product of local sensitivities.

required_elements.description: A circle labeled x, the input variable, on the left.
A circle labeled y in the middle, with y = g of x.
A circle labeled z on the right, with z = f of y.
An arrow from node-x to node-y, the forward map g.
An arrow from node-y to node-z, the forward map f.
A backward arrow from z to y annotated dz/dy, the local sensitivity of z to y.
A backward arrow from y to x annotated dy/dx, the local sensitivity of y to x.

diagrams.purpose: Show that when x and y are vectors, a single component of x reaches z through every component of y, so we must sum over all paths — the Jacobian.

required_elements.description: A single input node labeled x sub i on the left.
An intermediate node labeled y sub one.
An intermediate node labeled y sub two.
An intermediate node labeled y sub three.
The scalar output node labeled z on the right.
Edge from x sub i to y sub one.
Edge from x sub i to y sub two.
Edge from x sub i to y sub three.
Edge from y sub one into z.
Edge from y sub two into z.
Edge from y sub three into z.
A boxed n-by-m grid labeled Jacobian, dy/dx, overlaid to show all the partial derivatives bundled together.

choreography.narration: When a deep network gets something wrong, how does a weight buried twenty layers deep know it was even partly to blame? The answer is one of the cleanest ideas in all of calculus, and once you see it, the entire training engine falls into place.
Start with the simplest possible chain. You take a number x, push it through a function g to get y, then push y through a function f to get z.
So z lives at the end of a little assembly line. <<SECTION:Scalar chain rule|id=sec-1>>The question we care about is: if I nudge x by a tiny amount, how much does z move at the far end?

Here's the trick. The nudge can't teleport from x straight to z. It has to pass through y first. So watch the sensitivity flow backward: z reacts to y at a rate dz/dy, and y reacts to x at a rate dy/dx.

Multiply those two local rates together and the y in the middle conceptually cancels, leaving exactly how z responds to x. That product IS the chain rule. <<WRITE_KEY:dz/dx = dz/dy times dy/dx|id=key-1>>
Now the real world isn't made of single numbers. Let x be a vector of m components and y a vector of n components. A single input, x sub i, no longer touches just one y.
Watch it fan out. Nudging x sub i ripples into y sub one, y sub two, y sub three, all of them at once.
And every one of those then funnels into z. So the total effect on z is the sum of the effect along every single path. Miss a path, and you get the wrong gradient.
We bundle all those path derivatives, every partial of every y with respect to every x, into one n-by-m grid. That grid is the Jacobian matrix.

And here is the beautiful part: summing over all those paths is exactly a matrix-vector product. The gradient of z with respect to x is just the Jacobian times the gradient of z with respect to y. <<SECTION:The vector chain rule|id=sec-2>>

Pause on that, because it's the whole game. The gradient arriving at a node equals the local Jacobian of the next node times the gradient that node already received. <<WRITE_KEY:grad_x z = (dy/dx) transpose times grad_y z|id=key-2>>
So what does back-propagation actually do? It walks backward through the computational graph and performs exactly one Jacobian-times-gradient product at every single operation. Nothing more.

And tensors? They change nothing. <<WRITE_TEXT:tensor = flatten, backprop, reshape|id=text-1>>Imagine flattening each tensor into a long vector, running the same Jacobian products, then reshaping back. The indices become tuples instead of single numbers, but the engine is identical.

So that weight twenty layers deep learns its blame the same way every variable does: the error's sensitivity gets multiplied, Jacobian by Jacobian, all the way back to it. Master the chain rule, and you've mastered the engine that lets deep networks learn from their mistakes.

equations.explanation_in_words: The rate at which z changes with x is the rate z changes with y, multiplied by the rate y changes with x.

equations.latex: \frac{\partial z}{\partial x_i} = \sum_j \frac{\partial z}{\partial y_j}\,\frac{\partial y_j}{\partial x_i}
equations.explanation_in_words: To find how z responds to one input component, add up its contributions through every intermediate component.
Summing over all the paths is exactly multiplying the Jacobian matrix by the gradient with respect to y.
For tensors the chain rule looks the same, just with index tuples standing in for single index numbers.

lesson_plans.title: Recursively Applying the Chain Rule to Obtain Backprop

hook.text: The chain rule already gives you the exact formula for every gradient in your network. So why does a naive implementation of that formula take exponential time to run?

crucial_facts: The chain rule tells you WHAT to compute; back-propagation is the discipline of computing it WITHOUT recomputing any shared subexpression more than once.
Repeated subexpressions in the gradient can recur exponentially many times, so storing each one once and reusing it turns an infeasible computation into a linear-time pass.

diagrams.purpose: A diamond-shaped computational graph where one node feeds two paths that re-converge, making it visually obvious that a downstream gradient flows back through that node along two routes and gets reused.

required_elements.description: Bottom input node labeled x, the shared variable whose gradient we want.
Left intermediate node y, a function of x: y = f(x).
Right intermediate node z, also a function of x: z = f(y)... arranged so x feeds both branches.
Top output scalar node w, a function of both y and z, where the two paths re-converge.
Directed edge from x up to y, the left branch out of x.
Directed edge from x up to z, the right branch out of x.
Directed edge from y up to w, the left path into the output.
Directed edge from z up to w, the right path into the output.
Highlight band over node x and its two outgoing edges marking the subexpression dw/dy and dw/dz that both feed dw/dx and would be recomputed by a naive expansion.

choreography.narration: The chain rule already hands you the exact formula for the gradient of your loss with respect to every single parameter. So here is the paradox: why does writing that formula down naively, and just evaluating it, blow up to exponential time?
<<SECTION:The diamond graph|id=sec-1>>Let me build the smallest graph that exposes the problem. Here is an input node x at the bottom.
From x we compute y, and then from y we compute z, but x also feeds forward again so that the output w depends on both y and z. Watch the two paths leave x and re-converge at the top.
Now I want the gradient of the output w with respect to x. The chain rule says: sum over every path from x to w, multiplying derivatives along each path. There are two paths, so two terms.

<<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}|id=eq-chain>>Here it is written out. Each term is a product of derivatives along one route from x up to w.

Now here is the trap. Suppose z is itself a function of y. Then the derivative of w with respect to y is not atomic; it must in turn account for the path through z. So the piece dw/dy secretly contains dw/dz inside it.

If you expand everything symbolically and then evaluate, that inner subexpression dw/dz gets written out, and computed, in two separate places. One diamond duplicates it once. Stack diamonds on diamonds, layer after layer, and ask: how many times does the deepest subexpression get recomputed?

It doubles at every layer. With n stacked diamonds you recompute the shared piece on the order of two-to-the-n times. That is the exponential blow-up: the formula is short, but the naive evaluation is astronomically wasteful.

<<SECTION:The fix: compute once, store, reuse|id=sec-2>>The cure is the move every smart student already makes. Do the shared sub-calculation once, write the answer in the margin, and copy it wherever it is needed instead of redoing the arithmetic.

<<WRITE_KEY:Chain rule = WHAT to compute. Backprop = compute each subexpression ONCE, store, reuse.|id=key-1>>That is exactly what back-propagation does. It computes the gradient at each node exactly once, stores it, and feeds it to the parents below. The chain rule tells you what to compute; back-propagation is the discipline of never recomputing a shared subexpression.

<<WRITE_TEXT:store -> O(graph) time, more memory; recompute -> less memory, more time|id=text-tradeoff>>Notice this is a genuine trade-off, not a free lunch. Storing intermediate gradients costs memory but makes the runtime linear in the size of the graph. Recomputing saves memory but pays in time, and for tangled graphs that time is the exponential cost we just saw.

So the algorithm proceeds backward through the graph in a careful order: visit the output, then each node once, accumulating the gradient flowing into it before passing it down. Same answer the chain rule promised, computed in a single sweep instead of an exponential explosion.

equations.latex: \frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}
equations.explanation_in_words: The gradient of the output with respect to x is the sum over both paths from x to w, multiplying the derivatives along each path.

lesson_plans.title: Back-Propagation in a Fully-Connected MLP: Why It's Fast

hook.text: The chain rule is one line of calculus you've known since high school. So why does running it backwards through a network make the difference between training a model in an hour versus a century?

crucial_facts: Back-propagation is the chain rule plus one decision: compute each repeated subexpression once and store it, instead of recomputing it. That single choice trades a little memory for an exponential cut in runtime.
Forward propagation caches the intermediate activations on the way in; back-propagation reuses those exact cached values on the way out to assemble every gradient in one sweep.

diagrams.purpose: Show the linear chain w to x to y to z where the same function f is applied at every step, so the student can literally see the subexpression f(w) reappear when the chain rule is expanded.

required_elements.description: Leftmost node labeled w, the scalar input to the graph.
Second node labeled x, equal to f of w.
Third node labeled y, equal to f of x.
Rightmost node labeled z, equal to f of y, the output.
Directed edge from w to x annotated as the operation f.
Directed edge from x to y annotated as the operation f.
Directed edge from y to z annotated as the operation f.
A dashed arrow flowing right to left from z back to w representing the gradient pass that reuses stored node values.

choreography.narration: The chain rule is one line of calculus you've known for years. So why does running it backwards through a network decide whether you train a model in an hour or in a century?
Let's strip the network down to its bones: a single chain, where we apply the very same function f at every step.
We start with an input w. Then x is f of w, y is f of x, and finally z is f of y. <<WRITE_TEXT:x=f(w), y=f(x), z=f(y)|id=text-chain>>
Now we ask the gradient question: if I nudge w, how much does the output z move? <<SECTION:Expanding the chain rule|id=sec-chain>>
The chain rule answers cleanly: multiply the local derivatives along the path, partial z over partial y, times partial y over partial x, times partial x over partial w.

Here's the moment to watch. Each of those local derivatives is f prime evaluated at the node before it, so written out fully, the gradient becomes f prime of f of f of w, times f prime of f of w, times f prime of w.
Stare at that expression and you'll see the same subexpression, f of w, appearing again and again, nested deeper each time.

So you face a genuine fork in the road. You can recompute f of w fresh every single time the chain rule asks for it, which costs no memory but explodes the work, or you can compute it once, store it as the value x, and reuse it everywhere downstream.

Back-propagation takes the second road. <<WRITE_KEY:Backprop = chain rule + store each repeated subexpression once|id=key-backprop>>It is exactly the chain rule, plus the single decision to compute every repeated subexpression once and store it. That one choice trades a little memory for an enormous cut in runtime.

And this is precisely why the forward pass matters beyond just producing a prediction. <<SECTION:Forward caches, backward reuses|id=sec-mlp>>As we push the input through each layer, multiplying by weights, adding biases, applying activations, we are quietly caching every intermediate activation.

Then the backward pass sweeps right to left through the same graph, and at every node it reuses the exact value the forward pass already stored, multiplying it by the local derivative to assemble each weight and bias gradient in a single sweep.

Here's an example from the chapter. Let w be the single input to the graph, and we use the same function f at every step of a chain. So x equals f of w, then y equals f of x, and z equals f of y. Our goal is to compute the derivative of z with respect to w. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: x = f(w), y = f(x), z = f(y) — find dz/dw|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by applying the chain rule. That gives us a product: the derivative of z with respect to y, times the derivative of y with respect to x, times the derivative of x with respect to w. <<WRITE_STEP:dz/dw = (dz/dy)(dy/dx)(dx/dw)|id=ex-step-1-1>>
Now we rewrite each factor using f. This equals f prime of y, times f prime of x, times f prime of w. <<WRITE_STEP:= f'(y) · f'(x) · f'(w)|id=ex-step-1-2>>

If we expand it fully by substituting x equals f of w and y equals f of f of w, watch what happens: f of w appears multiple times in the expression. <<WRITE_STEP:= f'(f(f(w))) · f'(f(w)) · f'(w)|id=ex-step-1-3>>

Here's the payoff. Back-propagation computes the value of f of w only once and stores it in the variable x, then reuses it. The alternative approach recomputes f of w each time it is needed, which wastes work. <<PAUSE:short>> So the answer is the same product either way, but back-propagation gets it more efficiently. <<WRITE_ANSWER:dz/dw = f'(f(f(w))) · f'(f(w)) · f'(w), with f(w) computed once and stored|id=ex-ans-1>>
In a fully-connected MLP this is the whole story repeated layer by layer: one forward pass fills the cache, one backward pass drains it into gradients, and nothing is ever computed twice.

This toy chain uses one function and one input on purpose. Real frameworks generalize the same idea to any computational graph and process a whole minibatch at once, but the engine underneath is exactly what you just saw: store once, reuse everywhere.

equations.latex: \frac{\partial z}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\,\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\,\frac{\partial x}{\partial w}
equations.explanation_in_words: Multiply the local derivatives along the path: partial z over partial y, times partial y over partial x, times partial x over partial w.
Each local derivative is f prime evaluated at the node before it, so the whole thing becomes f prime of f of f of w, times f prime of f of w, times f prime of w.

lesson_plans.title: Symbol-to-Symbol Derivatives

hook.text: What if back-propagation never touched a single number — and instead handed you back a brand-new graph that already knows how to compute every gradient?

crucial_facts: Symbol-to-symbol differentiation builds new nodes in the computational graph that symbolically describe the derivative, rather than returning numbers at fixed input values.
Because the derivative is itself a computational graph in the same language, you can run back-propagation on it again to get higher-order derivatives.

diagrams.purpose: Show the original forward chain z = f(f(f(w))) and the new derivative nodes back-prop appends, so students see the derivative IS more graph in the same language.

required_elements.description: Input node labeled w at the bottom of the forward chain.
Intermediate node x = f(w).
Intermediate node y = f(x).
Output node z = f(y) at the top of the forward chain.
Upward arrows w to x to y to z, each labeled with the local function f.
New node computing dz/dy = f'(y), appended by back-prop.
New node computing dy/dx = f'(x).
New node computing dx/dw = f'(w).
Multiply node combining dz/dy and dy/dx into dz/dx.
Multiply node combining dz/dx and dx/dw into the final dz/dw.
Arrows wiring the derivative nodes together and back into the forward-graph nodes they depend on.

choreography.narration: What if back-propagation never touched a single number, and instead handed you back a brand-new graph that already knows how to compute every gradient?
<<SECTION:Symbols versus numbers|id=sec-1>>Think about a formula like velocity equals u plus a times t. The letters are symbols; they stand for values without committing to any actual number yet.
A computational graph is exactly the same kind of object: it's the recipe for a calculation, drawn as nodes and edges, before you plug in any ingredients. Here's one for z equals f of f of f of w.
Only when you actually run or train the network do you replace the symbol w with a concrete list of numbers, like one point one, two, and three point seven six five.
<<SECTION:Two styles of differentiation|id=sec-2>>So when we want gradients, here's the honest question: does back-propagation have to know those numbers to give us derivatives?

In one style, called symbol-to-number differentiation, the answer is yes. You hand it the graph plus actual inputs, and it crunches through and returns numbers, the gradient at exactly those values. Torch and Caffe work this way.

<<WRITE_KEY:Symbol-to-symbol: back-prop adds new graph nodes that symbolically describe the derivative|id=key-1>>But there's a cleverer style. Symbol-to-symbol differentiation never looks at a number. Instead it takes your graph and appends new nodes that are themselves a symbolic description of the derivative.
Watch what back-propagation actually builds. It walks the chain and, for each link, creates a node holding the local derivative: f prime of y, then f prime of x, then f prime of w.
Then it wires those local pieces together with multiply nodes, chaining d z d y times d y d x into d z d x, and multiplying once more by d x d w to get d z d w. That's the chain rule, drawn as graph.

<<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{dz}{dw} = f'(y)\,f'(x)\,f'(w)|id=eq-1>>And notice: not one number was needed to build any of this. The result is just a bigger graph that computes both the original expression and its derivative.

<<SECTION:Why this is powerful|id=sec-3>>The first payoff is uniformity: the derivative is written in the very same language as the original. A generic evaluation engine can later plug in any numbers you like; nothing special required.
Here's the truly beautiful part: if the derivative is just another computational graph, what stops you from running back-propagation on it again?

Here's an example from the chapter. When we actually use or train a neural network, the symbols alone aren't enough — we have to assign specific values to them. In particular, we replace a symbolic input to the network, x, with a specific numeric value. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Replace symbolic input x with a concrete numeric vector|id=ex-q-1>>

So we start by taking x, which up to now has just been a symbol, and we swap it for an actual vector of numbers. Here that vector is one point one, two, three point seven six five, and negative one point eight. <<WRITE_STEP:x is symbolic — assign a concrete vector|id=ex-step-1-1>>

And the answer is: the symbolic input x now becomes the numeric vector one point one, two, three point seven six five, negative one point eight, which is exactly what flows through the network when we run it. <<WRITE_ANSWER:x = [1.1, 2, 3.765, -1.8]|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. We begin with a graph that represents z equals f of f of f of w. So it's the same function f composed with itself three times, applied to w. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Start from a graph for z = f(f(f(w))); build a graph for dz/dw|id=ex-q-1>>

Now we run the back-propagation algorithm, but here's the twist: instead of asking it for a number, we instruct it to construct the graph for the expression corresponding to the derivative of z with respect to w. The key point is that no specific numeric values are accessed during this construction. <<WRITE_STEP:Run back-prop in symbol-to-symbol mode: emit graph nodes for dz/dw|id=ex-step-1-1>>

And the result is exactly what we wanted: a brand-new computational graph that gives a symbolic description of the derivative of z with respect to w. Back-propagation has simply added new nodes that describe how to compute the derivative, rather than computing the derivative itself. <<WRITE_ANSWER:A graph that symbolically describes dz/dw, with no numbers ever evaluated|id=ex-ans-1>>

<<WRITE_KEY:Derivatives are graphs, so differentiate them again for higher-order derivatives|id=key-2>>Nothing stops you. You feed the derivative graph back into the same machinery and get the derivative of the derivative, and so on, for arbitrarily high-order derivatives. The machinery composes with itself.
That self-composing flexibility, derivatives that are themselves differentiable graphs, is exactly why symbol-to-symbol systems like Theano and TensorFlow became the backbone of deep learning.

equations.explanation_in_words: The chain rule, drawn as graph, says the derivative of z with respect to w is the product of the local derivatives at each link in the chain.

lesson_plans.title: General Back-Propagation on a Computational Graph

hook.text: A deep network can share the same intermediate quantity across thousands of paths to the loss — so a naive gradient would recompute it an exponential number of times. Yet back-propagation gets every gradient in the same time as a single forward pass. How?

crucial_facts: Back-propagation visits each edge of the computational graph exactly once, so its cost scales linearly with the number of edges — the same order as the forward pass.
The gradient at any node is assembled by summing, over all of its children, the child's already-computed gradient times the local derivative of the child with respect to that node.

diagrams.purpose: Show a small computational graph with a shared subexpression, so the student sees forward values flowing up and gradients flowing back down, and sees that one node feeds multiple children.

required_elements.description: Top node labeled u^(n), the scalar loss, the quantity whose gradient we want.
A child node of the shared node, feeding into the loss along one path.
A second child node of the shared node, feeding into the loss along another path.
A shared interior node u^(j) that has two children (node-child-a and node-child-b), illustrating a reused subexpression.
An input/parameter node at the bottom whose gradient we ultimately want.
Forward edge from node-shared to node-child-a, carrying local derivative d child-a / d shared.
Forward edge from node-shared to node-child-b, carrying local derivative d child-b / d shared.
Forward edge from node-param up into node-shared.
Backward gradient marker at the loss node showing gradient equals one.
Backward gradient marker at the shared node, the accumulated gradient flowing in from both children.

choreography.narration: A deep network can route the same intermediate quantity to the loss through thousands of different paths — so if you differentiated naively, you would recompute that quantity an exponential number of times. Yet back-propagation finds every gradient in roughly the time of one forward pass.

Forget neural networks for a moment. Picture any computation as a graph: each node holds a number computed by applying some operation to the numbers flowing in from its parents, and at the very top sits a single scalar we care about — the loss.
<<SECTION:The shared subexpression|id=sec-1>>Now look at this interior node. Notice it has two children — its value feeds upward along two different paths to the loss.
<<WRITE_TEXT:want df_loss / d every input|id=text-1>>What we want is how the final loss changes when we nudge each input node — in practice, each parameter of the model.
Here is the honest question: if that shared node influences the loss through both of these children, how do we account for both paths without walking the whole tree of paths separately?
The trick is to run a second graph in exactly the reverse order. We start at the top, where the gradient of the loss with respect to itself is simply one, and then we work our way down.

<<SECTION:Gradient flows backward|id=sec-2>>To get the gradient at our shared node, we collect contributions from each of its children. From this child we take the gradient already computed there and multiply by the local derivative of that child with respect to the shared node.
We do the same along the second child, and then we add the two contributions together. That sum is the gradient at the shared node — both paths handled, no tree walked.

<<WRITE_KEY:grad[node] = sum over children of grad[child] times local derivative|id=key-1>>That summing rule is just the chain rule applied across all children of a node, and it is the entire engine of back-propagation.
We store every gradient in a table as we compute it, so when a node lower down needs the gradient of its child, it is already sitting there — never recomputed.
<<SECTION:Why it is cheap|id=sec-3>>Now count the work. Each edge of the graph is touched exactly once: one local partial derivative, one multiplication, one addition.

So the total cost scales with the number of edges — the same order as the forward pass. That is how back-propagation defeats the exponential explosion: it remembers shared subexpressions instead of recomputing them, trading memory for speed.

equations.latex: \frac{\partial u^{(n)}}{\partial u^{(j)}} = \sum_{i\,:\,j \in Pa(u^{(i)})} \frac{\partial u^{(n)}}{\partial u^{(i)}}\,\frac{\partial u^{(i)}}{\partial u^{(j)}}
equations.explanation_in_words: The gradient of the loss with respect to a node equals the sum, over every child of that node, of the loss-gradient already known at the child times the local derivative of the child with respect to the node.
In practice we read each child's gradient straight out of a stored table and accumulate it into the entry for the current node, so nothing is computed twice.

lesson_plans.title: Forward Propagation: The Relay Race Through a Deep Network

hook.text: Every prediction a deep network ever makes is just one input, passed hand to hand down a chain of layers — like a baton in a relay race, transformed at every exchange.

crucial_facts: Each layer computes a pre-activation by an affine map, then bends it through a nonlinearity, and that output becomes the next layer's input.
The final activation is the prediction y-hat, and the cost adds the data loss to a lambda-weighted regularizer on the parameters.

diagrams.purpose: Show the layer-by-layer flow of activations from input through hidden layers to prediction and cost, so each affine-plus-nonlinearity step is visually one link in a chain.

required_elements.description: The input vector x, labeled as the activation of layer zero, h-zero.
Arrow from input into layer one, annotated with weight matrix W-one and bias b-one.
Pre-activation node a-one for the first layer.
Activation node h-one, the output of the first layer's nonlinearity f.
Arrow carrying h-one forward into the next layer.
Activation node h-two of an intermediate hidden layer.
Arrow representing the repeated layers up to the final layer L.
Final-layer activation h-L, which equals the prediction y-hat.
Arrow from the prediction into the cost computation.
Cost node J, combining the loss between y-hat and y with the regularization term.

choreography.narration: Every prediction a deep network ever makes is just one input, passed hand to hand down a chain of layers, like a baton in a relay race, transformed at every exchange.
Before the race even starts, the network needs four things: how deep it is, the depth l, a weight matrix and a bias vector for every layer, and the input x with the target y we are aiming for.
<<SECTION:Forward Propagation|id=sec-fwd>>Here is the first, almost silly move: the activation of layer zero is just the input itself. The input is the very first runner holding the baton.
Now we hand off. The signal flows along this edge, where it gets multiplied by the weight matrix and shifted by the bias.

<<WRITE_STEP:a-one equals b-one plus W-one times h-zero|id=step-preact>>That mixing gives us the pre-activation: take the bias for the layer, and add the weight matrix times the activation coming in. It is a pure affine map, a linear combine plus a nudge.
If we stopped there, stacking layers would collapse into one big linear map. So we bend the pre-activation through a nonlinear activation function f, and that bent output is the activation h-one.

<<WRITE_KEY:Each layer: affine map, then nonlinearity, then pass forward|id=key-recipe>>And here is the whole engine in one sentence: each layer computes a pre-activation by an affine map, bends it through a nonlinearity, and that output becomes the next layer's input.
We just keep repeating the same two steps, layer after layer, the baton moving down the chain, until we reach the final layer.
The activation of that last layer is the finish line: it is our prediction, y-hat.
<<SECTION:Measuring the Result|id=sec-cost>>But how do we know if the prediction is any good, and what stops the weights from blowing up to fit every quirk in the data?

<<WRITE_KEY:Cost equals loss plus lambda times regularizer|id=key-cost>>We answer both with the cost. Its first part is the loss, comparing y-hat to the true y. Its second part is a regularizer, scaled by lambda, that gently penalizes large parameters so the network learns instead of memorizes.

Add those two together and you have the full cost the network drives downward. One input, walked forward through every layer, ending in a single number measuring how wrong we were: that is one complete forward pass.

equations.explanation_in_words: The activation of layer zero is defined to be the input itself.
The pre-activation of layer k is the bias plus the weight matrix times the previous layer's activation.
The activation of layer k is the pre-activation passed through the nonlinear function f.
The prediction is simply the activation of the final layer.
The total cost is the loss between prediction and target plus lambda times a regularizer on the parameters.

lesson_plans.title: Complications: What the Clean Picture of Back-Propagation Leaves Out

hook.text: The back-propagation you've learned is correct, complete, and elegant — and yet if you typed it up exactly as we drew it, no serious deep learning library would ship it. Why not?

crucial_facts: The clean back-propagation algorithm is conceptually complete, but production implementations layer engineering subtleties — multi-output ops, in-place accumulation, type policies, and undefined-gradient tracking — on top of it.
Each complication is not a flaw in the theory but an answer to a real systems constraint: memory, compute passes, numerical types, and mathematical well-definedness.

diagrams.purpose: Show a small computational graph and use it to localize exactly where each real-world complication bites: a node that emits two outputs, a node where many gradients fan in and must be summed, and an edge whose gradient may be undefined.

required_elements.description: A computation node f in the middle of the graph, taking one input and feeding several downstream consumers.
A single operation node that emits two outputs simultaneously, e.g. value and argmax, drawn with two outgoing result tensors.
A node whose gradient is the sum of contributions arriving back along multiple outgoing edges (the fan-in point during the backward pass).
One backward gradient-contribution edge arriving at the fan-in node.
A second backward gradient-contribution edge arriving at the fan-in node.
A third backward gradient-contribution edge arriving at the fan-in node.
A running-sum buffer sitting at the fan-in node into which each incoming gradient is added as it arrives.
An edge through a non-differentiable operation, marked as having an undefined gradient.

choreography.narration: The back-propagation you've learned is correct, complete, and elegant — and yet if you typed it up exactly as we drew it, no serious deep learning library would ship it. Why not?

<<SECTION:Complications under the hood|id=sec-1>>The answer is that our clean algorithm answers the mathematical question — what is the gradient — but stays silent on four engineering questions that every real implementation must confront. Let me walk you through them on a graph.
First wrinkle. We defined an operation as a function returning a single tensor. But suppose you want both the maximum value in a tensor and the index where it lives.

Scanning that memory twice would be wasteful, so a good implementation does both in one pass and returns two outputs from a single operation — which means the graph machinery must allow a node to emit more than one result tensor.

<<WRITE_TEXT:op may emit several output tensors|id=text-1>>So the very first generalization is structural: an operation is a map from input tensors to a tuple of output tensors, and every output carries its own gradient contribution backward.
Second wrinkle: memory. Look at this node — during the backward pass, gradient contributions arrive along three separate edges, and back-propagation must sum them.

The naive recipe computes all three, holds every one in memory, then adds them at the end. For a node with thousands of consumers, that peak memory is brutal. So how do we add them without ever storing them all at once?

<<WRITE_KEY:Accumulate in place: one buffer, add each gradient as it arrives|id=key-1>>You keep one running buffer at the node and add each contribution into it the instant it's computed, then free that contribution — so peak memory is one tensor, not the whole crowd of them.

<<WRITE_STEP:in-place sum trades a second pass for O(1) extra tensors|id=step-1>>This is the same idea as accumulating a running total instead of building a list and summing later — a constant-memory reduction folded directly into the backward traversal.

<<SECTION:Types and undefined gradients|id=sec-2>>Third wrinkle: numbers themselves. The same edge might carry thirty-two-bit floats, sixty-four-bit floats, or integers, and each type needs its own carefully designed policy for casting, accumulation, and overflow during the backward pass.

Fourth wrinkle: some operations have no well-defined gradient at all — think of an integer rounding step or an argmax index. The software must mark such edges and decide whether the gradient the user actually requested even exists.

Notice the pattern: none of these are flaws in the theory. Multi-output ops, in-place accumulation, type policies, undefined-gradient tracking — each is the answer to a concrete systems constraint sitting on top of the math.

<<WRITE_KEY:Clean theory complete; production layers engineering on top|id=key-2>>So the clean algorithm you learned is genuinely complete as an idea — it gives you the real intellectual machinery for computing derivatives. When you open a professional library, the extra complexity isn't confusion; it's engineering serving memory, compute, and numerical correctness, and now you know exactly why each piece is there.

lesson_plans.title: Differentiation Outside the Deep Learning Community

hook.text: Back-propagation can compute the gradient of a billion-parameter network for roughly the price of one forward pass — and yet it is provably NOT the optimal way to compute a gradient. Both of those statements are true at the same time.

crucial_facts: Back-propagation is reverse-mode automatic differentiation: for a single scalar output it computes the full gradient in time of the same order as the forward pass, O(number of edges).

Reverse mode and forward mode are the same chain rule evaluated in opposite orders; the cheaper order depends entirely on the shapes — many inputs and one output favors reverse, the reverse situation favors forward.

diagrams.purpose: Show that a chain of Jacobians ABCD can be multiplied left-to-right (forward mode) or right-to-left (reverse mode), and that the cheaper order depends on the matrix shapes — this is the geometric heart of the whole lesson.

required_elements.description: Leftmost Jacobian A, drawn as a tall-or-short rectangle whose height represents number of outputs.
Second Jacobian B in the chain.
Third Jacobian C in the chain.
Rightmost Jacobian D, drawn as a tall column-vector-like rectangle (single output case).
Bracket grouping (C times D) first, indicating right-to-left / reverse-mode association producing matrix-vector products.
Bracket grouping (A times B) first, indicating left-to-right / forward-mode association producing matrix-matrix products.
Arrow flowing right-to-left across the chain labeled reverse mode / backprop.
Arrow flowing left-to-right across the chain labeled forward mode.

choreography.narration: Back-propagation can compute the gradient of a billion-parameter network for roughly the price of one forward pass, and yet it is provably not the optimal way to compute a gradient. Both of those are true at once.

The deep learning world grew up a little isolated, and invented its own habits for derivatives. But step outside, and there's an entire field called automatic differentiation whose only job is computing derivatives by algorithm. <<SECTION:Automatic Differentiation|id=sec-ad>>Back-propagation is just one member of that family.

Specifically, back-propagation belongs to a class called reverse mode accumulation: we evaluate the chain rule starting from the output and work backwards toward the inputs. <<WRITE_TEXT:backprop = reverse-mode autodiff|id=text-rev>>Other methods just evaluate the same chain rule pieces in a different order.
Here's the cleanest way to see what order means. Think of the chain rule for a deep composition as a product of Jacobian matrices, A times B times C times D.
Suppose the rightmost factor D is a tall column vector and the leftmost A has many rows: that's a graph with many inputs and a single scalar output, exactly our loss.
So in which order should we multiply this chain to spend the least arithmetic?

Multiply from the right: C times D first. Because D is a vector, every product stays a cheap matrix-times-vector. Keep going right-to-left and you never build a single big matrix-matrix product. That is exactly reverse mode, exactly back-propagation.

Multiply from the left instead, A times B first, and you're grinding out full matrix-matrix products, vastly more expensive when there's only one output. <<WRITE_KEY:Cheapest order depends on the shapes: many inputs, one output favors reverse mode|id=key-shapes>>The answer is identical; only the cost differs.

Flip the situation. If A is short, few outputs, but D is wide, many of them, then multiplying left-to-right is the cheap direction. That is forward mode accumulation, and it also saves memory because you don't store the whole graph.

Now the guarantee that makes reverse mode beloved. When the graph has one output and each local partial derivative costs a constant, every edge's derivative is computed exactly once, with one multiply and one add. So the gradient costs the same order as the forward pass: order, number of edges.

But beloved is not optimal. Picture building a softmax from exponentials, a sum, and a division, then a cross-entropy loss on top. A human spots that the derivative of the loss with respect to a logit collapses to a gorgeous q minus p.

Back-propagation can't see that shortcut. It dutifully pushes gradients through every logarithm and exponential in the graph. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial J}{\partial z_i} = q_i - p_i|id=eq-qmp>>Libraries like Theano and TensorFlow bolt on pattern-matching heuristics to simplify, but plain back-prop won't.

Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose we have variables p one through p n representing probabilities, and variables z one through z n representing unnormalized log probabilities. We define q i equals exp of z i divided by the sum over i of exp of z i — that's the softmax, built out of exponentiation, summation, and division operations. From these we construct a cross-entropy loss J equals negative sum over i of p i times log of q i. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the derivative of the softmax-plus-cross-entropy loss J with respect to z i.|id=ex-q-1>>

A human mathematician looks at this whole expression and notices something beautiful. We start by writing down the loss and the softmax together. <<WRITE_EQUATION:J = -\sum_i p_i \log q_i, \quad q_i = \frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_i \exp(z_i)}|id=ex-eq-1>> When you differentiate J with respect to z i by hand, all the logarithms and exponentials cancel against each other algebraically, and the messy expression collapses. <<WRITE_STEP:Differentiate J w.r.t. z_i; logs and exps cancel|id=ex-step-1-1>>

And the answer is wonderfully simple: the derivative of J with respect to z i equals q i minus p i. <<WRITE_ANSWER:dJ/dz_i = q_i - p_i|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's the catch. Back-propagation cannot spot this shortcut. Instead it will explicitly propagate gradients through every single logarithm and exponentiation operation in the original graph. Some software libraries, such as Theano, can perform some kinds of algebraic substitution to improve over the graph that pure back-propagation proposes.

And finding the truly cheapest evaluation order in general? That's N P complete, because it can require simplifying the algebra into its least expensive form. So nobody has a fast, general optimal method.

One last cultural difference: outside machine learning, people differentiate raw Python or C code directly. Deep learning libraries instead use explicit graph structures, which forces a hand-written backward rule for every operation. That limits you to defined ops, but it lets experts hand-craft clever rules for speed and numerical stability. So back-propagation isn't the only way, nor the optimal way, but it is wonderfully practical and serves us extremely well.

equations.explanation_in_words: The gradient of a deep composition is a product of Jacobian matrices, one per layer, chained from output back to input.
With one scalar output and constant-cost local derivatives, reverse mode computes the whole gradient in time of the same order as the forward pass, growing with the number of edges in the graph.
A human notices the softmax-plus-cross-entropy gradient with respect to a logit simplifies to predicted probability minus true probability — a shortcut pure back-propagation cannot find on its own.

lesson_plans.title: General Back-Propagation: A Graph That Computes Its Own Derivatives

hook.text: Here's a strange idea: instead of building a graph that spits out numbers, what if we built a graph that spits out its own derivatives — and then never had to decide when to run anything?

crucial_facts: Back-propagation is gradient times Jacobian, accumulated backwards through the graph, starting from the seed dz/dz equals one — and where paths merge, the gradients SUM.
Symbol-to-symbol builds a derivative graph whose nodes are themselves differentiable operations, which subsumes symbol-to-number — same computation, but the graph is exposed.

diagrams.purpose: Show a small computational graph with a fork-and-merge so that the backward pass, the Jacobian multiplications, and the summing of gradients at a shared node are all visible on one picture.

required_elements.description: Input variable node x at the bottom, the ancestor we want the gradient with respect to.
Intermediate node y1, one of two operations consuming x.
Intermediate node y2, the second operation consuming x, creating a fork.
Final scalar output node z at the top, where back-propagation seeds dz/dz equals one.
Forward edge from x into y1, carrying the operation whose Jacobian multiplies on the backward pass.
Forward edge from x into y2, the second path.
Forward edge from y1 into z.
Forward edge from y2 into z.
Annotation at node z marking the seed gradient dz/dz equals one.
Annotation at node x showing the two incoming backward gradients being summed.

choreography.narration: Here's a strange idea: instead of building a graph that spits out numbers, what if we built a graph that spits out its own derivatives — and then never had to decide when to run anything?

<<SECTION:Symbol-to-symbol|id=sec-1>>The trick is what each node contains. In the ordinary view, a node holds a number. In the symbol-to-symbol view, a node holds another operation — so the derivatives themselves live inside the graph as differentiable nodes you can keep evaluating.
And because the derivative graph is just more graph, you don't decide ahead of time when each operation fires. A generic engine evaluates any node the instant its parents are ready.
<<SECTION:The backward pass|id=sec-2>>Now the heart of it. Suppose z is our final scalar and we want to know how z responds to some earlier variable x. Where do we even start?

<<WRITE_KEY:Seed the backward pass with dz/dz = 1|id=key-1>>We start at z itself, and we seed the gradient with the most obvious fact in mathematics: the gradient of z with respect to z is one. Anything changes itself one-for-one.
Then we walk backwards along an edge. At each operation, we multiply our current gradient by that operation's Jacobian — the matrix that says how the operation turned its inputs into its outputs.
We keep multiplying Jacobians, edge after edge, traveling backwards through the graph, until we finally arrive at x. That product of Jacobians is the gradient.
But look — x feeds two operations, not one. So going backward, two gradients arrive at x along two different paths.

<<WRITE_STEP:At a shared node, SUM the gradients from every path|id=step-1>>When a node is reached by more than one backward path, you simply add the arriving gradients. That sum is not a detail — it's the chain rule honestly accounting for every way x influenced z.
So the whole rule, written out, is a sum over consumers: for each operation that used x, transpose its Jacobian, apply it to that operation's gradient, and add them all up.
To make this general in code, each node holds a tensor — scalar, vector, matrix, whatever — and knows three things: which operation created it, who its parents are, and who its consumers are.

And every operation carries one back-propagation rule that computes exactly that Jacobian-vector product. Those tiny pieces — seed at one, multiply by Jacobians, sum at the merges — assemble into the entire algorithm.

equations.explanation_in_words: We start the backward pass with the simplest fact there is: the gradient of z with respect to itself is one, because anything changes itself one-for-one.
To get the gradient at any node, take each operation that consumed it, push the gradient backward through that operation's Jacobian, and add up the contributions from every path.

lesson_plans.title: Why Depth Works: Architecture as Prior

hook.text: Take two networks with the exact same number of parameters. Make one shallow and wide, the other deep and narrow. The deep one keeps winning. Why should rearranging the same parameters into more layers matter at all?

crucial_facts: Choosing a deep architecture is itself a prior: it encodes the belief that the target function is a composition of many simpler steps, where later features reuse earlier ones.
Every architectural choice — depth, weight sharing, specialized layers — is a way of expressing a prior that nudges the model toward the solutions we expect to be correct.

diagrams.purpose: Show that a deep network expresses the prior that the target function factors into a composition of reused feature stages, contrasting with a shallow network that must represent everything in one flat layer.

required_elements.description: Input x feeding the network on the left.
A single wide hidden layer representing the shallow network drawn along the top path.
Output of the shallow network on the top path.
First hidden stage of the deep network: low-level features.
Second hidden stage: mid-level features built by composing stage-1 features.
Third hidden stage: high-level features composing stage-2 features.
Output of the deep network on the bottom path.
Arrow highlighting that a later stage reuses and combines features from the previous stage.
A schematic blob of the full space of functions, with a small shaded sub-region representing the compositional functions favored by depth.
The shaded sub-region inside function-space marking the functions the deep prior assigns high preference to.

choreography.narration: Take two networks with the exact same number of parameters. Make one shallow and wide, the other deep and narrow — and the deep one keeps winning. Why should rearranging the same parameters into more layers matter at all?
This isn't a one-off. Across many tasks, holding the parameter count roughly fixed, depth tended to beat width. The empirical result was clear long before the explanation was.

The honest answer comes from one word: a prior. <<SECTION:Depth as a prior|id=sec-1>>A prior is an assumption you bake into the model before it sees a single data point — a belief about what good solutions ought to look like.
Picture the whole space of functions the model could represent. A prior is just a statement that some corner of this space is far more plausible than the rest.

So what corner does depth bet on? Watch the deep path. The input enters, the first stage extracts low-level features, the next stage combines those into mid-level features, the next builds higher-level ones still.

<<WRITE_EQUATION:f(x) = f^{(L)} \circ \cdots \circ f^{(1)}(x)|id=eq-1>>Each layer is a function, and the network is those functions composed in a chain — the output of one becomes the input of the next.
The crucial move is right here. Notice how a later stage doesn't start from scratch — it reuses and recombines whatever the stage below it discovered.

That is the prior. <<WRITE_KEY:Depth = the prior that f is a composition of reused simpler steps|id=key-1>>Choosing depth quietly tells the model: I believe the function we want factors into many simple steps, each one building on the features below it.
Here's the question that makes this matter: why would such an oddly specific assumption ever help? Surely committing to compositional functions just throws away flexibility.

Because the problems we actually care about are built that way. Edges compose into shapes, shapes into objects; phonemes into words, words into meaning. The shaded region the deep prior prefers is exactly where the real-world target functions tend to live.
So depth isn't a lucky trick that happened to work. The structure of deep networks lines up with the structure of the problems, and that alignment is what makes the prior useful.

Carry this framing forward. <<WRITE_TEXT:depth, weight sharing, specialized layers = priors|id=text-1>>Almost every architectural decision you'll meet later — depth, weight sharing, convolution, attention — is the same move: a built-in belief that nudges the model toward the solutions we expect to be correct.

equations.explanation_in_words: A deep network just says the answer is built by passing the input through one stage, then feeding that into the next, again and again — a chain of composed functions.

segments.raw_narration: Here are four points and one rule a child can state in a sentence, yet the best linear model on Earth answers every one with a shrug.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:input-space-axes>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_1:xor_feature_spaces>> Here are four points and one rule a child can state in a sentence, yet the best linear model on Earth answers every one with a shrug. <<POINT:input-space-axes>>

segments.raw_narration: The rule is exclusive or: when exactly one of the two inputs is one, the answer is one; when both agree, the answer is zero.
segments.text_with_markers: The rule is exclusive or: when exactly one of the two inputs is one, the answer is one; when both agree, the answer is zero.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:The linear attempt|id=sec-1>>So let's try the simplest model: take each input, scale it by a weight, add a bias, and read off the prediction.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:point-10>> <<SECTION:The linear attempt|id=sec-1>>So let's try the simplest model: take each input, scale it by a weight, add a bias, and read off the prediction.

segments.raw_narration: We score the model by the average squared gap between its prediction and the true answer across all four points.
segments.text_with_markers: We score the model by the average squared gap between its prediction and the true answer across all four points. <<WRITE_EQUATION:J(\theta) = \frac{1}{4}\sum_{x \in X}\bigl(f^*(x) - f(x;\theta)\bigr)^2|id=eq-1|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: The linear model is just a weighted sum of the inputs plus a constant bias.
segments.text_with_markers: The linear model is just a weighted sum of the inputs plus a constant bias. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f(x; w, b) = x^\top w + b|id=eq-2|boxed>>

The two class-one points pile onto one spot while the class-zero points pull apart — they no longer lie on a single line. <<TRACE:folded-point-cluster>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:separating-line>> <<WRITE_KEY:One ReLU bend folds the points off their line so a linear layer can separate them|id=key-1>>And now a single straight cut does the job. With billions of parameters you cannot guess. So what changes when you have to actually learn them? <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter where we specify a complete solution to the XOR problem. Let W be the two-by-two matrix with all entries equal to one. Let c be the vector with entries zero and negative one. Let w be the vector with entries one and negative two, and let b equal zero. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Solve XOR with W (all ones), c = (0, -1), w = (1, -2), b = 0|id=ex-q-1>> We start by writing down the input matrix X, which contains all four points in the binary input space, one example per row: the rows are zero-zero, zero-one, one-zero, and one-one. Notice that in this space all of the examples lie along a line with slope one. As we move along that line the output needs to start at zero, rise to one, then drop back to zero, and a linear model simply cannot do that. <<WRITE_STEP:XW + c has rows (0,-1), (1,0), (1,0), (2,1)|id=ex-step-1-3>> To finish computing the hidden values, we apply the rectified linear transformation, taking the max of zero and each value, which gives rows zero-zero, one-zero, one-zero, and two-one. segments.raw_narration: Here is something strange: you almost never have to invent a loss function. The moment you decide what your network is allowed to predict, the loss is already chosen for you.
segments.text_with_markers: Here is something strange: you almost never have to invent a loss function. The moment you decide what your network is allowed to predict, the loss is already chosen for you.

segments.raw_narration: Start with the reassuring part. The cost functions we use for deep networks are essentially the same ones we use for linear models. Nothing exotic — you are reusing familiar ideas, just stacked on top of a more flexible function inside.
segments.text_with_markers: Start with the reassuring part. The cost functions we use for deep networks are essentially the same ones we use for linear models. Nothing exotic — you are reusing familiar ideas, just stacked on top of a more flexible function inside.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Maximum Likelihood|id=sec-1>>The key move is that in most cases the network does not output a single number — it outputs an entire conditional distribution, p of y given x, parametrized by theta. Given an input, it tells you how probable every possible answer is.
segments.text_with_markers: <<SECTION:Maximum Likelihood|id=sec-1>>The key move is that in most cases the network does not output a single number — it outputs an entire conditional distribution, p of y given x, parametrized by theta. Given an input, it tells you how probable every possible answer is.

segments.raw_narration: So what should we ask of that distribution? Just this: make the answers that actually appeared in the training data as probable as possible. That single demand is the principle of maximum likelihood.
segments.text_with_markers: So what should we ask of that distribution? Just this: make the answers that actually appeared in the training data as probable as possible. That single demand is the principle of maximum likelihood.

segments.raw_narration: Maximizing a product of probabilities is awkward, so we take the logarithm and flip the sign. <<WRITE_TEXT:cost = average penalty for low probability of the true answer|id=text-1>>Maximizing likelihood becomes minimizing the negative log-likelihood — penalize the model every time it assigns low probability to a correct answer.
segments.text_with_markers: Maximizing a product of probabilities is awkward, so we take the logarithm and flip the sign. <<WRITE_TEXT:cost = average penalty for low probability of the true answer|id=text-1>>Maximizing likelihood becomes minimizing the negative log-likelihood — penalize the model every time it assigns low probability to a correct answer.

segments.raw_narration: Written as an expectation over the training data, the cost is the negative expected log-probability the model assigns to the true outputs. This quantity is exactly the cross-entropy between the data distribution and the model.

segments.raw_narration: Now the beautiful consequence. Once you have committed to a form for p of y given x, there is nothing left to choose. The negative log of that distribution IS your cost function.

segments.raw_narration: Because depth is not extra power — it is a belief. <<WRITE_KEY:Depth encodes a prior: target = composition of many simpler functions|id=key-depth>>Choosing a deep model says you believe the function you want is built by composing many simpler functions: edges into corners, corners into shapes, or one sequential step feeding the next.

segments.raw_narration: When that belief matches reality, depth gives you generalization almost for free, while the wide model just memorizes. <<WRITE_TEXT:wide -> memorize; deep -> compose|id=text-prior>>That is why the same parameter count pays off so differently.

segments.raw_narration: Here is the main chain — input, layer i, i plus one, i plus two. Now add a skip connection: an edge that jumps from layer i straight to layer i plus two.

segments.raw_narration: Why bother? Remember that during training the gradient flows backward from the output toward the input. The skip edge gives that gradient a shortcut — a second, shorter path home, so it arrives at the early layers without being squeezed through every step.

segments.raw_narration: The second lever is how you wire a pair of layers. The default is fully connected: every input unit touches every output unit — maximum parameters, maximum computation.

segments.raw_narration: But you can deliberately make it sparse, so each input only connects to a small local group of outputs. Convolutional networks do exactly this — far fewer parameters, far less computation, and a pattern tuned to the structure of images.

segments.raw_narration: So the real lesson is this: architecture is how you spend your parameters and steer your gradients. <<WRITE_KEY:Architecture = controlling gradient flow + spending parameters wisely|id=key-arch>>Skip connections and sparse wiring are not decoration — they decide whether the gradient can flow and whether the parameters are spent on the right assumptions.

segments.raw_narration: A modern network has hundreds of millions of weights, and to take one training step you need the derivative of the loss with respect to every single one of them. Naively that's hundreds of millions of separate calculations — so how does a network train in milliseconds?

But step outside, and there's an entire field called automatic differentiation whose only job is computing derivatives by algorithm. <<SECTION:Automatic Differentiation|id=sec-ad>>Back-propagation is just one member of that family. Specifically, back-propagation belongs to a class called reverse mode accumulation: we evaluate the chain rule starting from the output and work backwards toward the inputs. <<WRITE_TEXT:backprop = reverse-mode autodiff|id=text-rev>>Other methods just evaluate the same chain rule pieces in a different order. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:matrix-A>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_9:jacobian_chain>> Here's the cleanest way to see what order means. segments.raw_narration: Here's a strange idea: instead of building a graph that spits out numbers, what if we built a graph that spits out its own derivatives — and then never had to decide when to run anything?

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Symbol-to-symbol|id=sec-1>>The trick is what each node contains. In the ordinary view, a node holds a number. In the symbol-to-symbol view, a node holds another operation — so the derivatives themselves live inside the graph as differentiable nodes you can keep evaluating.

segments.raw_narration: And because the derivative graph is just more graph, you don't decide ahead of time when each operation fires. A generic engine evaluates any node the instant its parents are ready.

segments.raw_narration: We start the backward pass with the simplest fact there is: the gradient of z with respect to itself is one, because anything changes itself one-for-one.
segments.text_with_markers: We start the backward pass with the simplest fact there is: the gradient of z with respect to itself is one, because anything changes itself one-for-one. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial z}{\partial z} = 1|id=eq-1|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Seed the backward pass with dz/dz = 1|id=key-1>>We start at z itself, and we seed the gradient with the most obvious fact in mathematics: the gradient of z with respect to z is one. Anything changes itself one-for-one.

segments.raw_narration: Then we walk backwards along an edge. At each operation, we multiply our current gradient by that operation's Jacobian — the matrix that says how the operation turned its inputs into its outputs.
segments.text_with_markers: Then we walk backwards along an edge. At each operation, we multiply our current gradient by that operation's Jacobian — the matrix that says how the operation turned its inputs into its outputs. <<TRACE:edge-y1-z>>

segments.raw_narration: We keep multiplying Jacobians, edge after edge, traveling backwards through the graph, until we finally arrive at x. That product of Jacobians is the gradient.
segments.text_with_markers: We keep multiplying Jacobians, edge after edge, traveling backwards through the graph, until we finally arrive at x. That product of Jacobians is the gradient. <<TRACE:edge-x-y1>>

segments.raw_narration: To get the gradient at any node, take each operation that consumed it, push the gradient backward through that operation's Jacobian, and add up the contributions from every path.
segments.text_with_markers: To get the gradient at any node, take each operation that consumed it, push the gradient backward through that operation's Jacobian, and add up the contributions from every path. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} z = \sum_{i} \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}_i}{\partial \mathbf{x}} \right)^{\top} \nabla_{\mathbf{y}_i} z|id=eq-2|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: But look — x feeds two operations, not one. So going backward, two gradients arrive at x along two different paths.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:edge-x-y2>> But look — x feeds two operations, not one. So going backward, two gradients arrive at x along two different paths. <<TRACE:edge-x-y2>> <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_STEP:At a shared node, SUM the gradients from every path|id=step-1>>When a node is reached by more than one backward path, you simply add the arriving gradients. That sum is not a detail — it's the chain rule honestly accounting for every way x influenced z.

That sum is not a detail — it's the chain rule honestly accounting for every way x influenced z. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: So the whole rule, written out, is a sum over consumers: for each operation that used x, transpose its Jacobian, apply it to that operation's gradient, and add them all up.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:node-x>> So the whole rule, written out, is a sum over consumers: for each operation that used x, transpose its Jacobian, apply it to that operation's gradient, and add them all up. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: To make this general in code, each node holds a tensor — scalar, vector, matrix, whatever — and knows three things: which operation created it, who its parents are, and who its consumers are.
