The input enters, the first stage extracts low-level features, the next stage combines those into mid-level features, the next builds higher-level ones still. <<TRACE:deep-stage-1>> A deep network just says the answer is built by passing the input through one stage, then feeding that into the next, again and again — a chain of composed functions. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f(x) = f^{(L)} \circ f^{(L-1)} \circ \cdots \circ f^{(1)}(x)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:deep-stage-3>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:f(x) = f^{(L)} \circ \cdots \circ f^{(1)}(x)|id=eq-1>>Each layer is a function, and the network is those functions composed in a chain — the output of one becomes the input of the next. <<POINT:deep-stage-3>> <<FOCUS:reuse-arrow>> The crucial move is right here. Notice how a later stage doesn't start from scratch — it reuses and recombines whatever the stage below it discovered. <<POINT:reuse-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:favored-region>> That is the prior. <<WRITE_KEY:Depth = the prior that f is a composition of reused simpler steps|id=key-1>>Choosing depth quietly tells the model: I believe the function we want factors into many simple steps, each one building on the features below it. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:function-space>> Here's the question that makes this matter: why would such an oddly specific assumption ever help? Surely committing to compositional functions just throws away flexibility. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:favored-region>> Because the problems we actually care about are built that way. Edges compose into shapes, shapes into objects; phonemes into words, words into meaning. The shaded region the deep prior prefers is exactly where the real-world target functions tend to live. <<TRACE:favored-region>> So depth isn't a lucky trick that happened to work. The structure of deep networks lines up with the structure of the problems, and that alignment is what makes the prior useful. <<POINT:reuse-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:function-space>> Carry this framing forward. <<WRITE_TEXT:depth, weight sharing, specialized layers = priors|id=text-1>>Almost every architectural decision you'll meet later — depth, weight sharing, convolution, attention — is the same move: a built-in belief that nudges the model toward the solutions we expect to be correct. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.our_understanding:
Let's start with a wonderfully simple problem that reveals something deep about neural networks: learning the XOR function. XOR stands for exclusive or, and it works on two inputs that are each either zero or one. The rule is this: when exactly one of the two inputs is one, XOR gives back one. If both are zero, or both are one, it gives back zero. So out of the four possible input pairs, two of them produce one, and two produce zero. That's the target we want our network to learn.

Here's the thing about this example: we're not worried about generalizing to new data. We have exactly four input points, and we just want our network to get all four right. The only challenge is fitting these four points perfectly.

To measure how well we're doing, we use mean squared error. That means we look at the difference between what the network predicts and the true answer, square that difference, and average it over all four points. The authors are honest with us here: mean squared error isn't really the right choice for binary data in real applications, but it keeps the math simple for teaching.

Now comes the interesting part. Suppose we try the simplest possible model, a linear model. A linear model takes each input, multiplies it by a weight, adds them up, and adds a constant called the bias. When we solve this perfectly using the normal equations, we discover something disappointing. The best the linear model can do is output zero point five everywhere. It just gives up and predicts the same middle value for every single input.

Why does this happen? Because XOR simply cannot be drawn as a straight line separating the ones from the zeros. No matter how you place a line, you can't cleanly split those four points the right way. This is the famous limitation of linear models.

So what's the fix? We need a model that first transforms the inputs into a new feature space, a new way of representing them, where a straight line can do the job. That's exactly what a hidden layer in a neural network does. The authors introduce a tiny feedforward network with one hidden layer containing two hidden units. By learning new features first, the network can then solve XOR with a simple linear step on top. This little example is the seed of why deep networks are so powerful.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's build up the idea of why neural networks need something special inside them. Imagine you have a simple feedforward network. It takes your input, let's call it x, and runs it through a first function to produce a layer of hidden units, which we call h. Then those hidden units get fed into a second function, the output layer, which is just a linear regression model. So you've got two functions chained together: the first one turns x into h, and the second one turns h into your final prediction y.

Now here's the big question. What should that first function do? You might think, since linear models have worked nicely so far, let's just make the first function linear too. But here's the catch, and it's important. If the first function is linear and the second is linear, then the whole network is still just one big linear function. Think about it this way: if h equals W times x, and y equals h times w, then the whole thing is just x times the product of W and w. You can fold those two weight matrices into a single set of weights. So you gained nothing. Stacking linear on top of linear is still linear.

That tells us we must use a nonlinear function to describe our features. The trick most neural networks use is this: first do an affine transformation, which means multiply by a weight matrix and add a bias, and then apply a fixed nonlinear function called an activation function. So we define h as g applied to W times x plus c, where W holds the weights and c holds the biases. Notice that since we're now producing a whole vector h instead of a single number, we need a whole vector of biases, not just one scalar.

The activation function g is usually applied element by element, so each hidden unit gets the activation function applied to its own affine combination. And what should g be? In modern networks the default recommendation is the rectified linear unit, or ReLU. It's beautifully simple: g of z equals the maximum of zero and z. In plain words, if the number is positive, keep it; if it's negative, turn it into zero. That little kink is the nonlinearity that gives the network its real power, letting it learn representations that a plain linear model never could.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about cost functions, which are at the heart of how a neural network learns. A cost function is basically a score that tells the network how badly it's doing. The whole point of training is to make that score as small as possible. Here's the good news: the cost functions we use for deep neural networks are pretty much the same ones we use for simpler models, like linear models. So you're not learning something brand new and exotic — you're reusing familiar ideas.

In most cases, our network defines a probability distribution. That means, given some input x, the network predicts how likely different outputs y are. When we set things up this way, we use a principle called maximum likelihood. The idea is simple: we want the network to assign high probability to the answers that actually appeared in our training data. The cost function that does this is called the cross-entropy between the training data and the model's predictions. Another way to say the same thing is that the cost is the negative log-likelihood. Think of it as a penalty: the network gets penalized whenever it assigns low probability to a correct answer.

Now here's something beautiful. Once you decide what kind of distribution your model predicts, the cost function is automatically determined. You don't have to invent a clever cost function from scratch for every new model. For example, if your model predicts a Gaussian — a bell-shaped distribution centered on its guess — then maximum likelihood gives you back the familiar mean squared error, the average of the squared differences between the true value and the prediction. That equivalence holds no matter how complicated the function inside is.

There's one more practical insight worth remembering. For learning to work well, the gradient of the cost — basically the slope that tells the network which way to adjust — must be large and predictable enough to guide the algorithm. When a function saturates, meaning it becomes very flat, the gradient shrinks toward zero and learning stalls. Many output units use an exponential function that can saturate when its input gets very negative. The negative log-likelihood is helpful here because the logarithm inside it undoes that exponential, keeping the gradient healthy. Often, the total cost also includes a regularization term, like weight decay, to keep the model well behaved.

The discarded constant is based on the variance of the Gaussian distribution, which in this case we chose not to parametrize.

topics.standalone_narration_text: Here is something strange: you almost never have to invent a loss function. The moment you decide what your network is allowed to predict, the loss is already chosen for you. Start with the reassuring part. The cost functions we use for deep networks are essentially the same ones we use for linear models. Nothing exotic — you are reusing familiar ideas, just stacked on top of a more flexible function inside. <<SECTION:Maximum Likelihood|id=sec-1>>The key move is that in most cases the network does not output a single number — it outputs an entire conditional distribution, p of y given x, parametrized by theta. Given an input, it tells you how probable every possible answer is. So what should we ask of that distribution? Just this: make the answers that actually appeared in the training data as probable as possible. That single demand is the principle of maximum likelihood. Maximizing a product of probabilities is awkward, so we take the logarithm and flip the sign. <<WRITE_TEXT:cost = average penalty for low probability of the true answer|id=text-1>>Maximizing likelihood becomes minimizing the negative log-likelihood — penalize the model every time it assigns low probability to a correct answer. Written as an expectation over the training data, the cost is the negative expected log-probability the model assigns to the true outputs. This quantity is exactly the cross-entropy between the data distribution and the model. The cost is the negative expected log-probability the model assigns to the true outputs — that is the cross-entropy between the data and the model. <<WRITE_EQUATION:J(\theta) = -\mathbb{E}_{x,y\sim\hat{p}_{\text{data}}}\,\log p_{\text{model}}(y\mid x)|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now the beautiful consequence. Once you have committed to a form for p of y given x, there is nothing left to choose. The negative log of that distribution IS your cost function. <<PAUSE:long>> Let me make that concrete. Suppose your model predicts a Gaussian centered on its guess f of x — a bell curve whose mean is the network's output. What cost does maximum likelihood hand back? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Write down the log of a Gaussian and almost everything is a constant. <<WRITE_EQUATION:J(\theta) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\,\lVert y - f(x;\theta)\rVert^2 + \text{const}|id=eq-mse>>What survives is one half the squared distance between the true value and the prediction — the mean squared error. You did not invent it; it fell out. <<PAUSE:short>> And this equivalence does not care how complicated f is. Linear model, hundred-layer network — if it predicts the mean of a Gaussian, maximum likelihood gives you mean squared error. <<WRITE_KEY:Choose the distribution, and its negative log-likelihood IS the loss.|id=key-1>>Specifying the distribution automatically determines the cost. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:sigmoid-curve>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_2_1:saturation_gradient_plot>> <<SECTION:Keeping the Gradient Alive|id=sec-2>>There is one more reason this framework is not just elegant but practical. For learning to work, the gradient must stay large and informative. Look at a typical output unit, the sigmoid: out in the far negative region it flattens completely. <<TRACE:sigmoid-curve>> <<FOCUS:saturated-region>> In that flat tail the slope is essentially zero. If our loss lived directly on this curve, the gradient would vanish and learning would simply stall — the model would get no signal to correct a confident, wrong prediction. <<POINT:saturated-region>> <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose our model's conditional distribution is a Gaussian, that is, p model of y given x equals the normal distribution N of y, with mean f of x semicolon theta, and covariance the identity matrix. So the mean of the Gaussian is exactly the network output f of x semicolon theta, and the covariance is the identity matrix. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: If p_model(y|x) = N(y; f(x;theta), I), what cost function do we recover from maximum likelihood?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by taking the negative log likelihood of this Gaussian. When you write out the log of a normal density, you get the squared difference between y and f of x semicolon theta, scaled by one half, plus a constant term that does not depend on theta. <<WRITE_STEP:-log p_model(y|x) = (1/2) ||y - f(x;theta)||^2 + const|id=ex-step-1-1>> That leading term is just the mean squared error, the squared difference between y and f of x semicolon theta, carrying the scaling factor of one half. The constant term comes from the variance of the Gaussian, which in this case we chose not to parametrize, so it does not depend on theta and we discard it. And the answer is that maximum likelihood here reduces to the mean squared error cost: J of theta equals one half, the expectation over x and y of the squared norm of y minus f of x semicolon theta, plus a constant, up to a scaling factor of one half and a term that does not depend on theta. <<WRITE_ANSWER:J(theta) = (1/2) E_{x,y ~ p_data} ||y - f(x;theta)||^2 + const  (mean squared error)|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:nll-curve>> Here is the rescue. The sigmoid hides an exp of a negative argument, which is exactly what saturates. The log in negative log-likelihood undoes that exp. <<TRACE:nll-curve>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:nll-slope-marker>> So instead of flattening, the cost keeps climbing with a steep, predictable slope right where the model is most wrong. The logarithm cancels the exponential and the gradient stays healthy. In practice you then add a regularization term, like weight decay, to keep the whole model well behaved. <<POINT:nll-slope-marker>> <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.our_understanding:
Let's start with a strange but important fact about the cross-entropy cost we use for maximum likelihood. Most of the time, this cost doesn't actually have a true minimum value. Think about a model predicting probabilities for discrete outputs, like logistic regression. Such a model can never quite output a probability of exactly zero or exactly one, but it can creep closer and closer. For real-valued outputs, if the model can learn how spread out its predictions are, it can pack an enormous amount of probability density right onto the correct training answers, and the cross-entropy can plunge toward negative infinity. That's why we need regularization later on, to stop the model from chasing this unlimited reward.

Now, sometimes we don't want the whole probability distribution. We just want one summary number, like the average value of y given x. If our network is powerful enough, we can think of it as able to represent almost any function. From that view, the cost function becomes a functional, which is just a rule that maps a whole function to a single number. So learning becomes choosing a good function, not just tuning numbers. There's a tool called calculus of variations for this, and you don't need to master it. You only need two results. First, if you minimize the mean squared error, the best function predicts the mean, the expected value, of y for each x. Second, if you minimize the mean absolute error instead, the best function predicts the median of y for each x. Different cost functions reward different statistics.

But both mean squared error and mean absolute error often behave poorly with gradient-based learning, because some output units saturate and produce tiny gradients. That's a big reason cross-entropy is so popular.

This brings us to output units. The cost function and the output unit are tightly linked. Linear units, which are just an affine transformation with no nonlinearity, are great for producing the mean of a Gaussian. With them, maximizing log-likelihood is the same as minimizing mean squared error, and since linear units never saturate, optimization stays smooth.

For binary outputs, we use a Bernoulli distribution, where the network only needs to predict the probability that y equals one. That number must stay between zero and one. If you just clip a linear unit to that range, the gradient becomes zero whenever you stray outside, leaving the learner with no guidance. Instead, we use a sigmoid output unit, which squashes the value smoothly and keeps a strong gradient even when the model is wrong.

topics.standalone_narration_text: Here is something strange about the cross-entropy cost we train almost every classifier with: most of the time, it has no minimum. You can always make it smaller, forever. <<PAUSE:short>> Think of logistic regression. To drive the cross-entropy down, the model wants to output a probability of exactly one on the correct class. But a sigmoid can only creep toward one — it never gets there, so there is always a little more reward to chase. <<WRITE_TEXT:cross-entropy has no true minimum|id=text-1>>For real-valued outputs it is even sharper. Let the model learn how spread out its predictions are, and it can pile unbounded probability density right onto the training answers, sending the cross-entropy toward negative infinity. That is exactly why we will later need regularization. <<PAUSE:short>> Now step back. Often we do not want the whole distribution — we want one summary number, like the average value of y given x. If the network is powerful enough to represent essentially any function, then the cost stops being a function of a few parameters and becomes a functional: a rule that takes an entire function and returns one number. <<SECTION:Which statistic does the cost reward?|id=sec-1>>So learning is now choosing a function. And here is the first quiet result from the calculus of variations: which function wins depends entirely on which cost you picked. So — if you minimize mean squared error, what function does the optimizer settle on? <<PAUSE:long>> If you minimize mean squared error over all possible functions, the winning function at every input is the one that returns the average value of y there. <<WRITE_EQUATION:f^* = \arg\min_f \; \mathbb{E}_{x,y \sim p_{\text{data}}} \, \lVert y - f(x) \rVert^2 \;\Rightarrow\; f^*(x) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_{\text{data}}(y \mid x)}[y]|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:MSE to mean, MAE to median|id=key-1>>It settles on the conditional mean: at every input x, the best function returns the expected value of y there. Switch to mean absolute error and you get a different statistic entirely — the conditional median. The cost function literally chooses what the network learns. <<PAUSE:short>> This is why the cost and the output unit are tied together at the hip. Suppose we want that conditional mean for real-valued targets. We model y as a Gaussian whose mean is produced by a plain linear layer — an affine map, no nonlinearity. <<PAUSE:short>> For real-valued targets we model y as Gaussian with a mean produced by a plain linear layer, and maximizing its log-likelihood is exactly minimizing mean squared error. <<WRITE_EQUATION:p(y \mid x) = \mathcal{N}(y; \hat{y}, I), \quad \hat{y} = Wh + b|id=eq-2|boxed>> Maximizing the log-likelihood of that Gaussian is then identical to minimizing mean squared error. And because a linear unit never saturates — its slope is constant everywhere — the gradient never dies, so optimization stays smooth. <<SECTION:Binary outputs and the sigmoid|id=sec-2>>But now switch to a binary target. We model y with a Bernoulli distribution, so the network only needs one number: the probability that y equals one. And that number is trapped — it must live between zero and one. <<FOCUS:clipped-curve>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_2_2:saturation_vs_sigmoid>> The naive fix is to take a linear unit and just clip it into that interval. Watch what that costs us. Out here on the flat shoulders, where the model is confidently wrong, the curve is perfectly flat — the slope is exactly zero. <<TRACE:clipped-curve>> <<POINT:clipped-curve>> <<FOCUS:dead-gradient-region>> A zero gradient is a catastrophe: the learning algorithm gets no signal telling it which way to move. Right when the model is most wrong, it learns nothing. <<POINT:dead-gradient-region>> For a binary target we squash the linear pre-activation through the logistic sigmoid so the output is always a valid probability with a gradient that never dies. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\hat{y} = \sigma(w^\top h + b)|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<FOCUS:sigmoid-curve>> The sigmoid solves exactly this. It also approaches zero and one, but it never goes flat — it only asymptotes. So even a badly wrong prediction sits on a curve with real slope. <<TRACE:sigmoid-curve>> <<FOCUS:wrong-answer-point>> Look at this point: the true label is one, but the model outputs almost zero. On the clipped unit this lives on a dead shoulder. On the sigmoid, paired with cross-entropy, there is still a strong gradient pulling it back toward the right answer. <<POINT:wrong-answer-point>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> So the whole chain locks together: the cost functional picks the statistic, and the output unit keeps the gradient alive while it learns. Linear units give you the Gaussian mean, sigmoid units give you a Bernoulli probability — and cross-entropy, even without a minimum, beats squared error precisely because saturating units would otherwise strangle the gradient. <<PAUSE:short>>

Gradient-Based Learning
Designing and training a neural network is not much diﬀerent from training any
other machine learning model with gradient descent. In section

how to build a machine learning algorithm by specifying an optimization procedure,
a cost function, and a model family.
The largest diﬀerence between the linear models we have seen so far and neural
networks is that the nonlinearity of a neural network causes most interesting loss
functions to become non-convex. This means that neural networks are usually
trained by using iterative, gradient-based optimizers that merely drive the cost
function to a very low value, rather than the linear equation solvers used to train
linear regression models or the convex optimization algorithms with global conver-

important to initialize all weights to small random values. The biases may be

topics.our_understanding: In this section, we finally pull all the pieces together and write down a complete little neural network that can solve the famous XOR problem. Remember, XOR is the puzzle where a plain straight-line model just can't separate the answers. The trick is to add a hidden layer with a nonlinear bend in it. Our whole network looks like this in words: you take the input, multiply it by a first weight matrix, add a bias, then squash it through a function that keeps positive numbers but turns negative numbers into zero. That squashing function is called the rectified linear unit, or ReLU. After that, you multiply by a second set of weights and add a final bias to get the output. The ReLU is almost a straight line, but it has one bend at zero, and that little bend is enough to give the network the power it needs. The book makes a lovely point here: just like a computer can build everything out of zeros and ones, we can build a universal function approximator out of these simple rectified linear pieces. Now, the beautiful part of this section is watching the network actually do its work. We hand it all four XOR inputs at once, stacked into a matrix, and we walk through each step: multiply by the first weights, add the bias, apply the ReLU bend, then multiply by the final weights. After the ReLU, something important happens. The four points, which used to lie along a single straight line, get rearranged so that a straight-line model can finally separate them. By the end, the network produces exactly the right answer for every input. The book is honest with you, though. Here we simply guessed the perfect solution to show it works. In real life, there might be billions of parameters and you can't just guess. Instead, you let a gradient-based optimization algorithm search for good parameters. The big difference from the simple models you've seen before is that neural networks have this nonlinearity, which makes the loss surface bumpy, or non-convex. That means gradient descent isn't guaranteed to find the perfect answer the way convex methods are. So we start the weights at small random values, set the biases to zero or small positive numbers, and let the algorithm gradually descend the cost. It usually won't land on a clean, tidy, integer answer like the one we wrote down by hand, but it will find a set of parameters that works very well.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about one of the most important building blocks in modern neural networks: the rectified linear unit, often called the ReLU. The idea is beautifully simple. The activation function takes an input and outputs the maximum of zero and that input. So if the input is positive, it just passes it straight through. If the input is negative or zero, it outputs zero. That's it.

Now why do people love this so much? Because it's almost like a plain linear function, and linear functions are easy to optimize. The only twist is that across half its domain, when the input is negative, the ReLU outputs zero. Whenever the unit is active, meaning the input is positive, the derivative is exactly one, and the second derivative is zero almost everywhere. That means the gradient flows through cleanly and consistently. There are no weird second-order effects messing up the learning direction, so the network learns more smoothly.

In practice, you use a ReLU on top of an affine transformation, which is just a weighted sum of the inputs plus a bias. A neat trick when you set up the network is to initialize all the bias values to a small positive number, like zero point one. This makes it likely that most units start out active, so gradients can pass through right from the beginning of training.

There's one drawback. If a unit's output is stuck at zero, it gets no gradient, so it can't learn from those examples. To fix this, people invented generalizations that give a small non-zero slope when the input is negative. The leaky ReLU uses a tiny fixed slope like zero point zero one. The parametric ReLU lets that slope be a learnable parameter. And absolute value rectification fixes the slope to negative one, which gives you the absolute value of the input, useful for image features that shouldn't care about light polarity.

Then there's the maxout unit, which goes even further. Instead of applying a function to each value separately, it splits the inputs into groups and outputs the maximum value in each group. This lets the network actually learn its own activation shape, building a piecewise linear convex function with up to k pieces. With enough pieces, it can approximate almost any convex function. The cost is more parameters, so maxout units usually need more regularization, but they also resist a problem called catastrophic forgetting.

The big lesson tying all of this together is that models are easier to train when their behavior stays close to linear. That same principle even helps recurrent networks, like the LSTM, which passes information through time using simple summation.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about two activation functions that were the stars of neural networks before rectified linear units came along: the logistic sigmoid and the hyperbolic tangent, which we usually just call tanh. The sigmoid takes any input and squashes it into a value between zero and one. The tanh does something similar but squashes its input into a value between negative one and positive one. These two are actually close cousins. In fact, you can write tanh in terms of sigmoid: tanh of z equals two times sigmoid of two z, minus one. So they're really the same shape, just stretched and shifted.

Now here's the key idea you need to hold onto: the word saturate. Both of these functions saturate across most of their range. What does that mean? When the input is very large and positive, the function flattens out near its top value. When the input is very large and negative, it flattens out near its bottom value. The function only really responds, only really changes much, when the input is near zero. Everywhere else it's nearly flat. And when something is nearly flat, its slope, its gradient, is close to zero. That's a big problem, because neural networks learn by following gradients. If the gradient is tiny almost everywhere, learning crawls to a halt. This is why we now discourage using sigmoid units as hidden units inside feedforward networks.

They're still fine as output units, though, as long as you pair them with a cost function that cancels out the saturation. We saw that earlier with predicting the probability of a binary outcome.

If you really must use a sigmoidal function in a hidden layer, tanh is usually the better choice. Here's why: tanh of zero equals zero, while sigmoid of zero equals one half. Because tanh passes through zero and behaves like the identity function near zero, a deep network built from tanh layers, when its activations stay small, behaves almost like a simple linear model. That similarity makes training easier in the early stages.

Finally, notice that sigmoidal functions still shine outside of feedforward networks. Recurrent networks, many probabilistic models, and some autoencoders have special requirements that rule out piecewise linear functions, so sigmoidal units remain appealing there, saturation and all.

6.3.3
Other Hidden Units
Many other types of hidden units are possible, but are used less frequently.
In general, a wide variety of diﬀerentiable functions perform perfectly well.
Many unpublished activation functions perform just as well as the popular ones.
To provide a concrete example, the authors tested a feedforward network using
h = cos(Wx + b) on the MNIST dataset and obtained an error rate of less than
1%, which is competitive with results obtained using more conventional activation
functions. During research and development of new techniques, it is common
to test many diﬀerent activation functions and ﬁnd that several variations on
standard practice perform comparably. This means that usually new hidden unit
types are published only if they are clearly demonstrated to provide a signiﬁcant
improvement. New hidden unit types that perform roughly comparably to known
types are so common as to be uninteresting.
It would be impractical to list all of the hidden unit types that have appeared
in the literature. We highlight a few especially useful and distinctive ones.
One possibility is to not have an activation g(z) at all. One can also think of
this as using the identity function as the activation function. We have already
seen that a linear unit can be useful as the output of a neural network. It may
also be used as a hidden unit. If every layer of the neural network consists of only
linear transformations, then the network as a whole will be linear. However, it
is acceptable for some layers of the neural network to be purely linear. Consider
a neural network layer with n inputs and p outputs, h = g(W x + b). We may

Another key design consideration for neural networks is determining the architecture.
The word architecture refers to the overall structure of the network: how many
units it should have and how these units should be connected to each other.

topics.our_understanding:
In this section, the textbook steps back and reminds us of something important: rectified linear units and sigmoids are not the only choices for hidden units. In fact, an enormous variety of differentiable functions work perfectly well as activation functions. Many activation functions that never even got published would do the job just fine. To prove the point, the authors ran a feedforward network on the famous MNIST handwritten-digit dataset using the cosine of W times x plus b as the activation, and they got an error rate of less than one percent. That's competitive with the usual choices! The lesson here is honest and a little humbling: because so many functions work about equally well, researchers usually only bother publishing a new hidden unit type when it clearly beats the existing ones. New units that merely tie with old units are so common that nobody finds them interesting.

The section then highlights a few distinctive units. First, you can choose to have no activation at all, which is the same as using the identity function. We've seen linear units used at the output, but they can also be used in hidden layers. If every layer were purely linear, the whole network would just be one big linear function. But it's fine for some layers to be linear. Here's the clever trick: if you take a layer that turns n inputs into p outputs and split it into two linear stages with an intermediate size of q, you're factoring the big weight matrix into two smaller ones. The original needs n times p parameters, but the factored version needs only n plus p, all times q. When q is small, that's a big savings. The cost is that you've forced the transformation to be low rank, but often that's good enough.

The section also mentions softmax units, which usually act as outputs but can serve as a kind of switch inside advanced memory networks. Then it lists a few more units: radial basis function units, which fire when the input is close to a template but saturate to zero almost everywhere, making them hard to optimize; softplus, a smooth version of the rectifier that, counterintuitively, performs worse than the plain rectifier despite being smooth everywhere; and hard tanh, which simply clamps its input between negative one and one. The big takeaway: hidden unit design is still an open, active research area, and the best architecture for any task is found through experimentation, watching your validation error.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's start by tying off a loose end from the previous discussion. Sometimes we want a neural network to predict something much bigger than a single number or a single category. Imagine you want the network to output a whole sentence, a sequence of characters strung together. To handle that, we still use the same guiding idea we've leaned on all along, called maximum likelihood, where we set up a probability model for the output given the input and then push the network to make the real answers as likely as possible. But the models we'd need for rich, structured outputs like sequences get complicated fast, so the book sets those aside for later chapters. There's also a neat picture worth mentioning, where a network learns a mixture of several bell-shaped Gaussian distributions and lets all their means, spreads, and mixing probabilities change in nonlinear ways depending on the input.

Now we shift to something special to feedforward networks: how to choose the hidden units, the little computing pieces in the middle layers. Here's an honest truth the book shares: this is an active research area without many firm rules. The practical advice is simple, though. The rectified linear unit, which just outputs zero when its input is negative and outputs the input itself when it's positive, is an excellent default. There are many other choices, and you usually can't predict in advance which works best. So the real method is trial and error: pick a unit you think might work, train the network, and check how it does on a validation set.

There's a subtle worry to address. The rectified linear function has a sharp corner at zero, where the slope suddenly jumps. At that exact point it isn't differentiable, meaning the gradient isn't cleanly defined. You might think that breaks gradient-based learning. In practice, it doesn't matter. Training never actually lands exactly on that corner, and software just returns one of the one-sided slopes anyway. Think about it: the left derivative at zero is zero and the right derivative is one, and the computer simply picks one. Because computers already round numbers and carry tiny errors, the value was almost never truly exactly zero. So we can safely ignore these non-differentiable points.

One last framing: most hidden units work the same basic way. They take an input vector, compute an affine transformation, which means multiply by a weight matrix and add a bias, and then apply some nonlinear function element by element. What distinguishes one hidden unit from another is mostly just the choice of that nonlinear activation function.

topics.standalone_narration_text: The rectified linear unit has a sharp corner at zero where its derivative literally does not exist. So why is it the single most trusted building block in modern deep learning? But before we open up that unit, let's tie off a loose end. Everything we have built so far predicts a single number or a single category — yet sometimes we want a network to output something far richer, like a whole sentence, a sequence of characters strung together. The guiding idea does not change at all: we still write down a probability model for the output given the input, p of y given the parameters omega of x, and we push the network to make the real answers as likely as possible. <<SECTION:Rich structured outputs|id=sec-outputs>>That is still pure maximum likelihood. What changes is that the model for a structured y gets complicated fast — so we set those cases aside for later chapters. There is one beautiful picture worth holding onto, though: a network can output the parameters of a mixture of several Gaussian bells, letting every mean, every spread, and every mixing weight bend nonlinearly with the input. Now we turn to something special to feedforward networks: how to choose the hidden units, those little computing pieces in the middle layers. And here is an honest truth — this is an active research area with very few firm theoretical rules. So what is the practical method, if theory can't tell us which unit is best in advance? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> It is trial and error, plain and simple. You intuit that some unit might work, you train the network with it, and you check its performance on a validation set. And the default you reach for first, almost always, is the rectified linear unit. <<SECTION:The anatomy of a hidden unit|id=sec-anatomy>>Here is the unifying view. Strip away the names, and almost every hidden unit does the same three things: it takes an input vector x, computes an affine transformation — multiply by a weight matrix W and add a bias b — and then applies a nonlinear function g element by element. <<PAUSE:short>> A hidden unit takes the input vector, multiplies it by a weight matrix and adds a bias to get z, then applies the nonlinearity g element by element to get the unit's output. <<WRITE_EQUATION:z = Wx + b, \quad h = g(z)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Hidden unit = affine transform then element-wise nonlinearity; only g changes|id=key-anatomy>>So the entire zoo of hidden units differs in essentially one place: the choice of that activation function g. Everything else is shared scaffolding. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:relu-curve>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_4:relu_corner>> Now back to our opening puzzle. Let's actually draw the most common g, the rectified linear unit: g of z equals the max of zero and z. <<WRITE_EQUATION:g(z) = \max\{0, z\}|id=eq-relu>> <<TRACE:relu-curve>> <<FOCUS:kink-point>> Watch what happens right here at the origin. To the left, the function is flat, so its slope — the left derivative — is exactly zero. To the right, it climbs at forty-five degrees, so the right derivative is exactly one. The two don't match, and that is precisely what makes the function non-differentiable at this corner. <<POINT:kink-point>> <<POINT:kink-point>> Just to the left of zero the slope is zero, and just to the right of zero the slope is one — the left and right derivatives disagree, which is exactly why the function is not differentiable at the corner. <<WRITE_EQUATION:g'_-(0) = 0, \quad g'_+(0) = 1|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:left-slope-label>> You might think that single broken point kills gradient descent. Here is why it doesn't. <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. Take the rectified linear function, g of z, which outputs the maximum of zero and z. The book points out that this function is not differentiable at z equals zero. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Is g(z) = max(0, z) differentiable at z = 0?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's look at the two sides of that corner. Coming in from the left, where z is negative, the function is flat at zero, so the left derivative at zero is zero. Coming in from the right, where z is positive, the function rises like z itself, so the right derivative at zero is one. <<WRITE_STEP:Left derivative at z = 0 is 0|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Right derivative at z = 0 is 1|id=ex-step-1-2>> Because the left derivative, zero, doesn't match the right derivative, one, the slope jumps at the corner and the derivative is technically undefined there. But this is harmless in practice: software implementations of neural network training usually just return one of the one-sided derivatives rather than reporting that the derivative is undefined or raising an error. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Not differentiable at z = 0 (left deriv 0, right deriv 1) — software returns one one-sided value|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:right-slope-label>> Training never actually arrives at a clean local minimum, and it essentially never lands on z exactly equal to zero — a digital computer carries rounding error anyway, so the value was almost certainly some tiny nonzero number that got rounded. When the corner is hit, the software simply returns one of the two one-sided slopes and moves on. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:relu-curve>> So the corner is a mathematical curiosity, not a practical obstacle: we can safely disregard the non-differentiability of these activation functions. <<WRITE_TEXT:non-differentiable points: ignore them|id=text-ignore>>Remember the two takeaways — every hidden unit is an affine map followed by an element-wise g, and ReLU's broken derivative simply does not bite. <<PAUSE:short>>

Universal Approximation Properties and Depth
A linear model, mapping from features to outputs via matrix multiplication, can
by deﬁnition represent only linear functions. It has the advantage of being easy to
train because many loss functions result in convex optimization problems when
applied to linear models. Unfortunately, we often want to learn nonlinear functions.
At ﬁrst glance, we might presume that learning a nonlinear function requires
designing a specialized model family for the kind of nonlinearity we want to learn.
Fortunately, feedforward networks with hidden layers provide a universal approxi-
mation framework. Speciﬁcally, the universal approximation theorem (Hornik
et al.,

amount of error, provided that the network is given enough hidden units. The
derivatives of the feedforward network can also approximate the derivatives of the
function arbitrarily well (

continuous function on a closed and bounded subset of Rn is Borel measurable

activation functions that saturate both for very negative and for very positive
arguments, universal approximation theorems have also been proved for a wider
class of activation functions, which includes the now commonly used rectiﬁed linear
unit (

We may also want to choose a deep model for statistical reasons. Any time

set of prior beliefs we have about what kind of function the algorithm should
learn. Choosing a deep model encodes a very general belief that the function we

topics.our_understanding:
Let's start with a simple kind of model: a linear model. A linear model takes your inputs, multiplies them by some numbers, and adds them up. That's it. The nice thing is it's easy to train, because the math works out cleanly. The problem is that a linear model can only ever represent straight-line, linear relationships. But the real world is full of curves and twists and complicated patterns. We want to learn nonlinear functions.

Now here's the beautiful idea. You might think every new kind of curve needs a custom-built model. But feedforward networks with at least one hidden layer give us something amazing called the universal approximation theorem. In plain words, this theorem says: a neural network with one hidden layer and a squashing activation function, like the logistic sigmoid, can approximate almost any reasonable function you want, to any level of accuracy you want, as long as you give it enough hidden units. Later work extended this to other activations, including the popular rectified linear unit. So no matter what function you're trying to learn, a big enough network can represent it.

But here's the honest catch. Being able to represent a function is not the same as being able to learn it. Training can still fail. The optimization algorithm might never find the right settings, or it might overfit and pick a function that memorizes the training data but doesn't generalize. The theorem also doesn't tell us how big the network needs to be. In the worst case, a single hidden layer might need an exponential number of hidden units. Think about binary inputs: the number of possible binary functions explodes incredibly fast, so distinguishing them all could demand a staggering number of units.

This is where depth comes in. Going deeper, adding more layers, can dramatically cut down how many units you need. There are families of functions that a deep network handles efficiently, but that a shallow network would need an exponentially larger size to match. Researchers showed that deep rectifier networks fold the input space over and over, creating an exponentially large number of linear regions that capture repeating patterns. The number of these regions grows exponentially with depth.

There's also a thoughtful reason to prefer depth. Choosing a deep model encodes a belief that the function we want to learn is built by composing several simpler functions, like a computer program where each step uses the output of the step before. And in practice, across many tasks, deeper networks really do generalize better.

This is exactly where depth earns its keep. <<FOCUS:fold-line>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_4_1:folding_regions>> Picture the input as a single axis. A hidden unit with an absolute-value rectifier picks a fold line, and folds the space across it — so whatever pattern lives on one side gets mirrored onto the other. <<TRACE:fold-line>> <<POINT:fold-line>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:mirrored-pattern>> Watch: the bump on the right reflects across the fold line into an identical copy on the left. One fold turned one pattern into two regions — and stacking another layer folds those, giving four, then eight, doubling with every layer. <<TRACE:mirrored-pattern>> <<PAUSE:short>> The number of linear regions a deep rectifier network carves out grows exponentially in the depth l — that is the formal statement of the folding picture. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\#\text{regions} = O\!\left(\binom{n}{d}^{d(l-1)} n^{d}\right)|id=eq-3|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. 6.4.2
Other Architectural Considerations
So far we have described neural networks as being simple chains of layers, with the
main considerations being the depth of the network and the width of each layer.
In practice, neural networks show considerably more diversity.
Many neural network architectures have been developed for speciﬁc tasks.
Specialized architectures for computer vision called convolutional networks are
described in chapter
. Feedforward networks may also be generalized to the
9
recurrent neural networks for sequence processing, described in chapter

10
have their own architectural considerations.
In general, the layers need not be connected in a chain, even though this is the
most common practice. Many architectures build a main chain but then add extra
architectural features to it, such as skip connections going from layer i to layer
i+ 2 or higher. These skip connections make it easier for the gradient to ﬂow from
output layers to layers nearer the input.

rithms
When we use a feedforward neural network to accept an input x and produce an
output ˆy, information ﬂows forward through the network. The inputs x provide
the initial information that then propagates up to the hidden units at each layer
and ﬁnally produces ˆy . This is called forward propagation. During training,
forward propagation can continue onward until it produces a scalar cost J(θ).
The back-propagation algorithm (
,
), often simply called
Rumelhart et al. 1986a
backprop, allows the information from the cost to then ﬂow backwards through
the network, in order to compute the gradient.
Computing an analytical expression for the gradient is straightforward, but
numerically evaluating such an expression can be computationally expensive. The
back-propagation algorithm does so using a simple and inexpensive procedure.
The term back-propagation is often misunderstood as meaning the whole
learning algorithm for multi-layer neural networks. Actually, back-propagation
refers only to the method for computing the gradient, while another algorithm,
such as stochastic gradient descent, is used to perform learning using this gradient.
Furthermore, back-propagation is often misunderstood as being speciﬁc to multi-
layer neural networks, but in principle it can compute derivatives of any function
(for some functions, the correct response is to report that the derivative of the
function is undeﬁned). Speciﬁcally, we will describe how to compute the gradient
∇xf(x y
, ) for an arbitrary function f , wherex is a set of variables whose derivatives
are desired, and y is an additional set of variables that are inputs to the function
but whose derivatives are not required. In learning algorithms, the gradient we most
often require is the gradient of the cost function with respect to the parameters,
∇θJ(θ). Many machine learning tasks involve computing other derivatives, either
as part of the learning process, or to analyze the learned model.
The back-
propagation algorithm can be applied to these tasks as well, and is not restricted
to computing the gradient of the cost function with respect to the parameters. The
idea of computing derivatives by propagating information through a network is
very general, and can be used to compute values such as the Jacobian of a function
f with multiple outputs. We restrict our description here to the most commonly

topics.our_understanding:
Up to now, we've been picturing a neural network as a simple chain of layers, where the only real choices are how deep to make the network and how wide to make each layer. But in practice, networks are much more varied and creative than that. This section is really a heads-up that there's a whole world of architectural choices beyond the basic chain.

Let me point out a few of these. First, special networks have been designed for special jobs. For computer vision, we use convolutional networks. For sequences, like text or audio over time, we use recurrent networks. Each of these has its own design rules.

Second, layers don't have to be wired up one after another in a straight line. A common trick is to add skip connections, where the output of an earlier layer jumps ahead and connects to a layer two or more steps later. Why bother? Because during training, the gradient has to flow backward from the output toward the input, and skip connections give that gradient an easier path to travel. This helps the network learn.

Third, there's the question of how to connect two layers. In the standard layer, every input unit is connected to every output unit, which is called fully connected. But many specialized networks deliberately use fewer connections, so each input unit only links to a small group of output units. This cuts down the number of parameters and the amount of computation needed. Convolutional networks do exactly this with clever sparse patterns that work beautifully for images.

There's also a deeper lesson here about why depth matters. Experiments transcribing multi-digit street numbers from photographs showed that deeper networks generalize better. And importantly, this wasn't just because deeper networks are bigger. When researchers made networks wider, adding millions of parameters without adding depth, the improvement was nowhere near as strong. Shallow models started overfitting around twenty million parameters, while deep models kept benefiting past sixty million. The takeaway is that choosing a deep model expresses a useful belief: that the function we want to learn is built from many simpler functions stacked together, like recognizing corners from edges, or doing one step after another in sequence. So depth isn't just more power, it's a smarter assumption about how the world's patterns are structured.

Architecture = controlling gradient flow + spending parameters wisely

6.5
algorithm and modern generalizations of the back-propagation algorithm.
As with other machine learning models, to apply gradient-based learning we
must choose a cost function, and we must choose how to represent the output of
the model. We now revisit these design considerations with special emphasis on
the neural networks scenario.
topics.our_understanding:
This little section is really just an opening doorway into one of the most important ideas in all of deep learning: back-propagation. Think of it as the teacher clearing their throat before the big lecture. So let me set the stage for you, the way the book is setting it.

Here's the big picture. When we train a neural network, we want it to get better at its job. To do that, we need to measure how wrong it currently is, and then nudge all the little numbers inside the network, the weights, in a direction that makes it less wrong. That measurement of wrongness is called the cost function. And the way the network reports its answer at the end is called the output representation. These two choices matter a lot, because they shape what the network is even trying to do.

Now, to actually do the nudging, we use something called gradient-based learning. The word gradient is just a fancy way of saying slope, the direction that points downhill on our mountain of error. If we know which way is downhill, we can step that way and reduce the cost. But here's the catch: a neural network can have millions of these weights, all tangled together in layers. How on earth do we figure out the slope with respect to every single one of them efficiently? That is the problem back-propagation solves. It's a clever, organized way of pushing information backward through the network, from the output error back toward every weight, so we learn how each one contributed to the mistake.

Notice the language the book uses: it says this is the back-propagation algorithm and its modern generalizations. That hints there isn't just one rigid recipe, but a family of related techniques for computing these derivatives, all built on the same core idea.

So what this short passage is really telling you is: before we dive into the machinery, remember that two design choices always come first. You must choose a cost function, the way you measure error, and you must choose how to represent the output of the model. Everything that follows, all the careful math of back-propagation, exists to serve those choices in the specific setting of neural networks. Keep that in mind, and the upcoming details will feel like answers to a question you already understand.

topics.standalone_narration_text: A modern network has hundreds of millions of weights, and to take one training step you need the derivative of the loss with respect to every single one of them. Naively that's hundreds of millions of separate calculations — so how does a network train in milliseconds? <<PAUSE:long>> Before we answer that, remember the setup: to apply gradient-based learning we must make two choices first. <<SECTION:Two choices come first|id=sec-setup>>We choose a cost function — how we measure wrongness — and we choose an output representation — what form the model's answer takes. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:cost J = how wrong; backprop serves it|id=text-setup>>Everything that follows — all the careful machinery — exists only to compute slopes of that cost. Back-propagation is the servant of those two choices, not a thing unto itself. <<PAUSE:short>> The cost J is just a loss function comparing the network's output y-hat to the target y — that single scalar is what we differentiate. <<WRITE_EQUATION:J = L(\hat{y}, y)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:node-J>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5:comp_graph_mlp>> Here's the key reframing. Don't think of the network as layers of neurons. Think of it as a single long composition of functions, a computational graph, where the cost J is just the final node. Watch it flow forward. The input x maps to a pre-activation z, then through a nonlinearity to the hidden activation h, then to the output y-hat, and finally to the scalar cost J. <<TRACE:edge-x-z>> <<TRACE:edge-x-z>> <<TRACE:edge-x-z>> <<TRACE:edge-x-z>> <<FOCUS:node-x>> Now the honest question: J depends on a weight buried way back near x. The chain rule says its derivative is a product of local derivatives along the path. If I compute that product separately for every weight, am I doing redundant work? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:node-h>> Look at the path. Every weight near the front shares the same downstream factors — the derivative of J with respect to y-hat, of y-hat with respect to h, of h with respect to z. Compute those shared pieces once, store them, and reuse them. That's the whole trick. <<POINT:node-h>> The derivative of the cost with respect to a buried weight is a product of local derivatives along the path from that weight to the cost — and the front factors are shared by every early weight. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial J}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial \hat{y}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial h} \cdot \frac{\partial h}{\partial z} \cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial w}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:grad-J>> So we run the chain rule from right to left. <<WRITE_KEY:One backward pass computes ALL gradients, cost approx one forward pass|id=key-back>>Start at the cost with the trivial seed: the derivative of J with respect to itself is one. <<PAUSE:short>> We seed the backward pass with the only derivative we know for free: the derivative of the cost with respect to itself is one. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial J}{\partial J} = 1|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<FOCUS:backward-flow>> Then sweep that gradient backward across the graph. At each node we multiply the incoming gradient by the local derivative of that node's operation, and pass it further back. Every node is visited exactly once. <<TRACE:backward-flow>> <<FOCUS:backward-flow>> Because each shared sub-derivative is computed once and reused by everything upstream of it, a single backward pass delivers the gradient for all hundreds of millions of weights, at about the cost of one forward pass. That's the answer to our opening puzzle. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:node-J>> And notice — back-propagation isn't one rigid recipe. It's a family: the same right-to-left chain-rule bookkeeping generalizes to any computational graph, which is exactly why it scales from a tiny example to enormous modern models. <<WRITE_TEXT:choose cost + output -> backprop computes the slope|id=text-tie>>So hold two things together: you choose the cost and the output representation, and back-propagation is the efficient algorithm that turns those choices into a gradient for every weight in one organized sweep. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.orig_book_content:
6.5.1
Computational Graphs
So far we have discussed neural networks with a relatively informal graph language.
To describe the back-propagation algorithm more precisely, it is helpful to have a
more precise
language.
computational graph
Many ways of formalizing computation as graphs are possible.
Here, we use each node in the graph to indicate a variable. The variable may
be a scalar, vector, matrix, tensor, or even a variable of another type.
To formalize our graphs, we also need to introduce the idea of an operation.
An operation is a simple function of one or more variables. Our graph language
is accompanied by a set of allowable operations. Functions more complicated
than the operations in this set may be described by composing many operations
together.
Without loss of generality, we deﬁne an operation to return only a single
output variable. This does not lose generality because the output variable can have
multiple entries, such as a vector. Software implementations of back-propagation
usually support operations with multiple outputs, but we avoid this case in our
description because it introduces many extra details that are not important to
conceptual understanding.
If a variable y is computed by applying an operation to a variable x, then
we draw a directed edge from x to y. We sometimes annotate the output node
with the name of the operation applied, and other times omit this label when the
operation is clear from context.
Examples of computational graphs are shown in ﬁgure
.
6.8
topics.our_understanding:
Let's slow down and build a really useful tool: the computational graph. Up to now, when we've talked about neural networks, we've drawn them in a loose, informal way — circles for neurons, arrows between them, just enough to get the idea across. But when we want to describe back-propagation precisely, that loose picture isn't enough. We need a language that is exact, where every piece of the computation has a clear place. That's what a computational graph gives us.

Here's the core idea. In a computational graph, every node stands for a variable. And when I say variable, I mean it broadly. It could be a single number, what we call a scalar. It could be a vector, which is a list of numbers. It could be a matrix, which is a grid of numbers, or even a tensor, which is a higher-dimensional grid. The point is that a node just holds some value, whatever shape that value happens to take.

Now, nodes by themselves don't do anything. We need a way to connect them, and that's where operations come in. An operation is just a simple function that takes one or more variables and produces a result. Think of addition, or multiplication, or something a bit fancier. Our graph comes with a set of allowed operations, like a basic vocabulary. If we want something more complicated than a single operation can give us, we simply chain many operations together. That chaining is called composition, and it's how complex functions get built from simple parts.

Notice one convention the book chooses: each operation returns just a single output variable. You might wonder, isn't that limiting? Not really. That single output can itself be a vector with many entries, so we lose nothing important. Real software often allows multiple outputs, but for understanding the concept, sticking to one output keeps things clean.

The drawing rule is simple. If a variable y is computed by applying an operation to a variable x, we draw a directed arrow, an edge, pointing from x to y. Sometimes we label that arrow with the name of the operation, and sometimes, when it's obvious, we leave the label off. So the graph reads like a recipe: inputs flow in, operations transform them, and outputs flow out. This precise picture is exactly what we'll need to make back-propagation rigorous.

Node = variable, edge = operation
Complex function = composition of simple operations

A node just holds a value, whatever shape that value takes. <<POINT:node-w>> <<FOCUS:edge-dot>> Nodes by themselves are inert — they just sit there holding values. What gives the graph life is the edges. <<WRITE_TEXT:Node = variable, edge = operation|id=text-2>>An edge is an operation: a simple function of one or more variables. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:node-u>> Watch what happens with a real example — a logistic-regression prediction. topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about the chain rule of calculus, because this is the mathematical heart of how neural networks learn. Here's the core idea. Sometimes a function is built by stacking other functions together. Imagine you take a number x, feed it into a function g to get y, and then feed y into another function f to get z. So z depends on y, and y depends on x. If you want to know how z changes when you nudge x, the chain rule says: take how z changes with respect to y, and multiply it by how y changes with respect to x. In words, the derivative of z with respect to x equals the derivative of z with respect to y, times the derivative of y with respect to x. The middle pieces cancel in a sense, and you get a clean way to chain the effects together.

Now, why does this matter so much? Back-propagation, the algorithm that trains deep networks, is really just the chain rule applied in a clever, efficient order. Every operation in the network passes its sensitivity backward, and you multiply these sensitivities together as you go.

The chain rule doesn't just work with single numbers. When x is a vector and y is a vector, things get richer. To find how z changes with one component of x, you have to add up the contributions through every component of y. Each path matters. We bundle all those partial derivatives into a grid called the Jacobian matrix. So the gradient of z with respect to x is found by multiplying the Jacobian of y with respect to x by the gradient of z with respect to y. That's the key takeaway: back-propagation is performing one of these Jacobian-times-gradient products for each operation in the computational graph.

And here's a comforting fact. We usually don't work with neat vectors in deep learning; we work with tensors, which are just numbers arranged in higher-dimensional grids. But conceptually nothing changes. You could imagine flattening every tensor into a long vector, doing the back-propagation, then reshaping the result back into a tensor. So even with tensors, back-propagation is still just multiplying Jacobians by gradients. The notation gets fancier, with index tuples instead of single index numbers, but the spirit is identical. Once you really understand the chain rule, you understand the engine that lets deep networks learn from their mistakes.

When a deep network gets something wrong, how does a weight buried twenty layers deep know it was even partly to blame? The answer is one of the cleanest ideas in all of calculus, and once you see it, the entire training engine falls into place. <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:edge-xy>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_2:scalar_chain_graph>> Start with the simplest possible chain. You take a number x, push it through a function g to get y, then push y through a function f to get z. <<TRACE:edge-xy>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:edge-yz>> So z lives at the end of a little assembly line. <<SECTION:Scalar chain rule|id=sec-1>>The question we care about is: if I nudge x by a tiny amount, how much does z move at the far end? <<TRACE:edge-yz>> <<FOCUS:backflow-zy>> Here's the trick. The nudge can't teleport from x straight to z. It has to pass through y first. So watch the sensitivity flow backward: z reacts to y at a rate dz/dy, and y reacts to x at a rate dy/dx. <<POINT:backflow-zy>> Multiply those two local rates together and the y in the middle conceptually cancels, leaving exactly how z responds to x. That product IS the chain rule. <<WRITE_KEY:dz/dx = dz/dy times dy/dx|id=key-1>> <<POINT:backflow-yx>> <<PAUSE:short>> The rate at which z changes with x is the rate z changes with y, multiplied by the rate y changes with x. <<WRITE_EQUATION: rac{dz}{dx} =  rac{dz}{dy}\, rac{dy}{dx}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:node-xi>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_2:vector_fanout_graph>> Now the real world isn't made of single numbers. Let x be a vector of m components and y a vector of n components. A single input, x sub i, no longer touches just one y. Watch it fan out. Nudging x sub i ripples into y sub one, y sub two, y sub three, all of them at once. <<TRACE:path-xi-y2>> <<TRACE:path-xi-y2>> <<TRACE:path-xi-y2>> And every one of those then funnels into z. So the total effect on z is the sum of the effect along every single path. Miss a path, and you get the wrong gradient. <<TRACE:node-z-out>> <<TRACE:node-z-out>> <<TRACE:node-z-out>> <<POINT:node-z-out>> To find how z responds to one input component, add up its contributions through every intermediate component. <<WRITE_EQUATION: rac{\partial z}{\partial x_i} = \sum_j  rac{\partial z}{\partial y_j}\, rac{\partial y_j}{\partial x_i}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:jacobian-block>> We bundle all those path derivatives, every partial of every y with respect to every x, into one n-by-m grid. That grid is the Jacobian matrix. <<FOCUS:jacobian-block>> And here is the beautiful part: summing over all those paths is exactly a matrix-vector product. The gradient of z with respect to x is just the Jacobian times the gradient of z with respect to y. <<SECTION:The vector chain rule|id=sec-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> Summing over all the paths is exactly multiplying the Jacobian matrix by the gradient with respect to y. <<WRITE_EQUATION:
abla_x z = \left( rac{\partial y}{\partial x}ight)^{\!	op} 
abla_y z|id=eq-3|boxed>> Pause on that, because it's the whole game. The gradient arriving at a node equals the local Jacobian of the next node times the gradient that node already received. <<WRITE_KEY:grad_x z = (dy/dx) transpose times grad_y z|id=key-2>> <<POINT:jacobian-block>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:node-z-out>> So what does back-propagation actually do? It walks backward through the computational graph and performs exactly one Jacobian-times-gradient product at every single operation. Nothing more. <<PAUSE:short>> And tensors? They change nothing. <<WRITE_TEXT:tensor = flatten, backprop, reshape|id=text-1>>Imagine flattening each tensor into a long vector, running the same Jacobian products, then reshaping back. Recursively Applying the Chain Rule to Obtain Backprop
Using the chain rule, it is straightforward to write down an algebraic expression for
the gradient of a scalar with respect to any node in the computational graph that
produced that scalar. However, actually evaluating that expression in a computer
introduces some extra considerations.
Speciﬁcally, many subexpressions may be repeated several times within the
overall expression for the gradient. Any procedure that computes the gradient

wasted computations, making a naive implementation of the chain rule infeasible.
In other cases, computing the same subexpression twice could be a valid way to

topics.our_understanding:
Let's think about what it really takes to compute a gradient inside a neural network. Once you have a computational graph that produces some final number, like a loss, the chain rule from calculus gives you a clean recipe for the gradient of that number with respect to any node in the graph. Writing down that algebraic expression is the easy part. The tricky part is actually computing it efficiently on a computer.

Here's the key insight. When you expand the full gradient expression using the chain rule, you'll notice that the same little pieces, the same subexpressions, keep showing up over and over again. So now you face a choice. You could store each subexpression once you've computed it, and reuse it whenever you need it again. Or you could throw it away and recompute it from scratch every time it appears. Both are valid, but they trade off in different ways.

If you store the results, you save time because you never redo work, but you use more memory. If you recompute, you save memory but you do extra work. And for complicated graphs, that extra work can blow up dramatically. The number of repeated computations can grow exponentially, which means a naive approach, one that blindly recomputes everything, becomes completely impractical. This is exactly why back-propagation is designed the way it is. It computes things in a careful order and stores intermediate results, so each subexpression is calculated just once and then reused.

Think of it like solving a big homework problem where the same sub-calculation appears in five different places. A smart student does that sub-calculation once, writes the answer in the margin, and copies it wherever it's needed. A careless student redoes the same arithmetic five times. For a small problem the difference is minor, but for a huge problem the careless approach wastes enormous effort.

The section then sets up two ways to describe the algorithm. The first version specifies the gradient computation directly, in the exact order it will be performed, following the recursive use of the chain rule. You can either run those computations directly, or read the description as a symbolic recipe for building the back-propagation graph. The catch is that this first version doesn't really make clear how you'd construct that symbolic graph as an object you can manipulate. So a more general formulation comes later, one that makes the graph construction explicit. The big takeaway here is simple but powerful: the chain rule tells you what to compute, but smart back-propagation is all about computing it without wasteful repetition.

topics.standalone_narration_text: The chain rule already hands you the exact formula for the gradient of your loss with respect to every single parameter. So here is the paradox: why does writing that formula down naively, and just evaluating it, blow up to exponential time? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:node-x>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:deep_learning:deep_feedforward_networks:6_5_3:diamond_graph>> <<SECTION:The diamond graph|id=sec-1>>Let me build the smallest graph that exposes the problem. Here is an input node x at the bottom. From x we compute y, and then from y we compute z, but x also feeds forward again so that the output w depends on both y and z. Watch the two paths leave x and re-converge at the top. <<TRACE:edge-x-y>> <<TRACE:edge-x-y>> <<TRACE:edge-x-y>> <<TRACE:edge-x-y>> <<FOCUS:node-w>> Now I want the gradient of the output w with respect to x. The chain rule says: sum over every path from x to w, multiplying derivatives along each path. There are two paths, so two terms. <<PAUSE:short>> The gradient of the output with respect to x is the sum over both paths from x to w, multiplying the derivatives along each path. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}|id=eq-chain>>Here it is written out. Each term is a product of derivatives along one route from x up to w. <<POINT:node-x>> <<FOCUS:shared-subexpr>> Now here is the trap. Suppose z is itself a function of y. Then the derivative of w with respect to y is not atomic; it must in turn account for the path through z. So the piece dw/dy secretly contains dw/dz inside it. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:edge-z-w>> If you expand everything symbolically and then evaluate, that inner subexpression dw/dz gets written out, and computed, in two separate places. One diamond duplicates it once. Stack diamonds on diamonds, layer after layer, and ask: how many times does the deepest subexpression get recomputed? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:node-w>> It doubles at every layer. With n stacked diamonds you recompute the shared piece on the order of two-to-the-n times. That is the exponential blow-up: the formula is short, but the naive evaluation is astronomically wasteful. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:node-z>> <<SECTION:The fix: compute once, store, reuse|id=sec-2>>The cure is the move every smart student already makes. Do the shared sub-calculation once, write the answer in the margin, and copy it wherever it is needed instead of redoing the arithmetic. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:node-x>> <<WRITE_KEY:Chain rule = WHAT to compute. Backprop = compute each subexpression ONCE, store, reuse.|id=key-1>>That is exactly what back-propagation does. It computes the gradient at each node exactly once, stores it, and feeds it to the parents below. The chain rule tells you what to compute; back-propagation is the discipline of never recomputing a shared subexpression. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> <<WRITE_TEXT:store -> O(graph) time, more memory; recompute -> less memory, more time|id=text-tradeoff>>Notice this is a genuine trade-off, not a free lunch. Storing intermediate gradients costs memory but makes the runtime linear in the size of the graph. Recomputing saves memory but pays in time, and for tangled graphs that time is the exponential cost we just saw. <<FOCUS:node-w>> So the algorithm proceeds backward through the graph in a careful order: visit the output, then each node once, accumulating the gradient flowing into it before passing it down. Same answer the chain rule promised, computed in a single sweep instead of an exponential explosion. <<TRACE:node-w>> <<TRACE:node-w>>
